analytic-derivatives.note: [closed form] These are direct O(1), O(n) or O(np²) formulas: link cdf/pdf, analytic scores and Hessians, Wald/RD/BRS variances, ridit DeLong SE, lgamma sums. Each is at the lower bound of reading its inputs. Some are dead exports (beta_*_cpp, neg_loglik_nb_cpp). The micro-optimizations already noted (distinct-y lgamma caching in NegBinNoZiLikelihood, SYRK/weighted_crossprod reuse) are constant-factor and trivial.

lbfgs.note: [L-BFGS] The generic LBFGSpp driver uses backtracking strong-Wolfe. The Newton alternative for the concave ordinal/CR/AC/beta/logistic fits is already catalogued (catalog §2 TODO-1/2, §1 TODO-7). LBFGSpp releases add a More–Thuente / Nocedal–Wright line search but no performance claim. The literature found (arXiv 1911.04584, 2310.07296) suggests Wolfe/More–Thuente searches use more evaluations than Armijo backtracking, so switching the line search is not a demonstrated win.

log-sum-exp.note: [closed form (log-sum-exp)] The adjacent-category and stereotype log-likelihoods use a max-shifted log-sum-exp in O(n(K+p)). It is overflow-safe and cannot be done in less than linear time. Nothing faster that is also as accurate.

newton-raphson.note: [Newton–Raphson] cpoisson-combined and continuation-ratio are concave canonical-link Newton fits at small p with quadratic convergence. The open items are robustness (halving, LDLT info checks: catalog §1 TODO-2), not speed. No faster method in recent literature.

atkinson-da-biased-coin.note: [Atkinson D_A biased coin via full LU inverse] The two known speedups are already recorded. The Schur/block-inverse null-draw rewrite is Adopt (catalog P6 / TODO-5). For the per-arrival kernel, LDLT plus one solve is listed in catalog P5 with a ~3-5x estimate on the O(p^3) part, which the per-arrival O(tp^2) rebuild dominates. The Eigen dense-decomposition benchmark I fetched (https://libeigen.gitlab.io/eigen/docs-nightly/group__DenseDecompositionBenchmark.html) puts FullPivLU at 1.9x LLT at 8x8, so it adds no new evidence. A search for faster D_A computation found only the carat/covadap implementations, which use the same formula. Sherman–Morrison was already rejected for good reasons (drift, column-set changes). | [Atkinson D_A-optimal biased coin (LU inverse)] Same kernel as above. draw_ws_raw / generate_permutations_atkinson_internal are already Adopt via the Schur complement (O(r·n·p²)), which keeps the coin probabilities equal to roundoff and the RNG stream aligned. The per-arrival assign_wt costs O(tp²+p³) once per arrival and is not a hot path. No algorithm newer or faster than the tracked plan was found.

branch-and-bound-milp.note: The previous HiGHS-backend finding still stands and is re-reported. One update: CRAN highs 1.15.1-2 now exposes the HiGHS C API to other packages' compiled code, so EDI could call HiGHS from C++ without going through ompr/ROI. Two new items not in catalog §12 table (a). (1) A free MIQP/MIQCP solver now exists on CRAN: scip 1.10.1-1 (2026-10-04, Apache-2.0, SCIP 10 is Apache-2.0). It supports binary variables plus scip_add_quadratic_cons. This removes the 'MIQP needs a commercial solver' objection to the low-rank formulation (p continuous z = Mw, one convex quadratic). (2) For p = 1, mahal_dist/D/l1 reduce exactly to balanced number partitioning (Kallus 2018, eq. 2.8). That problem has a dedicated exact anytime algorithm, BLDM + complete Karmarkar-Karp (Mertens 1999). Neither speedup is quantified at EDI sizes. Also checked BiqBin (SDP B&B; serial beats Gurobi/SCIP on most of its benchmark instances, but the catalog already rejects SDP B&B as overkill at n ≤ 30) and Mallach's compact linearization (Glover-type, already in the table).

cholesky-ldlt.note: One-off O(np² + p³) whitening, already optimal. Searched low-rank incremental evaluation: the O(p)-per-swap use of the rank-p factor M is the enumeration/low-rank item already tracked (v1.0.5-TODO-1/-2). Nothing new since 2026-11-16.

dinkelbach.note: New check: the 'Accelerated Dinkelbach' method (arXiv 2510.26257, √5-order) assumes twice-differentiable parametric functions, which does not hold on a 0-1 feasible set, and it reports no combinatorial experiments. The Charnes-Cooper single-MILP alternative has no binary-case computational evidence. At these sizes the gains still come from cheaper subproblems (enumeration v1.0.5-TODO-1, seeding v1.0.5-TODO-13, a better MILP backend).

qr-decomposition.note: Runs once per setup. The only improvement is w'Pw = ||Q̂'w||² with the thin Q̂ kept instead of the dense n×n P, which is already recorded in the inventory (relevant to v1.0.5-TODO-1). Nothing new.

simulated-annealing.note: For p > 1, nothing newer overturns the tracked PT/tabu/polish items: 2025-26 QUBO benchmarks (enhanced PT beats SA and memetic tabu at equal time on Cauchy-coupled instances) are already covered by quantum_upgrade.md TODO-5, and threshold accepting is reported only as comparable to SA. New: for p = 1 the problem is balanced number partitioning (Kallus 2018). BLDM gives an O(n log n) solution, CKK improves it to a certified optimum (anytime), and both are deterministic. This replaces 4×20k-move SA for the p = 1 quadratic/D/l1 kinds at n > 20; see the finding. GKK+ (AISTATS 2026) is a randomized multi-arm design, a design change rather than a solver.

size-based-dispatch.note: Orchestration (trivial). The cutoff should depend on the solver (enumeration, HiGHS/SCIP backend) and, if the p = 1 finding is adopted, on p as well (route p = 1 to BLDM+CKK). There is no algorithmic alternative.

findings.candidate: Special-case p = 1 (one covariate) for the mahal_dist, D (P from [1,x] with fixed n_T) and l1 kinds. Each objective is then a monotone function of |Σ_T x̃ − Σ_C x̃|, i.e. the balanced number partitioning problem (Kallus 2018 eq. 2.8 shows the reduction and its NP-hardness). Use the balanced largest differencing method (BLDM, O(n log n)) as the start and Mertens' complete-Karmarkar-Karp extension (BLDM+CKK) to search to a certified optimum, an anytime algorithm that returns BLDM first. Equal-cardinality |m| ≤ 1 is exactly Mertens' 'balanced' case. Kapelner's own GreedyExperimentalDesign already ships a Karp method for one covariate.
findings.claimed_speedup: Not quantified for EDI. Mertens (arXiv cs/9903011) reports BLDM at O(n log n) time and O(n) space. CKK node counts peak near n_c ≈ 30 for 25-bit integers and fall beyond it. For ≤ 12 significant digits the exact search is 'arbitrary size in practice' (a claim adopted from Korf). With double-precision covariates the hard region extends to larger n, so certification may be exponential near n ≈ 50–60, but BLDM alone should already beat SA's discrepancy. No source compares it with SA or MILP on this problem.
findings.suggested_action: Prototype. Add a p = 1 branch in optimal_solve_auto that calls a C++ BLDM+CKK kernel with a node/time cap. Check against enumeration at n ≤ 24 and against SA at n = 50/100/200 (objective and wall time). Record it as a new row in catalog §12 table (a)/(b).

findings.candidate: Low-rank convex MIQCP solved by open-source SCIP via the CRAN package scip (1.10.1-1, published 2026-10-04, Apache-2.0; SCIP 10.0 is Apache-2.0): minimize θ subject to θ ≥ ||z||², z = Mw (p continuous variables), Σw = n_T, w binary, through scip_add_quadratic_cons. This removes all n²/2 auxiliary variables with no commercial dependency. Also usable through CVXR ≥ 1.8.2.
findings.claimed_speedup: Not quantified. The SCIP 10 report (arXiv 2511.18580) says it is faster than SCIP 9, with larger gains on nonlinear problems, but has no MIQP or balanced-allocation breakdown. The catalog itself predicted that 'MIQP solvers handle this well'.
findings.suggested_action: Re-look. Add 'scip' as an optional backend for the low-rank formulation behind requireNamespace. Benchmark it against GLPK Fortet at n = 15/20/25/30 (p = 5) and against the enumeration prototype. Update catalog §12 table (a), low-rank row, to record that an Apache-2.0 MIQCP solver is available.

findings.candidate: (Re-reported from the 2026-11-16 previous result, updated.) Add HiGHS (MIT) as a backend through ROI.plugin.highs (1.0-4, GPL-2|GPL-3), or the CRAN highs package (1.15.1-2, 2026-11-02, GPL ≥ 2). New in 1.15.1-2: other packages can call the HiGHS C API from compiled code, so EDI's C++ could build the models directly and skip ompr model construction. HiGHS still does not support MIQP (maintainer statement), so this helps only the linearized models.
findings.claimed_speedup: Not quantified. Mittelmann's MILP benchmark (previous run) puts HiGHS in SCIP's tier and does not include GLPK. A JuMP forum anecdote has GLPK about 100× faster than HiGHS on one linearized model and the ranking reversing after reformulation, so results depend on the formulation.
findings.suggested_action: Re-look, as the previous result recommended: benchmark GLPK against HiGHS on milp_solve_quadratic at n = 15/20/25 and on milp_solve_l1 at n = 20–200, then decide on the default and the per-backend linearization_max_n.

bayesian-bootstrap.note: [Bayesian bootstrap (Dirichlet weights)] Weight generation is one vectorized rgamma(B*n, 1) call, O(Bn), and is negligible next to the B weighted refits. Switching to rexp (R's rgamma at shape 1 takes the GD branch per rgamma.c, while rexp uses Ahrens–Dieter 1972) could be marginally cheaper but would change every realized draw, and the saving does not matter. QMC and antithetic Dirichlet weights only cut Monte Carlo variance; they are already the audit row J antithetic note and are not a speedup. No newer source found. The I13 per-draw context rebuild remains an implementation item. | [Bayesian bootstrap refits] The weighted logistic g-computation refit per replicate is warm-started. Fully iterated weighted MLE is required to keep the same estimand, and the one-step or linearized alternatives are estimator changes. Nothing newer than the 2026-11-16 review was found.

lbfgs.note: [L-BFGS] The generic LBFGSpp driver uses backtracking strong-Wolfe. The Newton alternative for the concave ordinal/CR/AC/beta/logistic fits is already catalogued (catalog §2 TODO-1/2, §1 TODO-7). Catalog O12 already covers the betareg recipe: moment φ start, then quasi-Newton, then a Fisher-scoring polish. betareg's newest NEWS entry (3.2-6) only adds analytic score/hessian methods to the BetaR distribution class (https://cran.r-project.org/web/packages/betareg/news/news.html). likelihood-factorization.note: [separate logit + beta regression fits] BB replicate calls the betareg::betareg formula interface per replicate although EDI already has fast_beta_regression_weighted_cpp for the same weighted interior-row MLE (EDI's own benchmark: 0.88 ms vs 24.85 ms for betareg.fit at N=1000). The two binary logits are fit even when the estimand is conditional and they are unused there. The PB simulator draws rbeta(1) in an interpreted per-row loop, which a single vectorized rbeta call over interior rows would replace. The two-logits-vs-multinomial parameterization mismatch is an estimator question (Investigate), not a speedup.

findings.candidate: Call EDI's existing fast_beta_regression_weighted_cpp(X_mid, y_mid, w_mid) (C++ L-BFGS, weights multiply each observation's log-likelihood contribution as betareg case weights do) on the interior rows, keeping betareg/lm.wfit only as fallbacks. Skip the two logits unless the estimand is marginal.
findings.claimed_speedup: Repo benchmark (fetched rawcdn.githack page, model-fit table, N=1,000): InferencePropBetaRegr 0.88 ms (EDI C++ beta regression) vs 24.85 ms betareg.fit, 28.38x. The formula betareg() used here adds model.frame overhead on top, so the per-replicate gain should be at least this order (not measured on this exact path). Skipping the unused logits saves two more IRLS fits per replicate under the conditional estimand (not quantified).

findings.candidate: Vectorize: idx = which(u >= p0 + p1); y_sim[idx] = rbeta(length(idx), pmax(mu[idx]*phi, 1e-4), pmax((1-mu[idx])*phi, 1e-4)). rbeta recycles shape arguments elementwise and draws in index order, so the RNG stream is consumed in the same order as the loop.

analytic-derivatives.note: Closed-form score Xᵀ(y−μ) and Hessian −XᵀWX (logit), plus the probit generalized-residual forms, are O(np²), which is the cost of reading X. No code commits since the 2026-11-16 result.

irls.note: The C++ LDLT IRLS (logit = Newton; probit = Fisher scoring) is still the right algorithm at EDI's small p. fastglm 0.1.4 (CRAN 2026-11-11; NEWS checked) runs the same IRLS + Cholesky with step-halving at the same per-iteration cost. Its 0.1.4 probit/cloglog changes (tail probabilities, capped scoring updates) back the existing Incidental 3 tail fix and the TODO-2 step-halving item, both already catalogued. Erdogdu-style scaled least squares, sketching and one-step bootstrap approximate the MLE, so each is an estimator change and was rejected. The prior finding still stands: inference_proportion_fractional_logit.R:165 still calls glm.fit(quasibinomial) on the estimate_only + harden=FALSE path, while line 257 uses the C++ kernel for the same QMLE. fastglm's benchmark vignette (dated 2026-11-06) still shows glm.fit at 2.75 ms vs Cholesky IRLS at 0.67 ms at n=1,000, p=30.

lbfgs.note: Re-verified in code. The R wrappers fast_logistic_regression and fast_logistic_regression_with_var (helper_glm_fit.R:852, :923) still default to optimization_alg = "lbfgs", while the C++ kernel defaults to "irls". KK21 calls the wrapper per covariate with p=2 (design_seq_one_by_one_KK21.R:431), and KK21 stepwise calls it at :345. The scikit-learn docs recommend newton-cholesky when n_samples >> n_features, which is EDI's regime. LBFGSpp's More–Thuente line search comes with no performance claim, so changing the line search is still not a demonstrated win. The previous finding stands.

lu-decomposition.note: determinant() (LU) on a p×p information matrix in the uncalled Firth evaluator. Cholesky is about 2× cheaper on an O(p³) term with p small, and Stan Discourse reports no practical gain for Jeffreys-penalized logistic. The evaluator has no caller, and the row is already Investigate for a sign issue. Rival Firth implementations (fastglm firth=TRUE, brglm2 1.1.0, logistf 1.26.1) use quasi-Fisher scoring, not an LU log-det objective. That matters only if the evaluator ever gets a caller.

The holdout's stats::hclust(dist(X), 'ward.D2') could use fastcluster, which claims to be a drop-in, faster replacement for hclust, but no speedup is quantified at EDI sizes. This is low priority.

branch-and-bound-milp.note: [MILP branch and bound (McCormick linearization)] solve_optimal_blocks (method='ompr') builds an n²B/2-binary McCormick MILP and solves it with GLPK. Table (c) of the catalog already lists four reformulations that are still open under TODO-5: continuous z with only the ≥ row, representative-ordering symmetry breaking, Grötschel–Wakabayashi clique partitioning, and column generation. This run found three things the catalog does not cover. (1) HiGHS is available on CRAN, GPL-compatible, as a drop-in ROI backend; nobody has considered it. (2) The 'euclidean' and 'mahal' kernels return squared distances (no sqrt in optimal_blocks_distance.cpp). So when n mod B = 0, the objective equals (n/B) × the equal-size minimum sum-of-squares clustering (MSSC) objective. That brings in exact clustering methods: Brusco's repetitive branch-and-bound, and Piccialli & Sudoso's SDP branch-and-cut (2023), which handles equal sizes as a special case. (3) For dist='sum_abs_diff' or a custom dist function, nothing beyond the existing table (c) options turned up.

greedy-blocking.note: [greedy column addition with quantile binning] Runs once per design to build strata keys, O(k·bins·n log n) on small n. Not a hot path, so nothing worth replacing. | [greedy nearest-pair blocking (blockTools optGreedy)] quickblock (GPL>=3, 0.2.2) claims to be 'more than an order of magnitude quicker' but does threshold blocking: it has a minimum block size, a variable block count and no fixed B or block sizes (https://cran.r-project.org/web/packages/quickblock/refman/quickblock.html). That is a different design, not a drop-in. blockTools 0.6.6 (2025-01-22) on CRAN shows no algorithm change. O(n²p) is fine at EDI's n.

General MIPLIB 2017 figures from Mittelmann's benchmark, as reproduced in Table form at https://arxiv.org/html/2312.13527v4: unscaled shifted geometric mean 7317 for GLPK vs 3114 for HiGHS (about 2.3×), with 6 vs 24 instances solved. These are large general MILPs, not this partition model at EDI's tiny n.

findings.label: MILP branch and bound (McCormick linearization)
findings.candidate: For dist ∈ {euclidean, mahal}, the kernels return squared distances, so when n mod B = 0 the objective is (n/B) × equal-size MSSC on X (or on whitened X for mahal). Specialized exact clustering methods then apply. (a) A Brusco-style repetitive branch-and-bound (Psychometrika 2006) written as a small deterministic C++ kernel, with the size bounds ⌊n/B⌋..⌈n/B⌉ added as a pruning rule. It needs no solver dependency. (b) Piccialli & Sudoso's SDP branch-and-cut for cardinality-constrained MSSC (Math. Programming 2023), which treats equal sizes as a special case.
findings.claimed_speedup: Not quantified against GLPK. The Cambridge abstract for Brusco 2006 says it solves 'poorly separated problems with no inherent cluster structure ... for up to 60 objects and six clusters' (well-separated: 240 objects, 8 clusters); unconstrained sizes, no runtimes given. Piccialli & Sudoso, Tables 2–3 of https://arxiv.org/html/2209.08901v3: cardinality-constrained instances solved exactly with n=75, k=4 in 3 s (1 node) up to n=1000, k=4 in 34396 s, with a 12 h limit. The paper does not benchmark against a plain MILP.
findings.suggested_action: Add a row to catalog table (c): 'squared-distance kinds with n mod B = 0 reduce to equal-size MSSC; Brusco RBBA-style B&B with size pruning (C++, no solver)'. Include it as an arm of the TODO-5 benchmark alongside the continuous-z and symmetry-breaking MILP. Do not pursue CC-SOS-SDP, because of its MATLAB/Gurobi dependency.

bca-interval.note: [BCa bootstrap (jackknife acceleration)] The z0, â and quantile steps are O(B log B), so the cost is in the jackknife refits. bcaboot::bcajack (CRAN, GPL-2/3) groups the n rows into m groups (typically 20 or 40) and averages mr = 5 random groupings. That is the catalog's 'grouped jackknife [cite needed]' option, and bcaboot can fill the citation. It costs about m·mr = 100–200 fits, so it only beats delete-one when n_units is above about 200. It changes â (randomly), so the earlier rejection stands. For least-squares statistics, the exact closed-form jackknife (see the delete-one finding) removes the refits without changing â. The influence-function option is already v1.0.5 TODO-7.

double-bootstrap.note: [double bootstrap calibration] Chang & Hall (Biometrika 2015, arXiv 1408.6327) show that single-inner-sample ('fast' or warp-speed) double bootstraps give third-order gains only for bias correction. Those gains are not available for confidence intervals, so cutting the inner bootstrap to one resample is not acceptable for this CI calibration. The prepivoting rewrite already planned (v1.0.5 TODO-2, about 5× fewer refits) is still the best option.

percentile-bootstrap-interval.note: [bootstrap confidence intervals (quantile)] Type-8 quantiles over B ≈ 501 values: R's quantile uses a partial sort, so this is effectively O(B) and microseconds against B refits. Balanced or importance resampling cut Monte Carlo variance, not run time, and are already tracked under audit J. | [bootstrap percentile / studentized intervals] Closed-form quantile and pivot work on a precomputed distribution, O(B log B) at most. Nothing faster exists, and the cost is dominated by the refits that produce θ* and se*. | [bootstrap tail-count p-value] Tail counts are O(B). The only way to save refits is to stop early. Davidson & MacKinnon's pretest (howmany.pdf, Table 1, B_min=99, B_max=12,799) averages B* ≈ 320–490 under the null and ≈ 570–2,400 under alternatives. At EDI's default B=501 that is no saving except under the null, and it gives a decision rather than a fixed-B p-value. The bootstrap distribution is also cached and shared with the CI types. Besag–Clifford/SMC stopping is already tracked (`performance_profiling_and_upgrades.md` TODO-156, catalog TODO-8). | [percentile bootstrap with Wald fallback] Type-8 quantiles plus an O(1) selection rule. The cost is the B refits, which are inherited from the generic bootstrap driver (row J). The Wald-fallback rule is a statistical choice, recorded as incidental. Nothing faster that gives the same interval. | [smoothed bootstrap] Adds N(0, sd(y)/√n) noise per replicate, so cost is B refits. No source gives a refit-free way to apply the kernel noise to a general statistic: kernelboot still evaluates the statistic on every resample, and bag-of-little-bootstraps style schemes are subsampling approximations, so they change the estimator. The cheap bootstrap (Lam) is a different CI, reported under the subsampling finding as an estimator change. The I7 serial/unseeded loop is an implementation issue that is already recorded.

cluster-block-resampling.note: [cluster bootstrap (bucketed group resampling)] O(n + G + output) with one counting pass is optimal. The only possible gain is batched Lemire draws for the G group indices, which is negligible at EDI's G (reported under the i.i.d. Lemire finding). | [pair (cluster) bootstrap] Resampling whole pairs is O(n_R + m) per replicate, which is already optimal. The cost is dominated by per-replicate clone + refit. Balanced bootstrap is already tracked (Keep-tracked J). Faster cluster methods such as the wild cluster bootstrap change the estimator and only apply to OLS-type statistics. | [pair-preserving (block) bootstrap] A precomputed pair table plus Lemire draws gives O(n + B(n_R + m)), which is optimal for generating indices. In the production path, the R sample() callbacks cost little next to the refit. The only open item is the balanced variant, already tracked.

iid-index-resampling.note: [i.i.d. bootstrap resampling (Lemire draws)] Batched ranged random integers (Brackett-Rozinsky & Lemire 2024) produce several bounded integers per word and report 1.5-2.5x on shuffles. This is a micro-level re-look only, because refits and per-call MT seeding dominate the bootstrap. See finding. | [i.i.d. multinomial bootstrap resampling] Index draws are O(n) per replicate. Poisson-weight bootstrap gives random replicate sizes, so it is an estimator change. Count-matrix vectorization (Chaibub Neto 2015) only helps moment statistics, not the refits EDI runs. Balanced bootstrap is already tracked (audit TODO-4 / catalog §7 TODO-1), and no new primary evidence was found. | [i.i.d. draws / rejection sampling without replacement] replace = TRUE (Lemire draws, O(k)) is optimal. For replace = FALSE, dqrng's benchmarks show the std::unordered_set duplicate check is the slowest of the known choices at intermediate-to-high sampling rates. A dense bitset or byte-vector 'seen' marker of length n keeps the accept/reject sequence, and so the output, bit-identical while removing hashing. The catalog's options table does not list this no-stream-change option; a partial Fisher–Yates (v1.0.5-TODO-2) is the stream-changing alternative for k > n/2.

largest-remainder-allocation.note: [largest-remainder (Hamilton) allocation] Closed form: floor, then sort the S strata remainders, O(S log S) once per call. It is negligible next to the draws and refits, so nothing faster matters. | [largest-remainder (Hamilton) rounding] Closed-form apportionment: G divisions plus a sort of G remainders, called once per allocation with G strata. G is small, so the cost is negligible. Any other rounding rule would change the allocation, i.e. an estimator change, not a speedup.

sort-and-sweep.note: [stable sort of index permutation] build_draw (exchangeable_resampling_draws.cpp:187-190) sorts row indices only when preserve_order is set. The only callers are the PRW subsampling paths (inference_ext_prw_subsampling.R:90,402), which run once per subsample beside a full refit. A counting sort keyed on row index (rows ≤ n) would be O(N+n) instead of O(N log N) and would give an identical order. The inventory already records this as immaterial, and nothing found changes that. No web search needed: the textbook alternative is already in the inventory.

stratified-resampling.note: [exchangeable-unit resampling + quantile pivot] Largest-remainder allocation is O(strata) and the draws are O(B·n); B fits dominate. The partial Fisher-Yates improvement for the without-replacement subsample is already catalog §7 TODO-2. No new evidence. | [stratified bootstrap] stratified_bootstrap_indices_cpp is O(n log S): std::map bucketing, Lemire draws, then a portable edi_rng Fisher–Yates (the libstdc++/libc++ std::shuffle issue in incidental #17 has since been replaced in this function). It is negligible next to the refits. Balanced resampling remains the only option, and it is already the audit J prototype (Davison–Hinkley–Schechtman; a secondary source repeats that stratified data need their own balanced variant, as the catalog already notes). | [stratified bootstrap / subsampling] With replace=TRUE it is optimal (Lemire draws). With replace=FALSE, the unordered_set rejection sampler already has a Prototype to replace it with partial Fisher–Yates (catalog TODO-2). The CRAN dqrng vignette adds quantified evidence for a rate-dependent hybrid: a bitset rather than a hash set at moderate rates, and partial Fisher–Yates above 50%. Recorded as a refinement of TODO-2. The end-to-end effect is negligible because the B·fit(b) refits dominate.

findings.label: i.i.d. bootstrap resampling (Lemire draws)
findings.candidate: Batched ranged random integer generation: several unbiased bounded integers from one random word, typically one multiplication and no division per value. Reference code is MIT-licensed (github.com/lemire/batched_random), which is GPL-3 compatible.
findings.claimed_speedup: arXiv 2408.06213v2 experiments: shuffles 1.4-2.5x with fast 64-bit generators (Lehmer/PCG), 2.6-4.7x with ChaCha, on in-cache arrays. Not benchmarked for repeated draws from one fixed range, nor with 32-bit MT19937. Not quantified at EDI sizes.
findings.suggested_action: No action unless RNG/index time is shown to matter in TODO-149 profiling. If it does, prototype a batched bounded_rand for sample_int_replace_internal and resample_group_rows_internal, and fold it into the same stream-change window as catalog §7 TODO-2/TODO-3.

findings.label: stratified bootstrap / subsampling
findings.candidate: Rate-dependent sampling without replacement, as in dqrng: partial Fisher–Yates on a reusable scratch copy when k/n > 0.5, and rejection against a reusable bitset (std::vector<char> or bitset of size n) instead of an unordered_set at moderate rates such as PRW's b=n^0.7 (~20–40% at n=200–1000).
findings.claimed_speedup: From the CRAN dqrng vignette: bitset rejection is about 6.4x faster than R's hashset at a 1% rate (102.62 µs vs 657.81 µs, m=1e6, n=1e4), and partial Fisher–Yates is about 6.2x faster than base R at a 60% rate (10.3 ms vs 63.7 ms). These populations are far larger than EDI's, so the gain at n≈100–1000 is not quantified. End to end it is negligible, because B·fit(b) dominates.
findings.suggested_action: When implementing catalog TODO-2 (partial Fisher–Yates), also use a reusable bitset in place of the unordered_set for k/n ≤ 0.5. Bundle it with TODO-2 rather than tracking it separately.

findings.label: i.i.d. draws / rejection sampling without replacement
findings.candidate: (a) Same rejection loop, but mark seen positions in a dense bitset or std::vector<uint8_t> of length n (scratch reused across b and strata). Same RNG calls in the same order, so the selected units are bit-identical and no seed-pinned test changes. (b) dqrng's rate-based dispatch: a partial Fisher–Yates on a scratch copy of ids above a 50% sampling rate (= v1.0.5-TODO-2; changes the stream), a bitset below.
findings.claimed_speedup: Not quantified for unordered_set vs bitset at EDI's sizes. The dqrng vignette (https://cran.r-project.org/web/packages/dqrng/vignettes/sample.html) reports, against base R sample.int: bitset rejection 102.6 µs vs 1.94 ms, and vs 657.8 µs for base R's hash variant, at m=1e6, n=1e4. Partial Fisher–Yates: 10.3 ms vs 63.7 ms at m=1e6, n=6e5. Those sizes are far above EDI's, so the ratio is indicative only.
findings.suggested_action: When v1.0.5-TODO-2 is picked up, first swap the unordered_set for a reusable dense marker, which keeps the output bit-identical, and microbenchmark it at k/n ∈ {0.25, 0.5, 0.9}, n ≤ 1e4. Adopt partial Fisher–Yates only if it is still materially faster at k > n/2. Add the bitset option to the catalog's P2 options table.

brt-monte-carlo.note: [bootstrap-randomization Monte Carlo (masked sums)] O(n) per replicate (gather + masked sums) is the floor for a fresh bootstrap resample per draw. The only known saving is hoisting the per-unit sharp-null transcendental out of the loop (catalog §7 Incidental #9, bit-identical), which is an implementation fix, not a new algorithm. No published faster BRT algorithm found. | [bootstrap-randomization draw materialization] Each draw re-runs the design on resampled covariates with its own per-draw w_seed. Running draws in parallel keeps results identical, and that is already Adopt under audit TODO-4. No algorithmic shortcut exists: the design must be replayed for each draw to get the BRT null. | [bootstrap-randomization test] B design-aware resamples plus fresh assignments plus B refits is what the test is defined as. The cost is dominated by the refits, which are covered by warm-start and batch-kernel items in rows A and D. Nothing found that keeps the same test and is faster. | [bootstrap-randomization test (C++ batch kernel)] OpenMP over B with per-draw seeds is already in place. Per-replicate algebra cannot be hoisted because X[i_b] changes every replicate (catalog P5). Weibull and robust warm starts are already Prototype items in row A and catalog §1/§5. Fast-and-robust bootstrap (Salibian-Barrera) linearizes the refit, so it changes the estimator and was not proposed. | [studentized bootstrap-randomization test] Costs B fits with an SE, using the C++ mean-diff kernel or a reused worker, with the SE fixed at δ=0. The studentized-permutation literature (Janssen; Chung & Romano 2013; Ritzwoller & Romano review) is about validity, not speed. I found no algorithm that keeps the studentized statistic and needs fewer fits.

kaplan-meier-product-limit.note: [bootstrap Kaplan–Meier (per-draw sort)] The audit's existing Adopt verdict (v1.0.5 TODO-18: presort once with rank0, then an O(n) counting pass per arm, bit-identical) is still the best option found. The new CRAN package FastSurvival 2.0.0 (2026-11-16) gets its claimed ~30x over survfit from presorting and skipping formula overhead in a single C++ pass, which is the same idea as the planned presort, not a new algorithm. Vectorized sorts (vqsort) only change the constant and are tuned for large arrays. Nothing beyond the planned presort.

logrank-sweep.note: [bootstrap log-rank (per-draw sort)] Already Adopt (v1.0.5 TODO-18 log-rank presort + merge). FastSurvival's survdiff_fast uses a two-pointer merge scan over per-arm sorted vectors, which corroborates the planned design but is not a faster one. ExaLT (arXiv 1309.4286) targets the exact permutation p-value, not the bootstrap-randomization (BRT) distribution, so it does not apply.

ridit-scoring.note: [bootstrap (per-draw ridit rebuild)] Each replicate gathers and rebuilds the ridit map in O(n log n). The O(n+L) counting/level-slot rebuild is already tracked as `ridit_kernel_level_slots.md` TODO-3 (v1.4.0 plan). It gives the same answer and is the only faster option; nothing beyond it was found.

sort-and-sweep.note: [bootstrap Mann–Whitney (sort + binary search)] Ordinal JT bootstrap-randomization (BRT) kernel. The known O(n+K) count-by-level variant (or a presort plus stable partition) is already recorded as a small optional win (TODO 9 / perm-stat-kernel table). No new method found. The fast rank-test literature (e.g. arXiv 2010.09712) targets other statistics.

streaming-moments.note: [textbook one-pass sum-of-squares variance] Closed form, O(n), bounded by reading the data. The accuracy fix (shifted one-pass, Chan–Golub–LeVeque) is already Adopt (catalog §7 P7 / TODO-4), and Welford was already rejected as slower in SIMD loops. The kk_bootstrap_reservoir_stats.cpp entries are dead code. Nothing new.

value-space-bisection-selection.note: [bootstrap (per-draw HL selection)] hl_from_groups materializes and runs nth_element up to 4096 pairs, otherwise sorts and does value bisection. The catalog already covers the alternatives: Monahan rank-space selection, Johnson–Mizoguchi/Frederickson–Johnson, the tie-safe early stop (`wilcox_hl_kernel_hoisting.md` TODO-3 and TODO-4) and the presort hoist (blocked by noise), and balanced indices are audit J. No new evidence overturns those decisions. The plain HL bootstrap kernel is dead code.

adaptive-quadrature.note: [adaptive quadrature oracle (QUADPACK)] Runs once per session per ordinal version: 2 clmm fits plus 80 one-dimensional integrate() calls. Its job is to be an oracle independent of GH, so swapping it for a GH rule would defeat the purpose, and the cost is negligible.

analytic-derivatives.note: [closed-form cumulative-link interval probability] Closed form, O(K) per observation per node; nothing faster exists. The upper-tail cancellation fix (survival-function form) and the probit closed-form marginal (catalog §4, TODO-4) are already recorded.

gauss-hermite-quadrature.note: [adaptive Gauss–Hermite quadrature (ordinal::clmm)] weighted_ordinal_random_intercept_fit makes up to 1+5+4 R-level ordinal::clmm(nAGQ=20) fits per Bayesian-bootstrap replicate, for both KKCLMM (inference_ordinal_KK_clmm_abstract.R:256) and KKGLMM (inference_ordinal_KK_combined.R:485). The candidate is a row-weighted variant of EDI's own C++ GH kernel. Its speedup is not quantified, and the weight semantics must be confirmed first. See the finding. | [Gauss–Hermite quadrature GLMM] Covered by the non-adaptive GH finding. Stringer (arXiv 2310.01589 v2, Nov 2024) gives an exact gradient for adaptive quadrature that works with L-BFGS (via LBFGSpp), which removes the obstacle the catalog recorded for v1.0.5 TODO-153. Against EDI's fixed 20 nodes the speed gain is not quantified and probably modest; against Poisson's 60 nodes it is likely larger. Not a drop-in: results change at quadrature tolerance. | [non-adaptive Gauss–Hermite quadrature] See finding: exact-gradient AGQ (Stringer 2024) makes TODO-153 workable with gradient-based optimizers, 2–4× faster than GLMMadaptive/lme4 at m=1000, n=5. The same paper says about 7–17 adaptive points are needed at small cluster sizes, so the expected win over the fixed 20 nodes is small. The bigger win is over the 60-node Poisson kernel, and the gain at large σ is accuracy.

lbfgs.note: [L-BFGS (single start)] Logistic, Poisson, clogit+GLMM and ordinal CLMM outer MLE. Stringer (arXiv 2310.01589) gives an exact gradient for adaptive-quadrature GLMMs with L-BFGS (LBFGSpp, the library EDI uses). That removes the catalog's objection to AGQ, which only adds weight to TODO-153. lme4 2.0-6/2.1-0 NEWS has no optimizer change. See findings.

model-simplification-surrogate.note: [fixed-effects cumulative-link surrogate] The inventory row is stale. At fa2fe36d, compute_weighted_clmm_estimate (inference_ordinal_KK_clmm_abstract.R:256) calls weighted_ordinal_random_intercept_fit, i.e. ordinal::clmm with a random intercept at nAGQ=20, not a fixed-effects surrogate. The KKGLMM weighted path (inference_ordinal_KK_combined.R:485) does the same. The estimand-mismatch Investigate looks resolved; the speed question now lives in the 'adaptive Gauss–Hermite quadrature (ordinal::clmm)' finding. Recommend updating or retiring this inventory row.

multistart.note: [multistart L-BFGS + damped Newton polish] The only real speedup is to replace the central-FD Hessian in the Newton polish (fast_ordinal_glmm.cpp:220-223, still present at fa2fe36d) with an analytic Louis-identity Hessian. That is already catalog §4 TODO-2 (Adopt). The ordinal NEWS at cran.r-project.org shows no optimizer changes in the 2025–2026 releases; clmm still uses nlminb/ucminf, not Newton. No new evidence against multistart (Keep-tracked).

findings.label: L-BFGS (single start)
findings.candidate: Stringer (arXiv 2310.01589v2, Nov 2024): exact gradient of the AGQ approximate log-likelihood for one grouping factor. It handles the mode through implicit differentiation of the stationarity condition and the Cholesky factor through reverse-mode AD. It is optimized with L-BFGS (LBFGSpp) from a GLM start, then one Newton step on a finite-difference-of-exact-gradients Hessian for the Wald SEs. With AGQ, far fewer nodes than 20–60 non-adaptive nodes would be needed.
findings.claimed_speedup: Paper §4–5: usually 2–4× faster than lme4 (BOBYQA) and GLMMadaptive. For the scalar random intercept (m = 1000, n = 5, σ² = 2) it is typically 2–4× faster than lme4. On toenail data (m = 294, n ≤ 7) it is up to 7× faster than lme4 and 2.5–10× faster than GLMMadaptive. These are relative to other packages, not to EDI's non-adaptive-GH L-BFGS, so the gain over EDI is not quantified.
findings.suggested_action: Add Stringer 2024 to the TODO-153 (adaptive GH) plan and catalog §4. It answers the 'exact AGQ gradient is not an envelope identity' objection while keeping L-BFGS (same LBFGSpp library), so the catalog's 1.2–1.6× estimate should be revisited. The gain is node reduction (60 → ~5–11) at the same or better accuracy. Prototype on the Poisson GLMM first, where 60 non-adaptive nodes are now required.

findings.label: adaptive Gauss–Hermite quadrature (ordinal::clmm)
findings.candidate: Add row (or group) weights to the native _glmm_engine.h GLMMObjective and fast_ordinal_glmm objective, and use them for the weighted replicates. For pair-level bootstrap weights that are constant within a group, this is w_g times the group's log-integral and its gradient. The replicate would then use the same estimator family as the point estimate (non-adaptive GH-20, the same links, EDI's cloglog convention without the TODO-31 link-swap probe).
findings.claimed_speedup: Not quantified. The expected gain comes from removing R model-frame and formula overhead and the multistart/refit ladder per replicate, inside a B-loop.
findings.suggested_action: Investigate: time one KKCLMM Bayesian-bootstrap replicate (clmm path) against an unweighted fast_ordinal_clmm_cpp fit at EDI sizes to bound the gain. Confirm clmm's weight semantics. If the gain is large, plan a weighted native kernel with an A/B against the clmm path. Also update the stale inventory row for compute_weighted_clmm_estimate, which is no longer a fixed-effects surrogate.

findings.label: non-adaptive Gauss–Hermite quadrature
findings.candidate: Adaptive GH with an exact gradient of the AQ log-marginal likelihood (Stringer, arXiv 2310.01589 v2, 2024-11-11). It differentiates the mode implicitly (implicit function theorem), reusing the inner Newton's Cholesky factor (one forward and one backward solve, ∂û never formed), plus closed-form third derivatives for the Bernoulli case, and feeds the result to quasi-Newton L-BFGS via LBFGSpp, the same family EDI already uses. The paper covers a single grouping factor, which matches EDI's pair/singleton random intercept.
findings.claimed_speedup: The paper benchmarks against GLMMadaptive (finite-difference gradients) and lme4 (BOBYQA), not against fixed-node GH. Sec. 4.3.2 / Fig. 2: typically 2–4× faster at m=1000 groups, n=5 per group. Toenail data (Fig. 4d): 2.5–10× vs GLMMadaptive and up to 7× vs lme4. Against EDI's fixed 20 nodes the gain is not quantified: the paper finds about 7–17 adaptive points are needed for stable inference at n=3–9 per group (App. C.1, Sec. 5), so the node saving over 20 is small. Over the 60-node Poisson default it is larger, roughly 3–8× fewer nodes, minus the per-group mode solve.
findings.suggested_action: Add Stringer 2024 (arXiv 2310.01589) to v1.0.5 TODO-153 and catalog T1 as the exact-gradient route for AGQ with L-BFGS, replacing the 'needs dû/dθ, lme4 sidesteps with BOBYQA' obstacle. Lower the expected node saving for the 20-node kernels (about 7–17 AGQ points are needed at small clusters), and prioritise the Poisson GLMM (60 fixed nodes) and the K=7 hurdle kernel (accuracy) as the first AGQ targets.

bernoulli-coin-flips.note: [Bernoulli trials (uniform threshold)] One unif_rand per subject from the R-parity MT19937 stream. Faster generators (xoshiro, SFMT, bit-packed coins) all break the R/Python seed stream; the catalog already rejected them (P1, inventory verdict). At prob_T ~ 0.5, geometric-skip sampling gives no gain. Nothing new found. | [cluster-level Bernoulli draws] One uniform per cluster plus an O(n) scatter: about G + n operations per draw, which is the floor for writing an n-length assignment column. Nothing faster exists. | [within-pair sign-flip randomization draws] Drawing is O(n) per draw with one uniform per pair, the floor for R-parity MT draws (catalog P1 already rejected bit-packed or non-MT generators for parity). The only new item is Koning & Hemerik (Biometrika 2024): a deterministic sign-flip subgroup gives an exact test that reaches the same power with about half the transformations. That changes the reference set and the p-value, so it is an estimator/reformulation change, not a speedup. Reported as such, low confidence. | [independent fair coin per pair] One MSB test per 32-bit word per pair, with per-draw-index seeding (deterministic for any thread count): O(n/2) words per draw, close to minimal without bit-packing, which would change the stream. Seeding a fresh MT19937 per column (~1.3k LCG/state steps) is comparable in cost to the draws when n is small. That is the RNG-throughput question already tracked as performance_profiling_and_upgrades.md TODO-149(c), not a coin algorithm choice. | [pair flips + Bernoulli reservoir] O(n·r) with one uniform per pair/reservoir subject, which is the minimum for general prob_T. Bit-packing coins only works for dyadic prob_T and changes the stream. The real lever is parallel per-index streams for the serial generate_permutations_matching_internal loop, already covered by TODO-149(c) and the catalog's child-stream verdict. | [per-column seeded coin flips (SplitMix64 + MT)] It uses one MT word per pair (the MSB). Taking 32 coins from each word would be about 32x fewer words but changes the stream. At n·r ≈ 1e5 words (n in the hundreds, r ≈ 501) generation takes well under a millisecond and is already OpenMP-parallel with index-derived seeds, so the win is immaterial at EDI sizes.

fisher-yates-shuffle.note: [batched complete randomization within blocks] block_ra_batch is already linear: R's order() defaults to radix for numeric vectors, so it is O(N·r) per block, not O(N·r log). What is left is a constant factor: N·r double uniforms, a two-key radix pass and several N·r temporaries. A C++ per-column partial Fisher–Yates over the existing RRng/bounded_rand would remove these with the same per-block law, but it changes the realized draws. The gain is not quantified at EDI's sizes. Low-priority re-look under v1.0.5-TODO-11. | [Fisher–Yates shuffle] The explicit Durstenfeld shuffle with Lemire bounded_rand is the standard method. The one newer result is batched ranged integer generation (Brackett-Rozinsky & Lemire, SP&E 2024), which reports 1.4–2.6× on shuffles with 64-bit PCG/Lehmer generators. It stays unbiased and deterministic but changes the seed-pinned stream again, and it is untested with 32-bit MT19937. The shuffle is not dominant in its callers: rerandomization spends O(np) per draw on the objective. Low confidence. | [Fisher–Yates shuffle / Bernoulli draws] iBCRD uses a full Fisher–Yates of the template; a partial shuffle was already judged marginal, and the batched-draw idea is covered under 'Fisher–Yates shuffle'. Bernoulli uses one uniform per subject; bit-packing was rejected in the catalog (breaks the stream for no material gain) and I found no new evidence against that. The factorial design's R sample() loop is O(nr) and not hot.

findings.label: within-pair sign-flip randomization draws
findings.candidate: Koning & Hemerik (Biometrika 111(2):441–458, 2024): replace the random sample of sign-flips with a deterministic, well-designed subgroup of the sign-flip group. The test stays exact because invariance under the group implies invariance under any subgroup, and it is fully replicable.
findings.claimed_speedup: arXiv v1 abstract (https://arxiv.org/abs/2202.00967v1): in simulations the subgroup test matches the power of a random-sample test with 'about half the number of transformations'. The paper gives no runtimes, and the result is not shown at EDI's pair counts.
findings.suggested_action: Note as an opt-in alternative next to catalog §7 TODO-6 (exact enumeration for small m). It could fill the gap for moderate m, where 2^m is too large to enumerate but refit-per-draw tests make r expensive. Do not change the default.

findings.label: Fisher–Yates shuffle
findings.candidate: Batched ranged random integer generation (Brackett-Rozinsky & Lemire, Software: Practice and Experience 55(1), 2024). Several unbiased bounded indices come from one random word, with one multiply and no division in the common case. With 32-bit words, two indices per word work while i·(i−1) < 2^32 (i ≲ 65k), which covers EDI's n.
findings.claimed_speedup: The paper reports shuffle_6 vs the unbatched shuffle across a range of array lengths: 1.4–1.8× (Lehmer) and 1.8–2.5× (PCG64) on Xeon, 1.5–2.3× / 1.9–2.6× on Apple M2. Only 64-bit generators were tested; it is not measured with MT19937 or 32-bit words, and the sizes in the 100–10,000 range are not reported separately.
findings.suggested_action: Record it as an option in the catalog P2 table. Consider it only if a profile shows shuffle or RNG words are a material share of rerandomization or null-draw time; bundle it with any other planned stream change (for example TODO-149(c) RNG throughput) so seeds are refreshed only once.

findings.candidate: A small C++ kernel: per draw column, a partial Fisher–Yates of k = min(n_T, N−n_T) positions per block with the existing edi_rng::bounded_rand, keeping the block_ra law (random rounding of N·prob_T, singleton Bernoulli). Seed per draw index for thread-count determinism.
findings.claimed_speedup: Not quantified at EDI's sizes. The R docs confirm the current order() is already linear (radix), so the gain is a constant factor only. For context, the dqrng vignette shows a partial Fisher–Yates at 10.3 ms vs base R sample's 63.7 ms (m=1e6, n=6e5).
findings.suggested_action: Update the inventory complexity to note the current path is linear (radix order). Profile block_ra_batch at typical sizes (N·r ≈ 1e5–1e6) and close v1.0.5-TODO-11 as Keep unless it is a measurable share of a design's draw time.

clogit-logistic-reduction.note: [clogit-as-logistic reduction] This is the exact identity: 1:1 conditional logit equals no-intercept logistic regression on within-pair differences of discordant pairs. Building the design is O(n_d p), which is optimal. A search found no newer fast 1:1 clogit method; recent work (e.g. clogitLasso) targets penalized or large-p cases. | [clogit-as-logistic reduction + Newton–Raphson (IRLS)] After the exact reduction the problem is a strictly concave logistic MLE with p in the tens. Newton/IRLS converges quadratically at O(np²) per iteration, which is the row-A Keep rationale. GLR recursion and enumeration both collapse to the same 2-term sum when m=2. | [conditional logit (discordant-pair logistic)] For 1:1 strata the exact conditional likelihood reduces to a no-intercept logistic fit on within-pair differences, at O(n_d p²) per Newton step. That is already minimal and exact. A 2026 search found only estimator changes (the bclogit empirical-Bayes prior, arXiv 2602.08212) and penalized coordinate descent (clogitL1). Neither is a same-estimator speedup.

closed-form.note: [closed form (pair-difference logistic)] For 1:1 discordant pairs, the exact conditional likelihood reduces to no-intercept logistic regression on within-pair differences. Each evaluation is O(n_d p), the minimum. Gail–Lubin–Rubinstein and enumeration both reduce to this same 2-term sum.

newton-raphson.note: [Newton–Raphson] cpoisson-combined and continuation-ratio are concave canonical-link Newton fits at small p with quadratic convergence. The open items are robustness (halving, LDLT info checks: catalog §1 TODO-2), not speed. No faster method in recent literature.

active-set-projection.note: [active-set projection (Fisher metric)] Reuses the iteration's LDLT, and the extra cost O(|A|p²+|A|³) is negligible next to the O(np²) IRLS step. A conic or QP solver would replace the whole scheme rather than speed up this step (see the IRLS finding).

cholesky-ldlt.note: [LDLT solve (QR fallback)] compute_diagonal_inverse_entry factors the information matrix once with LDLT and does one solve. Eigen's benchmark (libeigen.gitlab.io DenseDecompositionBenchmark) puts LDLT at 1.3x LLT at 8x8, so the only cheaper option is LLT, which is less robust on near-singular information. That is a micro-choice already tracked as v1.1.0-TODO-155, and the O(p^3) cost is dwarfed by the O(np^2) build of X'WX.

finite-differences.note: [central finite differences] Where these are costly (log/identity-binomial score and Hessian, using a 4-point ℓ stencil at O(2np³)), the closed-form X'diag(∂²ℓ)X is already Adopt (v1.0.5 row N, catalog O5), and nothing beats it. The generic numerical_gradient/numerical_hessian take central differences of the analytic gradient, so a Hessian costs only 2p gradient evaluations at p≤~25. AD and complex-step would not be cheaper (the catalog already rejected both). The R Cox FD helpers are dead code, and ordinal g-comp compute_md_gradient calls a cheap O(nK) functional; its cost is negligible.

irls.note: [IRLS with step-halving (constrained)] Log-/identity-binomial MLE. Schwendinger, Grün & Hornik 2021 (Comput Stat) benchmark conic (exponential-cone interior-point, ECOS) fits against glm/glm2 IRLS, logbin EM, constrOptim, ipopt and auglag. Conic was the reliable choice, and glm/glm2 were quick but often suboptimal at the boundary. Catalog O4 does not list conic programming. The gain is reliability at the boundary, not raw speed at p≈10; see the finding. | [Fisher scoring (IRLS) with step-halving] For the constrained log/identity-binomial MLE, a conic (exponential-cone) interior-point formulation was rated the preferred solver by Schwendinger, Grün & Hornik (Comput Stat 2021). It is not in the catalog's O4 options table. This is a re-look item for the v1.0.5 TODO-32 Prototype, not a proven win: the source gives no numbers I could read at EDI's sizes. BSW (CRAN, 2025-10-06) is an SQP/quadprog Newton variant, already covered by the catalog's 'active-set / projected Newton QP' option. It is pure R with no benchmarks, and its default constraint set (2^(m-1) range corners) changes the estimator, so it is not a separate finding. logbin 2.0.6 (2025-04) adds no new algorithm (EM/CEM, already rejected as slower).

kkt-boundary-analysis.note: [KKT conditions check] A small multiplier solve per check that reuses the LDLT. Nothing cheaper certifies a boundary MLE. An interior-point conic solver would return certified dual multipliers directly (see the IRLS finding). | [Karush-Kuhn-Tucker boundary score and information reduction] O(|C|p³) with tiny |C| and p, run once per test, so cost is not an issue. Side note, not speed: the loop drops every negative multiplier at once rather than following Lawson–Hanson NNLS. That can pick a different active set when constraints are degenerate. Worth a correctness look; not reported as a speed finding.

findings.label: IRLS with step-halving (constrained)
findings.candidate: Formulate the log-binomial MLE (concave log-likelihood, linear constraints Xβ≤0) as an exponential-cone program and solve it with a primal-dual interior-point conic solver (ECOS, GPL-3; Clarabel, Apache-2.0). This needs no feasible start, because the slack-variable formulation removes that requirement. The identity link is also a convex program, using log terms in exponential cones.
findings.claimed_speedup: Not a raw speedup at EDI sizes. Schwendinger, Grün & Hornik 2021 (Comput Stat, §4.6.2; n=500, 1000 reps; 10 and 100 covariates): only ecos, ipopt and auglag (with tuned settings) returned the optimum in every case, and their timings were 'rather similar' at 10 covariates. At 100 covariates ecos was 'among the quickest' and clearly beat ipopt/auglag. glm/glm2 were also among the quickest but 'tend to return suboptimal solutions' at the boundary. The paper gives no ratio versus IRLS at p≈10, and reads it only from a figure (not quantified in text).
findings.suggested_action: Add 'exponential-cone interior point (ECOS/Clarabel)' as an option row in catalog O4 and include it among the candidates for the row Z constrained-solver Prototype (TODO-32), A/B tested on boundary-MLE fixtures for converged rate and wall-clock at EDI's n and p. Do not adopt it without that measurement.

findings.label: Fisher scoring (IRLS) with step-halving
findings.candidate: Write the log-binomial (and identity-binomial) MLE as an exponential-cone program: the log-likelihood is a sum of log(μ) and log(1−μ) terms with linear constraints on Xβ. Solve it with a primal-dual interior-point conic solver; ECOS (GPL-3), Clarabel (Apache-2.0) and SCS (MIT) are all GPL-3 compatible. Such a solver needs no feasible start, handles boundary MLEs natively and returns KKT multipliers as duals.
findings.claimed_speedup: Not quantified in what I could fetch. The 2021 abstract (Schwendinger, Grün & Hornik, Comput Stat 36(3):1721–1754) names conic optimizers the preferred choice for reliability, no tuning and speed, but the runtime tables are behind a paywall. A 2024 talk on the same group's follow-up says conic solvers were more accurate and that the ROI interface added runtime overhead.
findings.suggested_action: Add 'exponential-cone interior point (ECOS/Clarabel)' to the catalog §1 O4 options table. In the v1.0.5 TODO-32 log-binomial constrained-solver Prototype, benchmark it as a fallback for the boundary or infeasible-start fits that IRLS fails to certify, at EDI's n and p. Get the paper's runtime tables before deciding.

analytic-derivatives.note: [information-matrix standard error] SE = sqrt([I⁻¹]_jj) from the already-computed information matrix, O(p³) with small p. It is cached through shared(). Nothing faster preserves the same estimator.

cholesky-ldlt.note: [LDLT inverse] Ordinal vcov at d≈3–15. Eigen rates LLT and LDLT both 'very fast' and LLT's blocking only helps large matrices (https://libeigen.gitlab.io/eigen/docs-nightly/group__TopicLinearAlgebraDecompositions.html), so there is no faster decomposition at this d. The only saving is implementation-level and already recorded as incidental: the Hessian is built twice, and one LDLT could serve both the diagonal entry and the full inverse. | [LDLT solve (QR fallback)] compute_diagonal_inverse_entry factors the information matrix once with LDLT and does one solve. Eigen's benchmark (libeigen.gitlab.io DenseDecompositionBenchmark) puts LDLT at 1.3x LLT at 8x8, so the only cheaper option is LLT, which is less robust on near-singular information. That is a micro-choice already tracked as v1.1.0-TODO-155, and the O(p^3) cost is dwarfed by the O(np^2) build of X'WX. | [LDLT inverse with eigen fallback] O(p³) at p ≲ 20, called once per fit. Eigen rates LDLT 'very fast'; plain LLT would save a constant factor at most and would change which inputs reach the pseudo-inverse fallback. Not worth it. | [LDLT solve against unit vector] One factorization plus a single-RHS solve is already the cheap way to get one diagonal entry of M⁻¹. The alternatives (selected inversion, LLT) save only constants at small p and change the fallback behaviour on indefinite inputs.

eigen-pseudo-inverse.note: [symmetric pseudo-inverse] Called once per fit post-fit on a d×d free information (d small); rank-awareness on possibly indefinite matrices needs an eigen/SVD-type decomposition. Eigen's benchmark (8x8: LDLT 1.3x LLT, COD 4.3x, SVD ~19x) shows the cheaper rank-revealing options give negligible absolute savings here and LDLT would lose rank-awareness. | [eigendecomposition pseudo-inverse] This is only a fallback in covariance_from_information after LDLT fails, and it is O(p³) with small p. SelfAdjointEigenSolver is the right rank-revealing tool for a symmetric matrix. COD/SVD pseudo-inverses use a different threshold semantics (they would change the answer on rank-deficient input) and are no faster for symmetric input. Not a hot path.

lu-decomposition.note: [LU inverse (FullPivLU)] invert_free_information does two factorizations: a FullPivLU check, then .inverse() (a partial-pivot LU). A single factorization (lu.inverse(), or LDLT/LLT on the SPD information) is cheaper. This is a constant-factor gain at p in the tens, already tracked as v1.1.0-TODO-155; the finding adds a published small-size benchmark. | [full-pivot LU inverse] No new option. Eigen's benchmark (fetched) quantifies the already-known gap: FullPivLU is 1.9x LLT at 8x8 and 10.6x at 100x100, while PartialPivLU is 1.5x and LDLT 1.3x. That supports the existing Keep-tracked item (performance_profiling_and_upgrades.md TODO-155: a single LDLT or reusing lu.inverse()). It is deliberately kept for bit-compatibility, and at EDI's p (≲ 20) the absolute cost is microseconds per fit, so this is not a new finding.

qr-decomposition.note: [QR rank check + inverse diagonal entry] O(p³) at p in the tens, post-fit only. Factorizing twice (QR rank check, then LDLT single-RHS solve) is a constant-factor issue already tracked as TODO-155. No algorithmic alternative is faster; one rank-revealing factorization reused for the solve is the known fix. | [pivoted QR inverse (chol2inv)] Closed form: chol2inv on an R factor that already exists, O(p³) with p in the tens. Nothing faster.

findings.label: LU inverse (FullPivLU)
findings.candidate: One factorization. Either reuse the FullPivLU (lu.inverse()), or, for an SPD information matrix, LDLT/LLT with a pivot-based check of definiteness/condition followed by solve(Identity).
findings.claimed_speedup: Eigen's dense decomposition benchmark (float, 8x8; the page says to roughly double the times for double): LLT 0.05, LDLT 0.07 (1.3x), PartialPivLU 0.08 (1.5x), FullPivLU 0.10 (1.9x). The current FullPivLU + PartialPivLU pair is therefore about 2.6x one LDLT on the factorization part at 8x8, before counting the inverse back-substitution. Not quantified at the whole-fit level, where the O(np^2) Hessian build dominates.
findings.suggested_action: No new work item. Attach this small-size benchmark to v1.1.0-TODO-155 (performance_profiling_and_upgrades.md) and, as the minimal fix, switch invert_free_information to lu.inverse() so it factors once. Consider LDLT only with an A/B on the existing vcov fixtures.

linear-scan.note: Trivial: a single O(n) pass. The O(n·S) which() loop has an O(n) split() alternative, already recorded as Incidental. The result is cached, and it is not on a hot path.

Moment-assisted subsampling (arXiv 2501.06924) and Bayesian Gibbs samplers (2604.06034, 2506.04675) are estimator changes, and exact Poisson-binomial ties (2502.18715) is an estimator change with no speed claim. Cyclops 3.7.1 (cyclic coordinate descent / MM) and coxstream 0.1.0 (memory only) target different regimes, and survival 3.8-12 NEWS has no fitting change. It already handles weights, Efron ties, strata and start times via reverse cumsums, so the kernel would not have to be derived and validated from scratch.

sandwich-estimator.note: Lin-Wei score residuals by prefix sums plus binary search, O(n log K + np + Cp²), is already the optimal form. sandwich 3.1-3 (2026-08-03), the SAS PHREG docs and rms robcov offer no faster algorithm. The I-6 forward-subtraction precision note is a robustness issue that is already catalogued. Recomputing the candidate ladder is a caching incidental, already recorded.

findings.candidate: Sort once by (stratum, time, dead desc), then take within-stratum reverse cumsums of exp(eta - max eta). This gives one risk sum per failure time (Breslow) for both the NLL and the cumulative hazard. The NLL is already implemented in C++ as compute_cox_neg_ll_only.
findings.claimed_speedup: Not quantified by any source. The complexity drops from O(n²) or O(nK) to O(n log n), or O(n) once sorted.
findings.suggested_action: Carried over from the previous run unchanged; the code is unchanged. Implement the Adopt verdict for .breslow_hazard (v1.0.5 audit TODO-7). Route kk_cox_fully_fixed_null_fit to the C++ reverse-cumsum NLL and verify it agrees to 1e-10.

findings.candidate: Build the rungs lazily, yielding the next rung only after the previous fit is rejected. The order is the same and the same design is accepted, so the result is bit-identical.
findings.claimed_speedup: Not quantified. It saves up to about 12 × O(np²) per call, multiplied by the number of randomization or bootstrap replicates.

The 4 extra refits per fit, including every estimate_only resampling draw, therefore cannot find a different optimum; they only repair non-convergence. A convergence certificate or Newton polish is cheaper and gives the same estimator (see finding). Stereotype (.stereotype_full_data_multistart / _candidates): the likelihood is genuinely nonconcave and no faster method with the same answer was found. The early-termination and global-optimality-test literature (arXiv 1906.00101) needs a generalized location family, which the stereotype model is not, and it is heuristic. The alternating algorithm was already rejected in the catalog. Keep.

newton-raphson.note: [Newton–Raphson / Fisher scoring] Cumulative-link and adjacent-category C++ Newton/Fisher kernels. ordinal (the reference CLM package, NEWS through 2026-07-26) still uses modified Newton–Raphson with no optimizer change since 2013. No newer algorithm found that beats Newton at n in the low thousands and K·p in the tens. | [Newton–Raphson with step-halving] PPO ladder rung ordinal::clm(nominal=): the modified Newton with step-halving is the reference algorithm (ordinal NEWS: unchanged since the 2013 clm.fit.NR redesign). The ladder runs only when nonparallel terms exist. Rungs after the first run only on failure, so speed depends on the first rung's success rate, not on the algorithm.

reparameterization.note: [covariate centering and scaling reparameterization] One O(np) pass for column means and SDs plus a linear parameter map M applied once. This is already below the cost of the ordinal fit it conditions, and nothing asymptotically or practically faster exists.

solver-fallback-ladder.note: [fallback ladder of PPO fitters] ordinal NEWS since 2023 (https://cran.r-project.org/web/packages/ordinal/NEWS) has no clm algorithm or nominal-effect changes. VGAM 1.1-14 (https://cran.r-project.org/web/packages/VGAM/NEWS) adds an optional 'bhhh' outer-product Hessian to vglm.control, an alternative information approximation with no claimed speedup. The ladder is a robustness device against improper PPO likelihoods, so Keep stands.

findings.label: Fisher scoring (VGAM IRLS)
findings.candidate: fastglm::fastglm_ordinal(nonparallel = ~terms) (fastglm ≥ 0.1.3, CRAN 0.1.4 dated 2026-11-11). It is a compiled C++ ML fit of the same partial-proportional-odds cumulative-link model (logit/probit/cloglog): observed-information Newton steps with step halving (max.halves), convergence certified by expected information, and robust or clustered vcov in C++. It could serve as the first rung, or as a faster first attempt before vglm.
findings.claimed_speedup: Not quantified. The ordinal vignette and NEWS give no timings against vglm, clm or polr. For context only, fastglm's benchmark vignette shows its C++ GLM fits about 2–4× faster than glm.fit at n=1,000, p=30 (logistic 0.67–1.26 ms vs 2.75 ms); that is a different model.
findings.suggested_action: Re-look: on EDI's PPO fixtures (n tens to low thousands, K 3–7), A/B fastglm_ordinal(nonparallel=) against VGAM::vglm for coefficient and SE agreement, convergence on the improper-fit cases, and wall-clock time. If it agrees on all regular cases, consider it as a faster first rung, with vglm kept as the fallback.

findings.label: deterministic multistart
findings.candidate: For the cumulative cloglog model, F(z) = 1 − exp(−exp(z)) has a log-concave density, so the log-likelihood is concave in the raw (α, β) parametrisation EDI uses (Pratt 1981, as cited in Kosmidis arXiv 1204.0105; that paper covers the G = 1 − exp(−exp(η)) case explicitly). When the MLE exists it is unique, and a restart that finds a strictly lower NLL means the primary solve stopped early, not that it found a different local optimum. Two cheaper checks fit this: (a) a convergence certificate on the primary fit, either the Newton decrement already in ordinal_scale_guard.h or a maximum-absolute-gradient plus positive-definite-Hessian test like ordinal::clm's maxGradient/cond.H, running the restarts only when it fails; or (b) a damped Newton polish from the primary solution, which is what clm does with step halving and gradTol 1e-6.
findings.claimed_speedup: Not quantified by any source. Based on the code structure, it avoids up to 4 extra fits per call when the primary fit passes the certificate, so up to about 5× fewer fits per estimate_only resampling draw. This is a theoretical figure, not a measurement.
findings.suggested_action: Re-examine the cloglog multistart. Gate the 4 restarts on a failed convergence certificate (gradient norm or Newton decrement with a PD Hessian), or replace them with a Newton polish. Before changing the default, A/B the result against the current multistart on the cases in ordinal_cumulative_link_null_refit_multistart.md. Apply the same reasoning to the cloglog fit_null 2-start, which is already marked Investigate.

linear-scan.note: [linear scan with early exit] which_cols_vary_cpp is an O(np) worst-case compare against row 0 that exits early, which is the lower bound for this problem. It also has no R caller outside RcppExports.

pairwise-correlation-filter.note: [iterated pairwise-correlation filter] Round 1 removes the second member of every flagged pair, and Pearson r for a pair depends only on those two columns. So round 2 can never flag anything: the second O(np²) cor() call is always redundant. Breaking after one round gives a bitwise-identical result.

qr-decomposition.note: [pivoted QR rank reduction] Eigen ColPivHouseholderQR is effectively tied with CompleteOrthogonalDecomposition at small sizes (Eigen dense-solver benchmark: 0.23 ms each at 8x8), and SVD is slower. The known O(n p³)→O(n p²) single-factorization rewrite of qr_reduce_preserve_cols_cpp is already catalogued (TODO-6), and the keep-set is cached, so this is not hot. No new evidence. | [pivoted QR rank detection + column dropping] R qr() uses LINPACK dqrdc2. LAPACK dgeqp3 is faster but does not report rank (R qr docs and R-devel threads), so it would break rank detection. The greedy refit-per-dropped-column loop only runs on rank-deficient designs (rare). Nothing faster that keeps the same keep-set. | [column-pivoted Householder QR] Eigen's benchmark (fetched) shows HouseholderQR ≈ ColPivHouseholderQR ≈ COD at 8x8 and 10000x8, and ColPivQR ~5x slower than LLT-on-normal-equations. The faster options (unpivoted QR, Cholesky) are not rank-revealing, or they square the condition number. Randomized CPQR (BQRRP) only pays at large sizes and changes the pivots. Keep for matrix_rank_cpp, qr_reduce_full_rank_cpp and robust_ols_solve. | [greedy column selection via repeated QR] LAPACK dgeqp3 supports 'leading' (fixed) columns through JPVT, so a single column-pivoted QR can force the required columns first and pivot the rest. QR column-append updating (Hammarling–Lucas) is the other route. Both turn O(n p³) into O(n p²) but can change the keep-set on near-collinear designs; this is the existing Prototype-lite TODO-6, now with a concrete library primitive. | [pivoted QR rank detection] drop_linearly_dependent_cols runs the second R LINPACK qr only when the matrix is rank-deficient, so the common full-rank path costs one factorization. On the Eigen benchmark page, ColPivHouseholderQR is about 4.3x LLT at 8x8 and the same speed as CompleteOrthogonalDecomposition and FullPivHouseholderQR, so no faster rank-revealing Eigen decomposition exists. A pivoted Cholesky of X'X would be faster but squares the condition number, which fails the accuracy criterion. The 'one pivoted QR would do' cleanup and the tolerance mismatch are already recorded in catalog §1. I could not confirm that Eigen 5.0 added blocking to ColPivHouseholderQR, and it would not matter at EDI's p.
labels: pivoted QR rank detection + column dropping
greedy column selection via repeated QR

streaming-moments.note: [two-pass mean/variance] scale_columns_cpp computes a column mean and SD in O(np), which is memory-bound. A one-pass Σx² form saves one read but loses accuracy through cancellation. Welford is slower per element and, per arXiv 2410.21922 (fetched in search results), less accurate than two-pass at large offsets. The function also has no R caller. Nothing faster that is also acceptable.

findings.label: iterated pairwise-correlation filter
findings.candidate: Compute cor once, drop unique(pairs[,2]) and return; delete the repeat loop. Pearson r_xy depends only on columns x and y, so removing columns leaves every remaining entry unchanged. Every flagged pair already lost its second member in round 1, so round 2 always finds zero pairs and breaks. NA correlations are dropped by which() in both rounds alike.
findings.claimed_speedup: Not quantified by any source. By the argument above, it removes exactly one of the two cor() calls, about 2× on this function. It matters because cox_design_candidates calls it 12× per call, per replicate (catalog §10 incidental note).
findings.suggested_action: Remove the repeat loop, leaving a single cor pass, and add a test asserting the keep-set is unchanged on the existing corpus. Treat the incidental #8 over-drop fix as a separate estimator-change item.

findings.label: greedy column selection via repeated QR
findings.candidate: Use a single column-pivoted QR with the required columns forced to the front. LAPACK DGEQP3 does this natively: JPVT(j) ≠ 0 marks column j as a 'leading' column, which is factored first, and the free columns are then norm-pivoted. Alternatively, append columns to an existing QR by updating it (Hammarling & Lucas, MIMS EPrint 2008.111) instead of refactoring.
findings.claimed_speedup: Hammarling–Lucas say updating is 'much faster' than refactoring but give no number on the abstract page. The O(n p³) → O(n p²) reduction is theoretical. Not quantified at EDI's sizes.
findings.suggested_action: When prototyping TODO-6 (Prototype-lite), use the DGEQP3 leading-column semantics as the reference. Drop the per-candidate re-QR after the residual QR and gate on keep-set equality across the test corpus, as the catalog already says.

clopper-pearson-interval.note: [Clopper–Pearson interval] Closed form via two qbeta calls, O(1); nothing is faster. The p-value/CI convention mismatch (F26) is a coherence issue, not a speed issue, and is already recorded.

exact-binomial-test.note: [sign test (closed form)] Unweighted path is closed form, O(m). The weighted BB path loops over pairs with which(m_vec==pid), which is O(n·m). Precomputing pair row indices once (split/match) makes it O(n) with an identical answer, but that is the already-recorded incidental, not a new algorithm; no external source needed or found. | [exact binomial test (minlike)] R's own binom.test minlike (fetched this run) evaluates dbinom over only the opposite side of the mode and uses pbinom for both tails, switching to a binary search for n≥1234. EDI's binom_two_sided_pval sums exp(dbinom) over all n+1 outcomes. The gain is about 2x to O(log n) per call. It matters only inside the Zhang CI bisection, and is microseconds at EDI's d. | [exact conditional binomial test] O(d) minlike sum over d+1 dbinom terms. R trunk's binom.test now has an O(log n) bisection path (Varadhan) that gives the same minlike p, but R itself uses it only for n >= 1234 (https://raw.githubusercontent.com/wch/r-source/trunk/src/library/stats/R/binom.test.R). EDI's discordant-pair counts d are far below that, so the per-call cost is microseconds even inside the Zhang CI bisection. Optional only if very large d ever matters.

noncentral-hypergeometric-enumeration.note: [exact CMH test (convolution of hypergeometrics)] R's mantelhaen.test (fetched this run) computes the central convolved density once in C (C_d2x2xk). Every noncentral evaluation inside uniroot is just a log-reweight plus a normalization, O(S). The only faster published alternatives are FFT methods, which Vollset/Hirji/Elashoff report lose accuracy, and arXiv:1508.05803, whose O(K log K) bound only covers a pruning bound for the asymptotic CMH, not the exact test. Nothing faster and acceptable. | [exact conditional test (noncentral hypergeometric)] O(S) log-weights plus log-sum-exp. No CDF closed form exists for the noncentral hypergeometric, so a full pass over the support is needed to normalize. Possible constant-factor gains: a ratio recurrence instead of 4 lgamma calls per term, or caching delta-free weights across the CI bisection (already noted in the verdict). Both are trivial at EDI sizes. | [Fisher exact test (noncentral hypergeometric enumeration)] pval_exact_fisher calls the full stats::fisher.test, which also runs uniroot for the CMLE and both CI limits, even when only the p-value at delta_0 != 0 is needed (cached only at delta_0 = 0, alpha = 0.05). R-devel adds fisher.test(pval.only = TRUE) for 2x2. EDI's own zhang_exact_fisher_pval_cpp computes the same minlike p in O(S).

findings.label: exact binomial test (minlike)
findings.candidate: R's stats:::.binom_test_two_sided_pval_minlike approach. It calls dbinom only on the side of the mode opposite x to count the boundary y, then takes pbinom(x) + pbinom(n−y, upper), or the mirrored form. For large n it finds the boundaries by binary search, O(log n) dbinom calls.
findings.claimed_speedup: Not quantified by the source. By construction it needs about half the dbinom calls and no exp-sum for n<1234, and O(log n) for n≥1234 (R source of binom.test).
findings.suggested_action: Low priority. If touching zhang_exact_speedups.cpp anyway, port R's one-sided boundary search plus the pbinom tails. Otherwise Keep.

findings.label: Fisher exact test (noncentral hypergeometric enumeration)
findings.candidate: For p-value-only calls, compute just the minlike p. Option 1: call EDI's existing C++ zhang_exact_fisher_pval_cpp(n11, n10, n01, n00, delta_0), which uses the same minlike rule with relErr 1e-7 (log-space log1p(1e-7) is equivalent to R's d <= d_obs*(1+1e-7)). Option 2: once EDI's minimum R allows it, use fisher.test(..., pval.only = TRUE), new in R-devel for the 2x2 exact case. Keep the full fisher.test for the CI and estimate calls.
findings.claimed_speedup: R-devel NEWS says pval.only gives 'substantial speed gains in the case of large counts'; it gives no number. In theory the p-only path drops the ~3 uniroot searches (roughly 30-90 extra O(S) pmf passes), so it should be several times to tens of times faster per p-value call. Not measured.
findings.suggested_action: Low priority. Route pval_exact_fisher for the single-stratum case through zhang_exact_fisher_pval_cpp, or a p-only R helper, instead of the full fisher.test. Gate it with an equality test against fisher.test(...)$p.value over a grid of small tables and delta_0 values. Revisit pval.only when EDI's minimum R version includes it.

closed-form.note: [cumulative log-factorial table] A single O(n) cumulative pass of log sums that is built once. lgamma per entry costs the same or more. Nothing is faster.

exhaustive-enumeration.note: [exact Jonckheere–Terpstra null distribution] This R wrapper delegates to exact_jonckheere_terpstra_pval_cpp. The faster algorithm, a polynomial DP over (level, treated-so-far, partial 2U), is already Adopt (algorithm_choice_audit.md TODO-15, catalog §6 TODO 1). Nothing new beyond that. EDISON-WMW (https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC4792850/) confirms that a DP over (subset size, rank sum) handles ties exactly. | [exhaustive composition enumeration (DFS)] No new option beyond the already-adopted polynomial DP (algorithm_choice_audit.md TODO-15). Since 2026-11-16 the kernel has an interrupt check and a 1e6-allocation guard (jt_exact_leaf_count_exceeds_limit) that stops and points to asymptotic inference. So until the DP lands, exact JT p-values are unavailable for moderate K. The DP would make those cases exact again in polynomial time. EDISON-WMW (PMC4792850) reports exact tied WMW at n = 100 in 2.87 s with a hash-map DP. EDI's level-count DP has a far smaller state space, so this is consistent with the theoretical sub-second estimate. The guard's own DP is O(K·n_T·max n_k), nothing faster needed.
