asymptotic-series-recurrence.note: [recurrence + asymptotic series] Boost.Math digamma (fetched) shifts into [1,2], uses a rational approximation there, and switches to the asymptotic series for x≥10. That is the same O(shifts) structure with about 1 ε error against EDI's ~1e-12 relative: more accurate, but not faster, and the page gives no timings. The FasterMath benchmark in search results showed SIMD digamma slower than scalar. The catalog already records EDI's version at 7–19× faster than R. No faster acceptable option.

closed-form.note: [closed form (lgamma differences)] Three fast_lgamma calls per observation is already cheap. The known gap is the near-Poisson cancellation at large size, an accuracy item already adopted as TODO 8 (R-style log1p / Poisson-limit branch, same speed). A log-rising-factorial sum for small integer x could avoid both cost and cancellation, but I found no source benchmarking it, so it is not reported as a finding.

continued-fraction-lentz.note: [modified Lentz continued fraction] Every EDI call site passes an integer chi-square df, so a = df/2 is always an integer or a half-integer. For those a, DLMF 8.4.10/8.4.14 give exact finite sums: erfc(√x) alone when df=1. Boost uses these sums for a<30 in place of the continued fraction, as 'more stable and more efficient'. See the finding. | [series / Lentz continued fraction] fast_pchisq_upper and fast_gammaq. Chi-square df is always an integer at every call site (lrt_ci_newton.cpp:53 with df=1, and _helper_functions.h:115/162/194). That allows the closed finite sums Q(n,x)=e^{-x}Σx^k/k! and Q(n+½,x)=erfc(√x)+…; for df=1 this is just erfc(√(T/2)) through the existing fast_erfc. Abergel–Moisan TOMS 1006 (2020) targets accuracy over huge ranges, not speed at small df, so it does not apply.

lanczos-stirling.note: [Lanczos + Stirling] Lanczos g=7/9 terms below x=8 and a 7-term Stirling series above is already a minimal-cost O(1) lgamma at ~1e-15 abs. SLEEF lgamma (1.0 ULP, vectorized) has no published timing, and the vec_cpp wrappers are dominated by R-call overhead. Side note, accuracy rather than speed: fast_lbeta computes lgamma differences, which cancel at large a,b; R's lbeta uses the lgammacor form there. | [Lanczos approximation] The x<8 branch: one log and nine divisions. Higher-order Lanczos sets (e.g. Boost lanczos13m53) cost more and give no accuracy that matters inside lgamma differences. Keep. | [Stirling series] Closed-form O(1) polynomial in 1/x² used for x≥8 and already accurate to about 1e-15. Fewer terms would help only marginally and at the cost of accuracy near x=8. Nothing faster.

power-series.note: [power series] This is the x<a+1 branch of the same fast_gammaq dispatch. The integer/half-integer finite sums replace this branch too (see the finding). On its own it is a standard power series and nothing faster was found for general a.

findings.label: series / Lentz continued fraction
findings.candidate: Branch on integer or half-integer a = df/2. These use the exact finite sums DLMF 8.4.10, Q(n,x)=e^{-x}Σ_{k<n}x^k/k!, and DLMF 8.4.14, Q(n+½,z²)=erfc(z)+e^{-z²}/√π·Σ_{k=1}^{n} z^{2k-1}/(½)_k. For df=1 this is just fast_erfc(√(x/2)); for df=2 it is exp(−x/2). Keep the series/continued-fraction path for non-integer a, or for a≥30 as Boost does.
findings.claimed_speedup: Not quantified. Boost.Math docs say these finite sums 'are both more stable and more efficient than the continued fraction alternative' (a<30), but give no number. For df=1 it replaces a CF loop plus lgamma/log/exp with one rational erfc evaluation. The caller's cost is dominated by the model refit, so the end-to-end gain is likely negligible; the gain is mainly accuracy (no lgamma prefactor cancellation at larger df).
findings.suggested_action: Re-look, low priority. Add an integer/half-integer fast path in fast_gammaq, with at least the df=1 → fast_erfc(√(x/2)) and df=2 → exp(−x/2) special cases. Gate it on a cross-check against R::pchisq(lower=FALSE) over df ∈ {1,…,60} and x ∈ [1e-8, 1e3]. It could be folded into the row-O accuracy TODO (v1.0.5 audit TODO-22).

golub-welsch.note: [Golub–Welsch algorithm] K=20 rule, O(K³) once per functor build. Caching it (catalog T2, already Adopt) is the only real saving. Townsend–Trogdon–Olver Newton/asymptotic methods only pay off at large n and use Golub–Welsch for starting values at small n. SciPy also uses eigenvalues plus one Newton polish up to n=150. Accuracy note only: lme4 2.0-6 (2026-07-16) now symmetrizes its GH nodes/weights, so EDI's glmer(nAGQ=20) equivalence references can move in the last digits. Symmetrizing EDI's rule when the shared cached rule is built would keep them aligned. | [Golub–Welsch eigenvalue method] Caching the rule (already adopted, TODO-1) removes the cost entirely. Two smaller drop-in options are recorded as a low-priority finding: Eigen's computeFromTridiagonal, which skips the dense tridiagonal reduction, and dedupe. Asymptotic O(n) methods (Townsend–Trogdon–Olver) do not pay off at n_gh = 7–60: SciPy itself uses Golub–Welsch up to n = 150.

findings.label: Golub–Welsch eigenvalue method
findings.candidate: Keep the adopted caching (TODO-1). If any uncached path remains, call SelfAdjointEigenSolver::computeFromTridiagonal(diag = 0, subdiag = sqrt((i+1)/2)), which skips the dense tridiagonal reduction that compute() performs. Asymptotic O(n) methods (Townsend–Trogdon–Olver) are not worth it at n_gh ≤ 60: SciPy uses Golub–Welsch for n ≤ 150.
findings.claimed_speedup: Eigen documents about 9n³ flops for compute() with eigenvectors and gives no figure for computeFromTridiagonal. The saving is not quantified, and caching makes it moot.
findings.suggested_action: No change to the plan: finish TODO-1 caching and dedupe, including fast_hurdle_poisson_glmm's copy. Optionally build the single shared cached rule with computeFromTridiagonal.

analytic-derivatives.note: [analytic observed information] Closed-form Hessians costing O(n·p²) (LMM trace identities, hurdle NB, ZIP/hurdle, ZOIB block-diagonal). The cost equals forming XᵀWX, which is optimal for an exact Hessian. Finite differences or BFGS approximations would be less accurate.

closed-form.note: [closed-form 2×2 inverse] O(1) stack-allocated 2×2 inverse. Nothing is faster.

generalized-least-squares.note: [exact Gaussian LMM likelihood + GLS fast path] The closed-form compound-symmetry marginal likelihood is O(n·p) per evaluation, and the frozen-variance-component GLS replicate path is O(np²+p³). Nothing is cheaper for the same estimator. lme4 NEWS 1.1-36 to 2.1-0 (https://cran.r-project.org/web/packages/lme4/news.html) and glmmTMB NEWS (https://cran.r-project.org/web/packages/glmmTMB/news.html) add no new LMM fitting algorithm. Profiled 1-D Brent (catalog §4 TODO-3) remains the tracked robustness prototype. | [generalized least squares (LDLT)] The compound-symmetry Sherman–Morrison normal equations Σ_g w_g[X_gᵀX_g − c_g s_x s_xᵀ] are algebraically the quasi-demeaning (random-effects GLS = OLS on quasi-demeaned data) form, at the same O(np² + p³). With p in the single digits to tens, LDLT on a p×p system is optimal. lme4-style sparse PLS only pays off with many or crossed random effects, which KK pair/singleton groups (m_g ≤ 2) never have.

laplace-approximation-tmb.note: [Laplace approximation + nlminb (glmmTMB)] Gaussian LMM: Laplace is exact and it is only the fallback; the closed-form C++ LMM plus the frozen-VC GLS replicate shortcut is already the fast path. Hurdle Bayesian bootstrap: the known faster option is the existing weighted hurdle-GLMM C++ (Prototype already recorded). No new glmmTMB/TMB optimizer evidence found.

lbfgs.note: [L-BFGS (joint, unprofiled ML)] Already Prototype: profiled 1-D Brent on λ=σ_b²/σ_e² with GLS β̂(λ), optional REML. lme4 itself profiles out β and σ. I found no newer one-parameter random-intercept algorithm that beats a bracketed 1-D search at EDI sizes (n up to thousands, p small). arXiv 2602.09247 (EM view of REML) is not faster.

sherman-morrison.note: [closed form (Sherman–Morrison per group)] The random-intercept ML NLL and gradient come from per-group sufficient sums via Sherman–Morrison on the compound-symmetry V_g. That is O(n p) per evaluation with no quadrature, the same O(n) Woodbury form general LMM codes reduce to for this model. Nothing is faster.

delta-method.note: [central finite differences + delta method] marginal_estimand_delta_se / numerical_gradient_central: the analytic gradient mean(μ_ai x_ai) is one O(np) pass and is already Adopt (v1.0.5-TODO-8). Complex-step was considered and rejected in the catalog. I found no new source that changes this. | [delta method (finite-difference gradient)] ordinal_gcomp_post_fit_cpp computes the md gradient by central FD over K−1+p parameters. Each evaluation is O(nK) and reuses the precomputed η, which is negligible next to the O(nd²+d³) Hessian and LU in the same call. The analytic gradient is already Adopt (low priority, v1.0.5-TODO-5). Nothing faster exists.

finite-differences.note: [central finite differences] Where these are costly (log/identity-binomial score and Hessian, using a 4-point ℓ stencil at O(2np³)), the closed-form X'diag(∂²ℓ)X is already Adopt (v1.0.5 row N, catalog O5), and nothing beats it. The generic numerical_gradient/numerical_hessian take central differences of the analytic gradient, so a Hessian costs only 2p gradient evaluations at p≤~25. AD and complex-step would not be cheaper (the catalog already rejected both). The R Cox FD helpers are dead code, and ordinal g-comp compute_md_gradient calls a cheap O(nK) functional; its cost is negligible.

g-computation.note: [g-computation + delta method] Ordinal PO g-comp: plug-in standardization is O(n(p+K)) and the central-FD gradient costs 2(p+K−1) cheap post-fit calls. The analytic gradient is already recorded (catalog §2 TODO-5) as a deterministic, low-priority drop-in. I found no faster method for the same estimator. | [g-computation + delta-method sandwich] One logistic or fractional-logit fit plus an O(np) standardization and an O(p²) analytic delta-method gradient is the minimal work for this estimator. CRAN 'risks' (0.4.3) and stdReg use the same standardization + delta method. The FD fallback fires only on failure. The covariate-sampling variance term (Incidental 16) is an estimand question, not a speed one. | [g-computation standardization (closed form)] A closed-form plug-in, O(np) (or O(n(p+K)) for PO): one or K−1 plogis evaluations per subject per arm. Nothing faster; the cost is dominated by the upstream model fit. | [g-computation (closed form) + drop-largest-coefficient] The plogis averages are a closed form, O(np), and nothing is faster. The only alternative to the separation fallback is Firth, which the catalog already rejected as an estimator change.

irls.note: [Fisher scoring + sandwich variance] Clusters have at most 2 members, the 2x2 V_g^-1 is closed form, and each iteration costs O(n p^2), the minimum for forming the p x p information. The one-step GEE of Lipsitz et al. (JCGS 2017) gets its 10x+ speedup (R-bloggers post: 0.087 s vs 1.946 s for geese at about 100 per cluster) by avoiding O(m^2) pair sums inside large clusters. That saves nothing at m <= 2, and it only approximates the iterated estimate (close but not identical), so it would be an estimator change. geepack NEWS through 1.3.13 (2025-10-14) has no solver changes. | [GEE (Liang–Zeger)] The C++ pairs-plus-singletons kernel is already the standard estimator at optimal per-iteration cost. The catalog T9 alternatives (GEE2, ALR, QIF, independence) are slower or change the estimator, and no newer evidence overturns that. One-step GEE is not acceptable for the same reason as above. The eager 12-threshold candidate ladder (inference_mixin_kk_gee_shared.R:298, still eager) is already recorded as an implementation note in catalog §11 and is not an algorithm-choice issue. | [GEE with local odds ratios (Fisher scoring)] Nothing faster replaces the estimator itself: multgee 1.9.0 (2023-09-02) is still current. However, multgee estimates the local-odds-ratio structure from response-only marginalized contingency tables and accepts LORstr='fixed' with LORterm. In randomization loops where y and the pairing m are unchanged, that RC-G(1)/IPFP step could be done once and reused instead of being refit on every permutation. Not quantified; see findings.

method-of-moments.note: [moment estimator (Liang–Zeger)] Closed-form O(n) pass over pair Pearson products. Nothing can be faster. The phi-scaling bug recorded in the audit (F20) has since been fixed in fast_gee.cpp (alpha = num / ((N_pairs - p) * phi)).

findings.candidate: Cache the estimated uniform LOR structure and pass it back as LORstr='fixed' with LORterm (built with multgee::matrixLOR from the cached fit). According to the CRAN reference manual, the structure is estimated by aggregating responses across clusters into marginalized contingency tables and fitting an RC-G(1) model; covariates do not enter. So the structure is the same whenever y and the cluster pairing (m) are unchanged, e.g. across ladder rungs, and across permutation draws at delta = 0 when the design does not redraw m.

findings.suggested_action: Profile one ordLORgee call at typical KK sizes to measure the share of time spent in LOR estimation versus Fisher scoring. If it is material, prototype a (y, m)-keyed cache with LORstr='fixed'/LORterm, used in the randomization loop and across ladder rungs, and A/B it against the current fits for identical coefficients within tolerance.

findings.label: damped Newton with step-halving
findings.candidate: Gradient-regularized Newton step (AN2CE/AN2CER, Gratton–Jerad–Toint): solve (H_k + sqrt(κ_a σ_k ||g_k||) I) s = −g. A negative-curvature/eigen step is added only when needed, using the shift (σ_k||g_k||^{1/2} + [−λ_min(H_k)]_+) I. This gives a concrete, essentially parameter-free τ rule for the 'add τI' branch of algorithm_choice_audit_catalog.md §1 TODO-9. A positive-definite system also allows LLT instead of FullPivLU (performance_profiling_and_upgrades.md TODO-155).
findings.claimed_speedup: Not quantified relative to EDI's current loop. Section 6 of https://arxiv.org/html/2302.10065 reports iteration-count performance-profile areas on 119 small OPM/CUTEst problems (2–49 variables): AN2CE 0.91 and AN2CER 0.88, against AR2 0.92 and trust-region TR2M 0.91. Reliability was 96.6% for both AN2C variants, 97.5% for AR2 and 95.0% for TR2M. AN2CER needed a single linear solve in about 93% of iterations. The source shows parity with standard safeguarded methods, not a win over them; the expected gain for EDI is fewer wasted halving cascades and fewer L-BFGS hand-offs on NB/beta Newton paths.
findings.suggested_action: When prototyping algorithm_choice_audit_catalog.md §1 TODO-9, consider the √||g|| regularization rule (with the [−λ_min]_+ shift on detected indefiniteness) as the τ choice. Factor with LLT, and keep step-halving and the L-BFGS fallback as the outer safety net. Judge it by halving-cascade and L-BFGS hand-off counts in the A/B harness. Do not expect a speedup on well-behaved concave fits.

gauss-hermite-quadrature.note: Re-checked today. New code-level finding: fast_poisson_glmm.cpp operator()/hessian (:199-206, :223-243, :258-300) computes exp(η_i+b_k), an all-n term vector and an X'·(n-vector) product at every one of the 60 nodes, so it costs O(n·K·p). With a log link, group g's integrand depends on b only through S_g=Σw·y, Λ_g=Σw·e^η and A_g=Σw(yη−log y!). That gives O(np + G·K) per evaluation with an identical estimator. The hurdle kernel already uses multiplicative exp sharing, and the catalog records no such note for the Poisson GLMM. The previous AGQ finding still stands (Stringer arXiv 2310.01589, no journal DOI yet). It is now backed by Rizopoulos 2012 pseudo-adaptive GHQ (doi 10.1016/j.csda.2011.09.007) as the frozen-mode route. Nothing newer turned up: the arXiv API had no 2025–26 GLMM quadrature speed paper; arXiv 2607.12184 (lme4 GLMM paper, Jul 2026) and 2606.15933 (package comparison) found no new algorithm; lme4 2.0-6/2.1-0 NEWS has only accuracy and symmetrisation changes; GLMMadaptive NEWS has none.

log-sum-exp.note: O(K) per group. SIMD/vectorised logsumexp threads report gains only for long vectors; at K=7–60 per group it is not a bottleneck. With the Poisson collapse it stays O(G·K).

louis-identity.note: Changed from no_faster_acceptable_found. For the Poisson GLMM Hessian, the Louis identity itself stays, but its β-β block can be one weighted_crossprod with weights w·e^η·E_g[e^b] instead of 60 per-node crossprods. The per-group E[GGᵀ] follows from G_gk = u_g − e^{b_k}v_g, with u_g=X_gᵀwy and v_g=X_gᵀwe^η, using posterior moments of e^b. So O(n·K·p²) → O(np² + G·(K+p²)), with the same matrix. Logistic and clogit+GLMM Louis Hessians are unchanged (no such factorization). Pan & Thompson 2003 (Comput Stat) remains the standard GHQ score/information reference; nothing faster found.

soft-barrier-penalty.note: O(1). The Chung et al. 2013 boundary-avoiding (log-gamma) penalties and blme change the estimator, not the speed. No new evidence.

findings.candidate: Collapse to cluster totals (log link). Per group g: S_g=Σw_i y_i, log Λ_g=log Σw_i e^{η_i} (via LSE), A_g=Σw_i(y_iη_i−log y_i!). Node log term = log w_k + A_g + b_k S_g − exp(b_k + log Λ_g), which is O(G·K). Gradient: β-part = Xᵀ[w⊙(y − e^{η}⊙E_g[e^b])], one GEMV. The σ-part comes from per-group posterior moments E_g[b(S_g−Λ_g e^b)]. Louis Hessian: β-β = −Xᵀdiag(w e^η E_g[e^b])X, one weighted crossprod. Cross and E[GGᵀ] terms come from u_g=X_gᵀwy, v_g=X_gᵀwe^η and E_g[e^b], E_g[e^{2b}], E_g[b e^b], E_g[b² ...]. This is the same quadrature-approximated likelihood algebraically; only the summation order changes. The cluster-total sufficiency is the Hausman–Hall–Griliches structure, and the per-group integral is a Poisson-lognormal-type 1-D function of (S_g, Λ_g, σ). EDI's hurdle kernel already uses the multiplicative e^{η}·e^{b_k} sharing.
findings.claimed_speedup: Not quantified by any source. This is my derivation from the code. The n-dependent work drops from O(n·K·p) to O(n·p) per evaluation, with O(G·K) left for the quadrature, so up to about K=60× on the dominant term when n ≫ G. In KK designs (pairs plus singletons, G≈n/2–n) the remaining G·K exp/LSE work is about half to all of the current n·K exp count. A realistic per-evaluation gain is then the removed K·p GEMV/crossprod work plus about 1–2× fewer exps, perhaps 3–10× on gradient+Hessian for p≈5–20. Must be measured.

findings.candidate: Adaptive GH with fewer nodes, by either of two routes. (a) Exact AQ gradient by implicit differentiation of the per-group mode, reusing the inner Cholesky, with L-BFGS (Stringer, arXiv 2310.01589v2, still a preprint with no journal DOI). (b) Pseudo-adaptive GHQ: centre and scale nodes once per group from an initial fit and keep them fixed, so the existing cheap fixed-node analytic gradient applies (Rizopoulos 2012, CSDA 56(3):491–501, doi 10.1016/j.csda.2011.09.007).

Rizopoulos: 'considerably faster than the standard Gauss–Hermite rule', not quantified on the abstract page; a later application cited in search results reports 6 pseudo-adaptive nodes ≈ 20 standard. Against EDI's 20 fixed nodes at m_g≤2 the gain is not quantified and probably small; catalog T1 estimates 1.2–1.6×.

best-improvement-swap.note: [best-improvement pairwise-swap local search] The best-improvement rule defines the design's allocation distribution, so any different search (first-improvement, KL, tabu) is a design change, not a speedup. The only speedups that keep the same local optimum (Gram G = M'M for O(1) per pair, plus routing through the pruned D-opt engine) are already tracked in catalog §8 P2 and small_kernel_hoists_batch.md Item A. I found no newer paper or software (the 2026-04-30 GreedyExperimentalDesign 1.6.1 on CRAN mentions only optional GPU acceleration) that offers a faster exact best-improvement scan at EDI's sizes. | [best-improvement swap search with bound pruning] The sorted-scan early break is already the standard exact pruning for an additive delta a_i + b_j − 2P_ij. Exact maximum-inner-product search on the low-rank P would only pay off at n far above EDI's sizes. A code-reading observation, not from the literature: the D prune threshold adds the global 2·max_P, and a per-row max_j P_ij would be a tighter bound that is still provably safe. That is an implementation tweak worth a look, not a new algorithm. | [greedy best-improvement pair flips] Pair-constrained mode costs O((n/2)·p) per round, already linear in the input with an O(p) incremental delta, so nothing faster is possible. Changing the flip rule would change the design. | [greedy best-improvement pair switching] The search is the design (Krieger, Azriel & Kapelner 2019). The follow-up literature I found (the 2023 CJS matching + greedy hybrid; GreedyExperimentalDesign 1.6.1 on CRAN, 2026-04-30) gives no faster algorithm that reaches the same local optimum. The O(1)-per-pair Gram trick and the pruned-engine route are already tracked (catalog §8 P2, TODO 2). | [greedy pruned best-swap search] This is the same shared engine as the bound-pruning entry: exact and already pruned, with the D bound adaptive and the A bound fixed per round as proven. The tighter per-row max-P bound noted above is the only cheap improvement I saw. No literature source offers a faster exact best-swap scan at n in the hundreds. | [pruned best-improvement swap search] The search rule defines the design's allocation distribution, so a different search would change the estimator. It already uses O(1) deltas with a sorted-scan prune. Nothing faster that keeps the same best-swap trajectory was found. | [incremental swap-delta objective] The O(1)-per-pair Gram trick (small_kernel_hoists_batch.md Item A) and routing through the pruned D-opt engine (P = 4G) are already tracked. Nothing faster found.

fisher-yates-shuffle.note: [Fisher–Yates shuffle] The explicit Durstenfeld shuffle with Lemire bounded_rand is the standard method. The one newer result is batched ranged integer generation (Brackett-Rozinsky & Lemire, SP&E 2024), which reports 1.4–2.6× on shuffles with 64-bit PCG/Lehmer generators. It stays unbiased and deterministic but changes the seed-pinned stream again, and it is untested with 32-bit MT19937. The shuffle is not dominant in its callers: rerandomization spends O(np) per draw on the objective. Low confidence.

findings.label: Fisher–Yates shuffle
findings.candidate: Batched ranged random integer generation (Brackett-Rozinsky & Lemire, Software: Practice and Experience 55(1), 2024). Several unbiased bounded indices come from one random word, with one multiply and no division in the common case. With 32-bit words, two indices per word work while i·(i−1) < 2^32 (i ≲ 65k), which covers EDI's n.
findings.claimed_speedup: The paper reports shuffle_6 vs the unbatched shuffle across a range of array lengths: 1.4–1.8× (Lehmer) and 1.8–2.5× (PCG64) on Xeon, 1.5–2.3× / 1.9–2.6× on Apple M2. Only 64-bit generators were tested; it is not measured with MT19937 or 32-bit words, and the sizes in the 100–10,000 range are not reported separately.
findings.suggested_action: Record it as an option in the catalog P2 table. Consider it only if a profile shows shuffle or RNG words are a material share of rerandomization or null-draw time; bundle it with any other planned stream change (for example TODO-149(c) RNG throughput) so seeds are refreshed only once.

Nothing new beyond the recorded option. | [linear-pass ID relabeling] compute_matching_grouping_cpp makes two O(n) passes over m_vec. Every subject must be read and written, so O(n) is the lower bound. | [pair extraction loop] The cost is an R loop running which(m_vec==pid) once per pair, O(n·m) per replicate. sort-and-sweep.note: [sort + unique] init_levels runs sort+unique once per fit, O(n log n) on doubles. The ordinal MLE that follows costs O(npK) per iteration, so this step is negligible. Counting or hashing would need an integer key range and would not preserve the sorted order the thresholds need, so the gain is immaterial at EDI's sizes. | [sort + unique, binary search] get_levels/map_y_to_1K run once per fit (or once per shifted y in a CI search, still dominated by the LBFGS fit that follows). They cost O(n log n + n log K) with K ≈ 3–7. Mapping with a hash or a sort-permutation would save at most a log factor on a step negligible next to the fit, and it would add complexity around floating-point key equality. | [stable sort + run-length grouping] This is a one-time O(n log n) layout step. A stable counting sort on dense integer group ids would be O(n + G), but the catalog already records it as immaterial next to the O(n·n_gh) GLMM objective evaluated many times per fit. Nothing new.

selection-algorithm.note: [Hodges–Lehmann estimator (selection)] EDI materializes the differences and runs introselect when n_T·n_C ≤ 4096, otherwise sorts and uses value-space bisection with two-pointer counts. The only asymptotically better options are Johnson–Mizoguchi/Monahan O(n log n) selection, already catalogued. No newer algorithm or benchmark found; the planned hoisting and early-stop TODOs remain the right levers. | [introselect (std::nth_element)] Floyd–Rivest selection in miniselect (Boost License, GPL-compatible) is claimed faster than libstdc++ nth_element, but only at 2^16 and 10^7 elements, with no published number at EDI's ≤4096 sizes (ClickHouse reported a 2.5% overall gain). It is a constant-factor change on an O(N) step that is dominated by materializing the differences. Not worth a dependency.

streaming-moments.note: [all-pairs one-pass variance] The variance of all n_T·n_C pairwise differences, and of all m(m+1)/2 Walsh averages, are exact functions of per-group sums of centered data, so each costs O(n) instead of O(n_T n_C) or O(m²). This is already tracked as Adopt (low priority, TODO 5). It is re-stated as a finding because the current naive sum/sum² over O(n²) terms is also numerically weaker.

value-space-bisection-selection.note: [value-space bisection selection (two-pointer count)] This is the hot path: per-replicate HL in compute_wilcox_hl_rand_bootstrap_parallel_cpp. Each bisection step is an O(n_T+n_C) two-pointer count with no extra memory, which is hard to beat at EDI sizes (n up to a few thousand). The asymptotically better options do not change that. Deterministic X+Y / sorted-matrix selection (Johnson–Mizoguchi, Frederickson–Johnson, and the simpler soft-heap version by Kaplan, Kozma, Zamir and Zwick, SOSA 2019, arXiv 1802.07041) only matches Frederickson–Johnson's O(n log n) bound for the median, with large constants. Its abstract (arXiv 1802.07041, fetched) gives no running time for selection in X+Y and no benchmark. The catalog already rejects this family. robslopes (CRAN 1.1.4, 2025-12-19, GPL-2|3) gets quasilinear medians of pairwise quantities with randomized Matoušek / Dillencourt-style algorithms. Those consume randomness, so they would need a private deterministic pivot to keep R streams untouched; that is the same trade-off as the catalog's Monahan rank-space option. The article reports speedups only against brute-force O(n²) implementations, not against an O(n·L) bisection. Nothing newer than the row's 2026-11-16 review overturns its verdict. The tracked wilcox_hl_kernel_hoisting.md TODO-3 (early stop, with the tie-safe criterion from Incidental 6) and TODO-4 (warm bracket) remain the right speedups. Same verdict for the one-sample Walsh-average variants (count_walsh_avgs_leq, max_walsh_avg_leq, select_walsh_avg_sorted), whose only caller is the legacy IVWC path.

walsh-average-enumeration.note: [Hodges–Lehmann estimator] stats::wilcox.test runs an exact sorted-Walsh path only for m<50 and uses the normal approximation with uniroot otherwise, which is cheap at EDI sizes. Monahan 1984 and Johnson–Mizoguchi are already in the catalog and pay off only at n in the thousands; the NAG and DescTools implementations found add nothing newer. The open item here is the SE scale (I2/F7), a correctness bug, not a speed one. | [weighted Hodges–Lehmann estimator] The weighted branch of hl_point_estimate (inference_all_simple_wilcox.R:256-279) appears to be unreachable at fa2fe36d. The class declares supports_bayesian_bootstrap = function() FALSE (line 231), and grep finds no caller that passes row_weights: all three call sites (lines 319, 341, 369) pass only (y, w). So there is no hot path to speed up. The inventory row describing it as 'weighted HL for the Bayesian bootstrap' looks stale and should be re-checked. If the branch is ever revived, there is a faster route that gives the same estimator. With product weights w_i·v_j, the weighted count of diffs ≤ x is Σ_j v_j · (prefix sum of w over y_T ≤ x + y_Cj). That can be computed with the existing two-pointer sweep plus prefix sums in O(n_T+n_C), so the existing value-space bisection and snap give the lower weighted median (smallest realized diff with cumulative weight ≥ 1/2, as the current code returns) in O(n log n + n·L). The current code does an O(n_T·n_C·log) outer+order in R. The answer matches up to floating-point summation order at an exact 1/2 boundary. This is not quantified by any source: I found no published weighted-X+Y-median algorithm (searches turned up only the sort-or-select weighted median, https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Weighted_median). It is not worth doing while the branch is dead.

findings.label: all-pairs one-pass variance
findings.candidate: Exact closed forms from per-group moments, computed on centered data. Rank-sum: the mean of the differences is x̄_T − ȳ_C, and the population variance of all differences is var_pop(T) + var_pop(C), so the sample variance is N/(N−1)·(var_pop(T)+var_pop(C)) with N = n_T n_C. Signed-rank: with S = Σd and Q = Σd² over m centered diffs, the sum of Walsh averages is (m+1)S/2 and their sum of squares is ((m+2)Q + S²)/4, divided by M = m(m+1)/2. Both use the shift invariance of the variance. Cost is O(n_T + n_C) or O(m), and Chan/Welford-style centering avoids the cancellation that affects the naive formula.
findings.claimed_speedup: Not quantified by a source. Algebraically, O(n_T n_C) becomes O(n_T + n_C), and O(m²) becomes O(m).
findings.suggested_action: No new decision is needed. When TODO 5 is picked up, replace both double loops with the centered O(n) closed forms. Verify against the current loop on fixtures, to 1e-12 relative, including a large-offset case where the naive formula loses precision.

icm-npmle.note: [ICM + Newton (icenReg ic_sp) + bootstrap SE] icenReg's JSS paper shows ic_sp converging in 11 iterations (0.023 s) at n=500, against 25 s for intcox at strict tolerance. Its fitter is ICM plus a constrained gradient-ascent step plus conditional Newton. The 200-refit bootstrap SE has only one alternative: the profile likelihood already listed in the catalog. ICsurv's Hessian/Louis SE uses a spline baseline, which is an estimator change. EDI's resampling loops already pass bs_samples=0 when only the estimate is needed. icenReg NEWS shows no new SE method.

turnbull-em.note: [Turnbull NPMLE (EM)] Nothing new beyond the already-recorded Prototype (v1.0.5 TODO-28 → icenReg::ic_np). New numbers do suggest reordering it: in icenReg's JSS paper (Table 1), ic_np takes 0.001 s at n=100 and 0.003 s at n=1,000, against 0.106 s and 8.3 s for Icens::EMICM, so the planned initEMICM first step is probably not worth doing. CNM/HCNM (npsurv, GPL, has w=) was checked: it is pure R and its published times (Wang & Taylor 2013, Table 4: 0.044–0.056 s at n=400) are not faster than ic_np's. | [per-draw NPMLE re-solve in randomization loop] Already Adopt (v1.0.5 TODO-11, not yet implemented at fa2fe36d). New detail from the interval manual: ictest() takes icFIT= (a precomputed pooled icfit, documented as being 'for increased computation speed'), and wlr_trafo() returns the scores. Also, methodRuleIC1 selects 'exact.network' when n ≤ 20, so each per-draw ictest call at small n also runs an exact network-algorithm p-value that EDI then discards.

On the per-draw estimate-only calls, also pass method='pclt' (or exact=FALSE) so no exact p-value is computed per draw. (b) The full v1.0.5 TODO-11 Adopt: get the scores c_i once with interval::wlr_trafo(L, R, scores=..., icFIT=pooled_fit), then compute each draw's statistic as a linear form in w (one matrix product over the draw matrix).

jackknife.note: [delete-one jackknife] For estimators that are least-squares fits (mean difference, OLS/Lin-type, and WLS), the exact delete-one-unit or delete-one-cluster estimates have a closed form, β^(g) = (X'X − X_gᵀX_g)⁻¹(X'y − X_gᵀy_g). This replaces n_units R6 refits with one pass over the data plus G small k×k solves (MacKinnon, Nielsen & Webb 2023, Eq. 15). The catalog only lists the approximate one-step and influence-function options; this exact identity is missing from it. See the finding. Nonlinear fits keep the refit loop. | [jackknife bias and variance (Quenouille–Tukey)] Closed-form moments of the jackknife vector, O(n_units) after the replicates are computed. Nothing faster exists. The unequal-unit weighting issue (I17) is an accuracy item that is already recorded. | [weighted delete-one jackknife] The alternatives (infinitesimal jackknife / empirical influence, ABC, regression-IJ, grouped jackknife, one-step approximate LOO) are all already in the catalog with their estimator-change caveats, and a search turned up nothing new from 2024–2026. The serial vapply could run through par_lapply, but that is parallelisation, not an algorithm change.

findings.label: delete-one jackknife
findings.candidate: For least-squares estimators, compute the exact delete-one-unit estimates in closed form: β^(g) = (X'X − X_gᵀX_g)⁻¹(X'y − X_gᵀy_g). This needs the per-unit cross-products X_gᵀX_g and X_gᵀy_g, formed once in O(n·k²), plus G k×k solves (MacKinnon, Nielsen & Webb 2023, Eq. 15–16). For a plain mean difference it reduces to O(n) arm-sum updates. Keep the refit loop for nonlinear fits.
findings.claimed_speedup: Not quantified against naive re-estimation. MacKinnon, Nielsen & Webb (arXiv 2301.04527, Section 4) benchmark only against other CV3 methods: the jackknife formula is about 12× (k = 20) and 26× (k = 40) faster than the score method for small clusters at N = 2²⁰. Against EDI's n_units refits with R6 overhead, the theoretical saving is the whole refit loop: n_units fits become O(n·k² + G·k³).
findings.suggested_action: Prototype an exact closed-form jackknife fast path for the least-squares classes (mean difference, OLS and Lin-type, WLS), behind a bit-tolerance test against the refit jackknife. Add the option to the catalog's NEW-jackknife-influence table, which today lists only approximate deletion methods.

greenwood-variance.note: [weighted Greenwood-type RMST variance] weighted_restricted_mean_se_diff computes weighted at-risk n_j via vapply(ut, sum(wt[y>=t])) and d_j via vapply(sum(wt[y==t & d==1])). That is O(n·D) ≈ O(n²) per BB replicate. Sorting once and taking a reverse cumulative sum gives O(n log n) with the same formula (FP summation order only), the same fix as v1.0.5-TODO-6 for the weighted KM median. | [Greenwood-type delta-method variance] Closed form after one sort plus suffix sums, O(n log n) once per call, not in a resampling loop. Alternative variance forms (Aalen-type, pseudo-values) would change the estimator, not speed it up. Nothing faster.

kaplan-meier-product-limit.note: [Kaplan–Meier median + Brookmeyer–Crowley CI] One grouped survfit plus quantile() costs O(n log n) per alpha and is memoised. The sort is the lower bound, so a faster algorithm is not possible. A C++ sweep that reused get_survival_stat_diff's sort would save only R/formula overhead (implementation, not algorithm). Alternatives such as the Su–Wei two-sample interval are different estimators, not speedups. survival NEWS up to 3.8-12 shows no change to quantile.survfit or BC limits that affects this. | [restricted mean survival time (KM area)] Point RMST is survival::survfit(weights=) (C code, O(n log n) sort) + O(D) area loop; nothing asymptotically faster exists since a sort is needed. The only overhead is survfit's formula/model.frame setup per BB replicate, which is unquantified. A hand-rolled weighted KM sweep would remove it, but that is an implementation tweak, not a better algorithm. Interval-censored SE stays tracked under v1.0.5-TODO-7 (row Y). | [weighted Kaplan–Meier (repeated tail sums)] Already Adopt (v1.0.5-TODO-6) but still not implemented at commit fa2fe36d. weighted_km_median still recomputes sum(row_weights[i:n]) at every distinct time and grows vectors with c(). A reverse cumsum after the sort, with early exit once S ≤ 0.5, gives O(n log n), identical up to FP order. | [Kaplan–Meier product-limit sweep] Single evaluation: one comparison sort plus an O(n) sweep, which is optimal for unsorted input. In resampling, the per-draw re-sort is already covered by the presort Adopt (TODO-11/-18). SIMD sorts (vqsort, x86-simd-sort) sort primitive keys and help int32 more than 64-bit keys (djbsort speed notes), and they don't apply directly to EDI's record comparator. The catalog already rejects this sort-swap option.

mover-interval.note: [Kaplan–Meier median + Brookmeyer–Crowley CIs combined by MOVER] Cost is dominated by the same O(n log n) survfit, and the MOVER combine is O(1). The 2025 arXiv work on Wald SEs from BC intervals (2503.03065) concerns how the SE is estimated, not speed. Nothing faster that keeps the estimator. | [MOVER (method of variance estimates recovery)] Closed form, O(1); nothing faster.
labels: Kaplan–Meier median + Brookmeyer–Crowley CIs combined by MOVER

findings.label: weighted Greenwood-type RMST variance
findings.candidate: Sort the arm once by y, use rowsum (or tabulate on match(y, ut)) for per-time weighted events and totals, and get the weighted at-risk n_j as a reverse cumulative sum of the per-time totals. Then apply the same cumprod / reverse-cumsum A(t_j) / variance formula. Alternatively, reuse the weighted n.risk/n.event from the survfit fit already built for the point estimate, if its weighted counts match.
findings.claimed_speedup: Not quantified by any source; complexity O(n·D) → O(n log n) per arm per replicate, the same pattern and rationale as the already-adopted v1.0.5-TODO-6 (weighted KM median).
findings.suggested_action: Adopt: fold into v1.0.5-TODO-6's scope (same reverse-cumsum fix) and update the inventory verdict from 'Not yet audited' to Adopt.

findings.claimed_speedup: Not quantified by a source; O(n·D) → O(n log n) (sort-bound) per replicate.

brute-force-distance.note: [brute-force weighted Euclidean distances] O(|R|d) SIMD scan, one query per arrival. The weights change with each arrival's KK21 refit, so a static tree is invalid for the same moving-metric reason. Per the scikit-learn guide, brute force wins at these N and with few queries. This is already the minimal exact cost.

mahalanobis-quadratic-forms.note: [batched Mahalanobis quadratic forms (GEMM)] One GEMM rowsum((D·S⁻¹)∘D) is O(|R|p²), the same order as Cholesky whitening. Swapping solve() for Cholesky is already tracked (kk14_incremental_covariance.md TODO-3). Nothing beats exact quadratic forms at |R| in the tens to hundreds; the only sub-linear methods found are approximate (see the next row). | [brute-force Mahalanobis nearest-neighbour + Hotelling T² threshold] The metric changes every arrival. The only dynamic-metric structure found, Qin/Reddy/Song 2023 (https://arxiv.org/abs/2309.01030), is randomized and approximate, so it breaks exactness and determinism. The scikit-learn guide (https://scikit-learn.org/stable/modules/neighbors.html) says brute force is competitive for N below ~30 and when there are few queries per structure; here there is one query per metric, which rules out amortizing a tree. The audit's Keep verdict holds. The covariance/QR rebuild is already tracked in kk14_incremental_covariance.md.
labels: brute-force Mahalanobis nearest-neighbour + Hotelling T² threshold

monte-carlo-pair-sampling.note: [Monte Carlo pair sampling (distance quantile)] At O(Bd) with B = 500 per arrival this is already trivial. Exact all-pairs enumeration when t(t-1)/2 <= B is the only alternative, and it is already a tracked Prototype (catalog §7, TODO-7; v1.0.5 TODO-35). It changes design draws for a given seed, which makes it a design-rule change rather than a speedup. I found no newer selection or incomplete-U-statistic result for weighted multivariate pair distances that would beat O(Bd) at EDI's sizes. Fetching the KK21 arXiv PDF to confirm the paper's threshold definition failed (binary PDF, no text extraction available), so that point is unverified.

alternating-irls-theta.note: [alternating IRLS and Newton on θ] The catalog already rejects joint Newton, Fisher scoring and profile-θ variants. A small constant-factor option remains: the θ Newton step in kk21_weights.cpp computes digamma/trigamma(y_i+θ) for every observation. The distinct-y table pattern (already used in fast_zinb.cpp and fast_hurdle_negbin.cpp, and the core of glmGamPoi's speedup) gives the same answer with D ≪ n special-function calls. Likely a small win, because IRLS O(inner·n·m²) dominates.

closed-form.note: [closed-form simple linear regression] Closed form, one O(np) pass, so nothing can be asymptotically faster. The only open issue is numerical: the one-pass Σx²−n·x̄² and the expanded-SSE form cancel badly when |mean|/sd is large (catalog §8 incidental 4). A centered two-pass form costs the same O(np) and is an accuracy fix, not a speedup.

forward-stepwise-selection.note: [forward stepwise (FWL residualization / score test)] FWL/MGS forward selection is O(np²), the optimal order, and the logistic path already uses one reduced fit plus Rao scores. Bernardi/Busatto/Cattelan, 'Fast QR updating methods for statistical applications' (https://arxiv.org/abs/2412.05905, v3 March 2026), updates only R. The abstract claims a 'substantial reduction' but gives no numbers, so the speedup is not quantified, and the method has the same asymptotic order. CRAN fastQR 1.1.5 (https://cran.r-project.org/package=fastQR, GPL≥2) assumes full column rank and has no pivoting in its update routines. Its Gram-based R-update also squares the condition number, the same objection as the rejected sweep-operator option in catalog P9. The stepwise beta/NB/ordinal full-refit paths (Prototype TODO-3) are a different algorithm and are not in this batch. | [cumulative-link fit via R callback (stepwise Wald)] The code at fa2fe36d no longer calls back into R. multivariate_ordinal_tstat now calls the C++ fast_ordinal_regression_internal directly, so the inventory 'details' text and the 'unprotected wrap' caveat are stale and should be refreshed. The stepwise path still refits every candidate (O(p²/2) fits). The faster scheme already tracked in v1.2.0-TODO-23 (score entry from one reduced fit per step) is what SAS PROC LOGISTIC does for cumulative-logit forward selection: a 1-df score chi-square from the current model's MLEs. The ordinal R package (2026.7-26) offers only LR add1/drop1, which refits each candidate, so it is no faster comparator. See finding. | [forward stepwise score (Rao) selection] This is already the fast design: one reduced fit per step plus O(nm) score work per candidate. The I-1 correctness issue looks fixed at fa2fe36d: the reduced fit now uses WeibullAFTLikelihood with Newton (kk21_stepwise_survival.cpp ~L37-46). The only remaining speedup is the constant-factor GEMM batching the catalog already lists. A side observation, not about speed and low confidence: I_jj.S projects out only the β block (XS'W XS), not the log-σ nuisance. β and σ are not orthogonal in the Weibull AFT, so the statistic may not be the efficient score. Worth a check alongside the inventory 'Keep' verdict. | [forward stepwise via full Wald refits] Beta and NB still refit [1, x_j, S, w] for every candidate at every step. The tracked score-test scheme (v1.2.0-TODO-23, catalog P3) is the known faster option. statmod::glm.scoretest (1.5.2, 2026-05) is a reference implementation: it computes score z for a matrix of candidate covariates from the null fit alone, and for NB it holds dispersion fixed, which matches the catalog's 'θ held at the reduced-fit value' plan. arXiv 2609.29335 (Sept 2026) also uses one ML refit per step and ranks every candidate against that fit's score vector, but with raw inner products rather than standardized Rao z, so that ranking would be an estimator change. No speedup number at EDI sizes was found. See finding. | [forward stepwise via FWL + Gram–Schmidt] O(np²) total, with O(np) per step for scoring and projection. That matches the cost of QR column-append forward selection. Fast QR-updating work (arXiv 2412.05905v3, revised 2026-03) and Woodbury-update stepwise (arXiv 1706.03265) do not beat O(np) per step when every candidate must be scored. The Gram/sweep alternative was already rejected for squaring the condition number. | [forward stepwise via Rao score tests] This is the standard fast scheme, the same as SAS PROC LOGISTIC score-chi-square entry and statmod::glm.scoretest: one warm-started reduced fit plus Rao z for every candidate. The only remaining options are constant-factor ones such as BLAS-3 batching of the X_S'W X_unused cross-products.

irls.note: [Newton–Raphson (IRLS)] fastglm 0.1.4 (CRAN, 2026-11-11) runs the same IRLS with Marschner step-halving. Its Cholesky path is the same per-iteration cost as EDI's C++ LDLT IRLS, so it is no faster than what EDI already has; its value is the step-halving pattern already in TODO-2. KK21 univariate logistic (2×2 IRLS, design-time only, O(p·iter·n)) is not a hot path. A logit(ȳ) start or a closed-form log-OR for two-valued columns would save only an iteration or two. | [quasi-binomial IRLS + grid search on log φ] Hot path (one fit per KK21 candidate covariate, per arrival). The only faster option known is Brent or safeguarded Newton on the 1-D log φ profile, using the digamma score and the trigamma curvature that betareg already uses: about 19 → 5–8 loglik-equivalents. It is already recorded in catalog P4 and tracked as a Prototype (v1.0.5 TODO 4), so it is not re-reported. betareg NEWS (https://cran.r-project.org/web/packages/betareg/news/news.html) adds no new faster φ method, only the Ferrari–Cribari-Neto start and a Fisher-scoring polish. Switching the mean model to the full beta MLE is an estimator change and is slower.
labels: quasi-binomial IRLS + grid search on log φ

newton-raphson.note: [Newton–Raphson (Weibull AFT MLE)] fast_weibull_regression / KK21 reduced fit / univariate_weibull_tstat use damped Newton on the analytic Hessian with an L-BFGS fallback, at p ≤ ~10. Newton is already the fastest-converging option. The BRT warm-start and Newton-default item was already reported by batch A.1 (2026-11-16). The Burridge reparametrization is already in the catalog (§ Weibull options) and changes robustness, not speed. survival 3.7-3 fixed survreg's step-halving NaN check, which is irrelevant to EDI's own kernel.

univariate-screening-fits.note: [independent univariate GLM fits] KK21 non-stepwise weights: p independent 2-parameter fits at tiny m, which is already the minimal structure (O(p·fit)). No closed form exists for univariate beta/NB/Weibull MLEs. The stepwise refit cost is a separate Prototype (catalog P3) that changes the weight values, so it is not a drop-in. | [per-covariate univariate fits + Monte Carlo quantile threshold] The univariate fits are closed-form or a few Newton steps each, O(p·t·iters). The 500-pair MC threshold costs O(500d), already less than an exact all-pairs quantile. Any exact or deterministic pairwise-quantile method, the catalog's own TODO-7 included, changes λ and so the design rule (an estimator change). No search result gives an exact sub-quadratic pairwise-distance quantile in d>1 dimensions. Warm-starting the fits stays the low-priority Prototype already recorded.
labels: per-covariate univariate fits + Monte Carlo quantile threshold

bisection.note: [bisection (test-inversion CI)] pval_invert_ci_cpp is still pure bisection, as of fa2fe36d (brent_ci_inversion.md TODO-1..3 are unimplemented). Brent remains faster, and that is already tracked. What is new: Chandrupatla and ITP, which the catalog's options table never considered. Sources say they match or beat Brent on smooth functions, and Brent's worst case on flat or jumpy functions is several times bisection's. See findings. | [bracketing + bisection test inversion] Same kernel as 'bisection (test-inversion CI)' (lrt_ci_newton.cpp pval_invert_ci_cpp), and the same Chandrupatla/ITP finding applies. The bracket phase (Wald seed, then doubling) is already cheap: 1–2 evaluations when the Wald seed brackets. | [generic test inversion on Gaussian refits] Nothing beyond what the audit already adopted. With σ² fixed at the full-fit value, LR = score = gradient = (β̂−δ)²/(σ̂²[(X'X)⁻¹]_jj), so the bounds are closed form and the LR null law is exactly F(1, n−p) (v1.0.5 TODO-16 → v1.1.0-TODO-50). At fa2fe36d the code still does generic per-δ lm.fit refits (inference_continuous_lin.R:460, KK_ols_one_lik.R:302) plus the param-bootstrap re-simulation, so the adopted fix has not landed. No new candidate.
labels: generic test inversion on Gaussian refits

brent-root.note: [Brent root-finding test inversion] Mislabelled in the inventory. inference_incidence_log_binomial.R:392 calls invert_gradient_ci_uniroot, which calls pval_invert_ci_cpp (inference_ext_ci_inversion.R:150-195). That is pure bisection, not uniroot or Brent. 'Keep (already Brent)' is therefore wrong, and this path belongs under the brent_ci_inversion.md plan. | [Brent's method (uniroot)] invert_ci_to_find_two_sided_pval_for_treatment_effect runs uniroot over α on a closed-form z/t CI (log-rank). The inventory already records the closed form 2Φ(−|z|) / 2·pt(−|t|,df), which needs zero root-finding. The cost (~10–15 O(1) CI evaluations) is negligible. Chandrupatla's gain over Brent on smooth functions is about 0–2 evaluations, so it is not worth it.

safeguarded-newton-root.note: [Newton–Raphson with bisection safeguard] Newer endpoint methods do not beat it at EDI's sizes. Fischer & Lewis 2021 (RVM, a trust-region Venzon–Moolgavkar) needed about 3× the likelihood evaluations of the fastest method on an 11-parameter logistic benchmark, and its authors say it may not win on well-behaved likelihoods; its gain is robustness. CICO (LikelihoodProfiler) uses hundreds of likelihood calls per bound. Newton on the signed root (v1.0.5 audit TODO 4) remains the cataloged improvement. | [safeguarded Newton test inversion] Same kernel as lrt_ci_nr_cpp / eval_lrt. RVM and CICO are not faster for smooth, small-p GLM-type likelihoods. findings.label: bisection (test-inversion CI)
findings.candidate: Chandrupatla's hybrid quadratic/bisection method (Chandrupatla 1997, Adv. Eng. Softw. 28:145–149; used by SciPy's elementwise find_root). Alternative: ITP (Oliveira & Takahashi 2021, ACM TOMS 47(1)) with n0=0 or 1, which guarantees no more than n0 evaluations beyond bisection's count. Use either in place of textbook Brent when implementing brent_ci_inversion.md TODO-2.
findings.claimed_speedup: From the evaluation-count table at https://degenerateconic.com/root-finding.html (15 test functions, tol 1e-15): bisection 574 total, Brent 260, ITP 303, Chandrupatla 178. Brent is worse than bisection on flat or near-multiple roots: x³ 40 vs 17, sin((x−7.14)³) 46 vs 18. Chandrupatla is never much worse than bisection: 17 and 18 on those two. The CRAN itp vignette has uniroot (Brent) at 65 iterations against itp's 35–36 on a repeated root, with parity elsewhere. Neither source benchmarks EDI's p(δ). The tie-in to EDI (the jump guard for isolated low-p null refits, and flat p near a ridge fallback) is my inference.
findings.suggested_action: Before implementing brent_ci_inversion.md TODO-2, re-look at the method choice: add Chandrupatla and ITP to the catalog's row-M options table, and consider Chandrupatla (or ITP with n0=1) as the Phase-2 solver. Keep bisection as the fallback. Add an evaluation-count test that includes a flat-near-root p(δ), to check that the new solver never needs many more evaluations than bisection.

closed-form.note: [Terrell gradient statistic (closed form)] Code (_helper_functions.h gradient_test_from_restricted_score) is O(1): score[idx]*(estimate-null) plus pchisq; no Schur complement or inverse. The inventory 'details'/'complexity O(p^3)' text was copied from the score-test row and should be corrected; nothing faster exists. | [closed-form score / LR / gradient statistics] These are closed forms computed from one null fit. The only cost is the p×p efficient-information step in score_test_from_score_information (_helper_functions.h:153), which forms covariance_from_information(I_nn) and then multiplies. A Cholesky solve would use about 3x fewer flops at p³, but p is in the tens and this runs once per test, not per replicate. That is a micro-choice already covered by performance_profiling_and_upgrades.md TODO-155. No faster algorithm exists for the statistic itself. | [likelihood-ratio test (closed form)] The LR statistic is a closed form 2*(nll0 - nll1) plus one chi-square tail, O(1); nothing is faster. The related Rao score test forms a full covariance_from_information(I_nn) and then a matrix-vector product, where one LDLT solve would be enough. irls.note: [Newton–Raphson (IRLS) + sandwich / dispersion variance] Parametric-bootstrap refits already warm-start β and Fisher info (get_fit_warm_start_*). The sandwich is O(np²) once per fit. One-step/k-step bootstrap would change the estimator (an approximation), so it is not acceptable as a drop-in.

multistart.note: [two-start constrained refit] Cloglog only: concave cumulative-link likelihood (Pratt 1981 / Burridge 1981, restated in the ordinal clm paper) stays concave when beta_T is fixed, so the second start is redundant whenever the first converges with a gradient-norm certificate; conditional second start halves null-refit cost. Stereotype (nonconcave) keeps multistart; no change there.

newton-raphson.note: [constrained Newton refits (score / LR tests)] The constrained refits already use C++ Newton with fixed_idx and are warm-started (get_backend_warm_start_args / start=), and Newton is optimal for a concave Poisson likelihood. The alternatives found are a bootstrap-calibrated Bartlett correction (spaMM/pbkrtest) and the modified approximate quasi-LR of Noma et al. 2025. Both change the test, so they are estimator changes, not speedups.

parametric-bootstrap.note: [Monte Carlo Bartlett correction] The literature I found (Rocke 1989, via arXiv 1501.07551; Birnbaum–Saunders and beta-regression studies) supports a mean-of-LR bootstrap factor at B ≈ 100. Nothing newer offers a cheaper estimator of E[LR|H0] that keeps the per-δ estimator. The audit's options (one factor per CI, analytic Cordeiro-type factors; v1.0.5 TODO-3) still cover the space.

ridge-regularization.note: [escalating ridge regularization] Up to 8 solves of a (p−1)×(p−1) nuisance block in R, called once per score test; the cost is trivial next to the model fits. One eigendecomposition reused across all ridge levels would save at most 7 small solves, a win that is not material at EDI's p. I found no source for a faster method with the same answer. Its calibration is the open question, and that is not a speed issue.

schur-complement.note: [Rao score test via Schur complement] Efficient information I_tt − I_tn I_nn⁻¹ I_nt equals 1/[I⁻¹]_tt, so it can be one LDLT solve instead of covariance_from_information(I_nn) followed by a matvec. That is the constant-factor change already noted on the inventory row (TODO-155). It is O(p³) at small p and the same statistic, with no new algorithm.

findings.label: two-start constrained refit
findings.candidate: Single refit with a certified convergence check (max |gradient| below tolerance, as clm's Newton uses gradTol), running the second start only when the first fails the certificate. Justified because the basic cumulative-link log-likelihood is concave with a unique global optimum (Pratt 1981; Burridge 1981), and fixing beta_T restricts it to an affine subspace, which preserves concavity.

power-series.note: [truncated atanh series] fast_log1pexp / log1pexp_array_fast cost one exp, one division and a 10-term Horner on s=z/(2+z), with s in (0,1/3]. The exp dominates. The alternatives are exact SIMD exp+log1p (e.g. Highway, Arm optimized-routines, 2-2.5 ULP), which adds a second transcendental call, or the exact Goldberg path, which the catalog already lists as ~1.5-2x slower. Neither is faster. A minimax polynomial in s² (the fdlibm e_log.c construction) could reach the same 5e-12 error with fewer terms, or near-ulp with the same 10 terms. That gains accuracy at the same cost, with at most a few FMAs saved. It is already listed in catalog P11 as 'cite needed' and is reported below only to supply that citation.

rational-approximation.note: [rational minimax approximation] fast_atan is Cephes range reduction plus a 5/5 rational minimax at about 1 ulp, O(1). It is the standard libm-quality construction. No faster method at the same accuracy turned up, and it sits only in the cauchit CDF.

stable-branch-evaluation.note: [piecewise log1p/expm1 evaluation] O(1) closed form; nothing faster. The current code (fast_hurdle_poisson_glmm.cpp:76-80) still uses log1p(-e^{-λ}) for all λ ≥ 1e-10, which loses relative precision for small λ. The Mächler log1mexp switch, log(-expm1(-λ)) for λ<ln2, costs the same and is already recorded as an incidental accuracy fix. Not a speed issue. | [branch-split stable evaluation] plogis and softplus in branch-split form cost one exp plus a divide or log1p per element: closed form, O(1) per element, nothing faster that is exact. The approximate atanh-series variant (fast_log1pexp) is already catalogued (P11). | [Goldberg log1p correction] Eigen 3.4.0's generic_plog1p is the same Kahan/Goldberg formula, and in 3.4.0 it is specialized only for Packet8f (float), so EDI's double-precision fast_log1p_arr is still needed. Eigen master adds EIGEN_DOUBLE_PACKET_FUNCTION(log1p, Packet4d), but that is the same algorithm (no speedup), and CRAN RcppEigen (0.3.4.0.2, 2024-08-24) has not moved to it. A later option is to replace the helper with .log1p() once RcppEigen bundles Eigen 5; that would simplify the code, not speed it up.

findings.label: truncated atanh series
findings.candidate: Minimax (Remez/fpminimax) polynomial in s² over [0,1/9], the same construction fdlibm uses for log: s=f/(2+f) with a degree-14 even polynomial (Lg1..Lg7, i.e. 7 coefficients) whose error is bounded by 2^-58.45 on s in [0,0.1716]. The same evaluation scheme as the current Horner, with fitted coefficients in place of the 1/(2k+1) Taylor ones.
findings.claimed_speedup: Not quantified by the source. At equal accuracy it would save a few FMAs per element (fewer terms); at an equal number of terms it gives much smaller error than the Taylor truncation. The exp call dominates the cost either way, so the speed gain is marginal. This is mainly an accuracy-at-equal-cost option.
findings.suggested_action: Fill the '[cite needed]' in catalog P11 with fdlibm e_log.c. Optionally refit the 10 Horner coefficients as a minimax polynomial on s² in [0,1/9] to bring fast_log1pexp close to ulp accuracy at the same cost. No speed-driven change is warranted.

An affine-invariant Newton-decrement test (gᵀH⁻¹g via one LDLT, as row AA kernels already do) would be slightly cheaper (p³/3 vs ~4p³/3 flops). But it changes which stalled fits are flagged as converged, so it is a policy change, not a speedup. I fetched no readable source for it this run, so I am not reporting it as a finding. | [column location/scale heuristic] One O(np) pass per column, about the cost of reading X once, and it runs once per fit. Nothing faster is possible. The separate 0/1 scan could be fused into the mean pass, but that is a negligible constant factor. | [Newton decrement check (LDLT)] A one-off post-fit certificate: one gradient, one Hessian and an O(p³/3) LDLT, run only when covariates look badly scaled. It is the standard affine-invariant stopping criterion (Boyd & Vandenberghe). Cost is negligible next to the fit, and a cheaper non-invariant check would lose the scale invariance that is the reason for the check. | [gradient-norm acceptance threshold] An O(1) threshold heuristic; there is nothing to speed up. | [limit-score boundary certification] Costs 3 objective/score evaluations and runs only on the boundary path. bisection.note: [bisection (Monte Carlo test inversion)] Glazer & Stark (arXiv 2405.05238 v3, Feb 2025; R package permutest, GPL>=3) prove that inverting one fixed Monte Carlo sample (common random numbers) with a conservative p-value gives conservative coverage. They also find it faster than Garthwaite's Robbins–Monro at n=30, N=6000 (Findings 1 and 2). The Zhang quantile CI still draws fresh sign flips for every δ. Zhang (arXiv 2602.20498, 2026) does not apply: it targets the risk-difference ATE, while EDI's Zhang-incidence path uses log-OR Fisher/binomial tests. | [bracketing + bisection (Monte Carlo test inversion)] Two leads. (1) Glazer–Stark evidence against prototyping Garthwaite–Buckland as a faster driver (Finding 1). (2) Xu (arXiv 2512.14024, Dec 2025) finds exact breakpoints for statistics that are rational in the parameter. That could extend the closed-form path to the studentized and symmetric-percentile-t BRT types on affine classes, which currently fall back to bisection (Finding 3). | [confirm pass + bisection refinement] It only corrects SMC early-stopping noise at the final bound: 2 full-r evaluations, more only on disagreement. The sequential-stopping alternatives (Besag–Clifford, Gandy 2009) are already in the catalog. No newer method found that is cheaper and keeps the decision. | [bisection test inversion] The Zhang exact p(δ) is a minlike sum of dbinom or noncentral-hypergeometric terms (zhang_exact_speedups.cpp:22,41). It is piecewise smooth in δ with jumps, not a step function as the inventory says. ITP with n0=0 is guaranteed never to need more evaluations than bisection and can be superlinear on the smooth pieces. The gain is small because each evaluation costs only O(d+S). Low priority.

breakpoint-inversion.note: [closed-form breakpoint inversion (affine statistics)] Xu 2025 (Algorithm 2) uses the same breakpoint computation, sorted by an O(M log M) sweep. This is the sweep the inventory already calls irrelevant at B ≤ low thousands. Nothing faster for the same exact answer.

brent-root.note: [candidate scan + golden-section/Brent maximisation of p(delta)] Three candidate evaluations cover the usual case. stats::optimize (golden section + parabolic) runs only when no candidate has p > α, and costs ~20–30 O(d+S) evaluations. No derivative-free 1-D maximiser is materially faster on a piecewise-smooth p(δ) with jumps. The real risk is a local rather than global maximiser on a non-unimodal minlike p, which is a correctness issue, not speed.
labels: candidate scan + golden-section/Brent maximisation of p(delta)

exponential-bracketing.note: [exponential bracketing (doubling)] Glazer–Stark 2025 use the same Wald-seeded doubling bracket. It costs a few evaluations (≤7 doublings) and is not the bottleneck. Nothing faster found.

findings.label: bracketing + bisection (Monte Carlo test inversion)
findings.candidate: Keep the fixed-sample (CRN) bisection, made conservative as in Glazer & Stark: p = (1+#{T≥t})/(1+N), endpoint returned on the rejecting side. This argues against prioritizing the Garthwaite–Buckland driver; it is not a new algorithm to adopt.
findings.claimed_speedup: Glazer & Stark, lizard data (n=30, N=6000), 100 runs: the new method took 0.33 s versus 0.47 s for Garthwaite's algorithm (≈1.4× in favour of fixed-sample bisection). Garthwaite's interval was approximate, [−0.29, 11.0]; the new one was conservative, [−0.20, 10.875]. Caveat: their per-δ evaluation used the mean-difference shift shortcut. For non-affine statistics, each bisection step costs N refits while each RM step costs one, so the comparison has not been measured there.
findings.suggested_action: Re-check the premise of garthwaite_buckland_ci_search.md (v1.2.0-TODO-21) against Glazer & Stark 2025. Either narrow its scope to non-affine, refit-heavy statistics (e.g. the parametric-bootstrap LR) or downgrade it. Record that Robbins–Monro gives up conservativeness and start-independence.

findings.label: bisection (Monte Carlo test inversion)
findings.candidate: Glazer–Stark fixed-sample inversion. Draw one sign-flip and permutation matrix per CI search and reuse it for every δ, with the conservative p = (1+#)/(1+N). Their Theorem 1 then gives coverage ≥ 1−α, and bisection runs on a deterministic function. The catalog's TODO-6a (common random numbers) is the same idea; this adds a published validity proof and a GPL-3 reference implementation.
findings.claimed_speedup: Not quantified for quantile regression. The evaluation count per bound stays about the same, but bisecting a noisy p(δ) to a width of 1e-6 spends many of the ~2×nsim_rand-rq-fit evaluations resolving Monte Carlo noise. On a fixed sample, those evaluations converge to a single breakpoint and can stop once the bracket holds one jump.
findings.suggested_action: Use Glazer & Stark 2025 as the supporting reference when prototyping catalog TODO-6a (common random numbers for the Zhang quantile CI). Also fix the inventory row's stale stopping-rule text (the code now uses a 1e-6 width and 100 iterations).

findings.label: bracketing + bisection (Monte Carlo test inversion)
findings.candidate: Xu (Dec 2025) inverts exactly with rational-function statistics. Each studentized draw is a ratio of an affine numerator to a null-dependent SE, so it is a rational (square-root-of-quadratic) function of δ. Crossings with the observed pivot are roots of a low-degree polynomial per draw. Sorting and sweeping them gives the exact step-function p-value curve, with no bisection.
findings.claimed_speedup: Xu claims 'an order of magnitude' over grid search, not measured; the paper reports no timings of its own. Cost would be O(B·n·p²) for the per-draw coefficients plus O(B log B) for the sweep, against 10–20 evaluations × B refits now.
findings.suggested_action: Re-look: check whether the studentized BRT pivots on OLS, mean-diff and Lin are rational in δ. If they are, consider extending closed_form_ci_from_affine_null_draws to rational breakpoints (Xu 2025, Algorithm 2) as a Prototype.

findings.label: bisection test inversion
findings.candidate: ITP with n0=0 (Oliveira & Takahashi 2021). It is guaranteed to need no more evaluations than bisection, and it is superlinear when the α-crossing lies inside a smooth piece. If the crossing is at a jump, it converges to the jump just as bisection does.
findings.claimed_speedup: Not quantified for this problem. The itp vignette has the Staircase discontinuous function at parity with uniroot (31 vs 31) and smooth examples at about 8 iterations, at tol 1e-10. Expected roughly 20 → 8–10 evaluations per bound when the crossing is smooth, and never worse than bisection.
findings.suggested_action: Correct the 'step function' rationale in the inventory and in catalog §6/§11 to 'piecewise smooth with jumps'. Optionally record ITP (n0=0) in the options table as a no-worse-than-bisection option, with the non-monotone-p caveat. Keep bisection unless a test grid shows identical bounds.

truncated-series-summation.note: [truncated series summation] expected_trigamma_y_plus_theta already does what the newest method in the literature does: one trigamma at θ, then the recurrence ψ₁(x+1)=ψ₁(x)−1/x² and the recursive NB pmf, at O(1) per term. That newest method is the trigamma-free tail-sum series E[ψ₁(ν+Y)]=ψ₁(ν)−Σ P(Y>y)/(ν+y)² from Yu, Dousti Mousavi & Yang (Statistical Papers 2024, arXiv:2306.04798). It is an equivalent reordering of the same sum with the same O(M) term count. Its Table 2 shows only ±25% timing differences against GFWL, and it never compares against a pmf sum that uses a recurrence. Its Theorem 2 bound, P(Y>M+1)/(ν+M), could serve as a stopping rule in place of the ad hoc μ+10·sd rule, but that is not a speedup. No O(1) exact method exists, and asymptotic expansions would change the estimator. The code is also unreachable from R: get_negbin_regression_expected_hessian_cpp has no R caller.

blossom-matching.note: [Derigs weighted non-bipartite matching] compute_binary_match_structure runs once per design build at n in the tens to low hundreds, where nbpMatching::nonbimatch (O(n^3) Derigs/Edmonds, GPL>=2, v1.5.6 2024-09-25 per https://cran.r-project.org/package=nbpMatching) takes under a second. Candidates checked: (1) Blossom VI (Arkhipov & Kolmogorov, arXiv 2604.20351 v2 Jul 2026, GPL-3, C++20, integer weights). Its benchmarks start at about 14k nodes and 10M edges, and on its smallest reported instance (TSP, 105k nodes) it is slower than Blossom V (0.23 s vs 0.20 s, https://arxiv.org/html/2604.20351v2). Nothing shows a gain at EDI's sizes, and it would add a C++20 and Boost dependency. (2) Blossom V is licensed for research only, so it is not GPL-compatible (https://pub.ista.ac.at/~vnk/software.html). (3) LEMON MaxWeightedPerfectMatching runs in O(nm log n), which on EDI's complete graph (m ~ n^2/2) is O(n^3 log n), no better than O(n^3) (https://lemon.cs.elte.hu/pub/doc/1.2.3/a00221.html). (4) The geometric/Euclidean O(n log n) algorithms (Hougardy & Tammemaa, https://arxiv.org/abs/2407.07749) are approximate, so they would change the pairs: an estimator/design change, not a speedup. The exact geometric route (Vaidya) was already noted and deferred by the audit. Also, an equally optimal solver can break ties differently, which changes the design's pairs; that is a further reason not to swap at these sizes. The p=1 sort-and-pair path is O(n log n) and optimal, so nothing is faster there. | [minimum-weight perfect matching (blossom)] compute_halves matches pairs of pairs on m = n/2 pair averages with nbpMatching::nonbimatch, once, and caches the result. It is not in the resampling loop: compute_bai_distr_parallel_cpp reuses the cached halves. With m in the tens, O(m^3) is negligible. The candidates are the same as for the Derigs entry: Blossom VI benchmarks only at 14k+ nodes (https://arxiv.org/html/2604.20351v2), Blossom V is research-only (https://pub.ista.ac.at/~vnk/software.html), LEMON is O(nm log n) (https://lemon.cs.elte.hu/pub/doc/1.2.3/a00221.html), and the Euclidean approximation algorithms change the matching, which would change the Bai–Romano–Shaikh variance estimate (https://arxiv.org/abs/2407.07749). Keep.

nonparametric-bootstrap.note: [nonparametric bootstrap] For the same interval and the same distribution, no faster method was found. Plain i.i.d. multinomial resampling plus B refits warm-started at the full-data MLE is the standard. Balanced resampling (v1.2.0-TODO-23 / audit TODO-4) remains the tracked Monte Carlo variance reduction, and no new evidence changes it. Two cheaper alternatives exist, but both change the estimator, so they could only be opt-in: the cheap bootstrap (B≈1–10) and the k-step bootstrap. See findings. | [nonparametric bootstrap (studentized)] No faster method gives the same (θ*, se*) pairs; each replicate needs its fit and its SE. The cost here comes from the implementation (serial loop, R6 duplicate per replicate, no seed: I7), not the algorithm. The k-step bootstrap (Andrews 2002) covers t-intervals and is higher-order equivalent, but it is an estimator change; see the k-step finding. | [KK compound bootstrap] The C++ kernel does one O(n) pass per replicate (IVW combination of the pair and reservoir means), which is optimal. The O(B·m·n) R index build is an implementation fix (I9: precompute the split once), not an algorithm choice. Balanced resampling is already tracked under TODO-4.

rejection-sampling.note: [nonparametric bootstrap (rejection resampling)] O(B·n) R loop, and effectively unreachable: the only caller returns NULL for KK (I10). Not worth optimizing; nothing faster is needed. | [nonparametric bootstrap with rejection] The cost is B × attempts × a C++ refit. Rejecting unusable resamples is a statistical choice: any scheme that avoided rejection (conditional or smoothed resampling) changes the bootstrap distribution, so it is an estimator change. Balanced resampling is already tracked under audit J. Nothing new found.

ridit-scoring.note: [bootstrap (per-draw ridit rebuild)] Each replicate gathers and rebuilds the ridit map in O(n log n). The O(n+L) counting/level-slot rebuild is already tracked as `ridit_kernel_level_slots.md` TODO-3 (v1.4.0 plan). It gives the same answer and is the only faster option; nothing beyond it was found.

value-space-bisection-selection.note: [bootstrap (per-draw HL selection)] hl_from_groups materializes and runs nth_element up to 4096 pairs, otherwise sorts and does value bisection. The catalog already covers the alternatives: Monahan rank-space selection, Johnson–Mizoguchi/Frederickson–Johnson, the tie-safe early stop (`wilcox_hl_kernel_hoisting.md` TODO-3 and TODO-4) and the presort hoist (blocked by noise), and balanced indices are audit J. No new evidence overturns those decisions. The plain HL bootstrap kernel is dead code.

findings.label: nonparametric bootstrap
findings.candidate: The cheap bootstrap (Lam 2022): ψ̂ ± t_{B,1−α/2}·S with S² = (1/B)Σ(ψ*_b − ψ̂)². It gives asymptotically exact coverage with B as small as 1 and is typically used at B ≈ 5–10. It would be offered as a new opt-in CI type for expensive refits (GLMM, survival, ordinal).
findings.claimed_speedup: Refits drop from 501 to about 10 (~50x fewer); this is arithmetic, not a measured benchmark. Coverage comes from the ar5iv HTML of arXiv 2202.00090 (0.6-quantile of Exp(1), n = 100, 95% nominal, 1,000 reps): coverage 0.92 at B = 5 and B = 10 with mean widths 0.63 and 0.53, against percentile-bootstrap coverage 0.69 and 0.80 at the same B. At B = 50 the cheap interval has width 0.50 and coverage 0.94.
findings.suggested_action: Consider adding an opt-in cheap-bootstrap CI type (B ≈ 10) for classes whose per-replicate refit is expensive. Document it as a distinct interval and validate its coverage against the B = 501 percentile and BCa intervals in the A/B harness.

findings.label: nonparametric bootstrap (studentized)
findings.candidate: The k-step bootstrap (Davidson & MacKinnon 1999; Andrews 2002, Econometrica 70:119–162): a fixed small number k of Newton (or line-search Newton) steps from the full-data estimate in each replicate. Andrews proves it is higher-order equivalent to the standard bootstrap for t-CIs (symmetric, equal-tailed, one-sided) and Wald tests, under the iid and block bootstraps. Batch A.1 raised this only for the Weibull kernel; this finding generalizes it to the shared bootstrap loop for smooth likelihood classes.
findings.claimed_speedup: Not quantified in the abstract; Andrews calls it 'a very attractive alternative computationally'. Because EDI already warm-starts at the MLE, the gain is only the iterations beyond k plus convergence checks. It is likely modest (≈1–3x) for Newton/IRLS families and larger for L-BFGS families, but not quantified.
findings.suggested_action: Measure how many iterations warm-started bootstrap refits actually take on representative fixtures. If it is well above 2–3 for some families, consider an opt-in k-step mode (k = 2–3 Newton steps) for studentized/t-based bootstrap CIs in smooth GLM-type classes, validated in the A/B harness. Otherwise record it as no gain at EDI's warm-start setup.

erfc-normal-cdf.note: [erfc-based normal CDF (clamped tails)] Not a speedup over the current clamped code. It is an implementation option for the already-adopted tail fix (v1.0.5-TODO-22 / catalog TODO 2): Johnson's MIT-licensed Faddeeva erfcx gives the tail at near-machine precision, where the planned 4-term asymptotic series is only ~1e-9 relative at x=-8. See the finding.

rational-approximation.note: [Cephes rational approximation] Scalar Cephes erfc is about 1e-15 abs at O(1) cost. SLEEF (Boost license) has vectorized erfc at 1.5 ULP (Sleef_erfcd4_u15, sleef.org/x86.xhtml), but the SLEEF paper benchmarks only trig, exp, log and pow, not erfc. EDI's call sites are scalar per-observation likelihood loops, so a win at EDI's sizes is not shown. Keep. | [Acklam rational approximation] Used only for optimizer warm starts and one Wilson z per CI. Exact AS241 for the Wilson CI is already adopted (TODO 7). Newer fast quantiles are either GPU-oriented and not benchmarked against AS241 (Shaw & Luu, arXiv 0901.0638) or low-precision (Voutier, ~1e-4). Nothing beats Acklam+AS241 for this job. | [Wichura AS 241 rational approximation] qnorm_std must match R's qnorm.c bit for bit, because RRng::norm_rand reproduces R's Inversion normal generator. Any other algorithm would break seed parity with R. Faster options I checked: Voutier (arXiv 1002.0567) has absolute error around 2.5e-5, which is far less accurate. Shaw & Luu (arxiv.org/abs/0901.0638) report a 2x speedup on GPUs against CUDA's function, not on CPUs, and do not claim full tail accuracy. R's NEWS (cran.r-project.org/doc/manuals/r-release/NEWS.html, read through about R 4.4) shows no qnorm change for non-log p. It is O(1) per call and not a bottleneck.

findings.label: erfc-based normal CDF (clamped tails)
findings.candidate: Use the scaled complementary error function erfcx from S. G. Johnson's Faddeeva package (MIT license). Its method is 100 Chebyshev polynomials on y=4/(4+x) for 0<=x<=50 and a continued fraction beyond 50. Then for x<0: Phi(x) = 0.5*exp(-x^2/2)*erfcx(-x/sqrt2), and log Phi(x) = -x^2/2 + log(0.5*erfcx(-x/sqrt2)). That gives near-machine-precision log Phi over the whole negative tail with no branch-boundary jump, and Phi down to underflow.
findings.claimed_speedup: Not quantified. The Faddeeva.cc header comment (Octave doxygen copy) says the erfcx routine 'seems to be substantially faster than either the SLATEC DERFC function' and Cody's CALERF (the basis of R's pnorm), at 'near machine precision'. Against the planned asymptotic series it is expected to cost about the same (one table lookup plus a polynomial), not to be faster.
findings.suggested_action: When implementing v1.0.5-TODO-22, compare a real-argument erfcx tail (Faddeeva erfcx, MIT) against the planned 4-term asymptotic series. Use the TODO's existing gate (grid vs R::pnorm(log.p=TRUE), 1e-12 rel on [-40,40]) and pick whichever passes at equal cost. The series is unlikely to reach 1e-12 at x=-8, so erfcx (or a later switch point for the series) may be needed to meet the gate.
