finite-differences.note: [FD Hessian + LU inversion] Only used for the ZINB vcov once per non-estimate-only fit (fast_zinb.cpp skips the Hessian when estimate_only=TRUE), so it is not in a resampling hot path. An analytic observed-information Hessian exists elsewhere (fastglm 0.1.0 NEWS: fastglm_zi has an 'analytical observed-information vcov'). It would save about 2k gradient evaluations of digamma-heavy work, but nobody has quantified that gain, and both cost O(n k²). The O(k³) LU is negligible at k in the tens. The ZINB optimizer and Hessian question stays tracked under row B. | [central finite differences] Where these are costly (log/identity-binomial score and Hessian, using a 4-point ℓ stencil at O(2np³)), the closed-form X'diag(∂²ℓ)X is already Adopt (v1.0.5 row N, catalog O5), and nothing beats it. The generic numerical_gradient/numerical_hessian take central differences of the analytic gradient, so a Hessian costs only 2p gradient evaluations at p≤~25. AD and complex-step would not be cheaper (the catalog already rejected both). The R Cox FD helpers are dead code, and ordinal g-comp compute_md_gradient calls a cheap O(nK) functional; its cost is negligible. | [central finite differences of gradient] For the ordinal GLMM / _glmm_engine observed information, the analytic Louis identity is already Adopt (v1.0.5-TODO-2), at about 1–2 gradient-equivalents versus 2d. Forward-mode AD costs about d gradient-equivalents and is no cheaper (catalog T5). For ZINB, an analytic Hessian costs about the same at k≈10 (Keep). A 2026 astrophysics paper (arXiv 2604.06318) reports AD Hessians 5–10× faster than FD, but that is against value-only FD with O(N²) evaluations, not FD of an analytic gradient, so it does not carry over. | [central finite-difference Hessian] fast_weibull_frailty runs 2P gradient evaluations (P=p+2) once per fit, which is never a bottleneck. An analytic Hessian, complex-step or forward-over-reverse AD would save at most a constant factor on a one-off step, at high derivation or dependency cost (catalog NEW-fd-hessian). Keep. | [forward finite-difference Hessian] Clayton and dep-cens forward FD of the analytic gradient takes P+1 gradient evaluations, once per fit, which is already the minimum-evaluation FD scheme. An analytic Hessian saves only a constant factor on a one-off step. The dep-cens analytic Hessian is unreachable dead code, deliberately disabled (I-3). Complex-step second derivatives are reported as not clearly more accurate than FD (Lai & Crassidis, via search). Keep.

cholesky-ldlt.note: [normal equations (LDLT)] fast_ols.cpp. Eigen's DenseDecompositionBenchmark (https://eigen.googlesource.com/mirror/+/03f646b7e352a68f26fff252615bedb4a2b359aa/doc/DenseDecompositionBenchmark.dox) puts LLT/LDLT on normal equations, with AᵀA formation counted, about 5x faster than HouseholderQR at 10000x8 and 4.3x at 10000x100. It is the fastest dense option at EDI's tall, small-p shapes. LLT is about the same speed. The known weaknesses (κ² conditioning, LDLT not flagging rank deficiency, SSE cancellation) are accuracy issues already recorded in catalog §1 O10 and Incidentals 6–7. They are not a speed gap.

qr-decomposition.note: [OLS (lm.fit / lm.wfit) + HC2] KK_ols_one_lik: R lm.fit/lm.wfit (Householder QR) followed by a C++ HC2 post-fit, which costs O(np²), the same order as the fit. Leverages need X(XᵀX)⁻¹Xᵀ diagonals, as the fixest vignette notes for HC2/HC3. No cheaper exact method was found. The real cost here is R overhead per draw, which is already tracked as catalog §10 TODO candidate 9 (C++ batch randomization kernel). That is not an algorithm-choice issue. | [OLS via QR] inference_continuous_ols.R. The R side delegates to fast_ols_cpp (normal equations + LDLT), and QR is only the hardened column-drop fallback. The fast path already uses the fastest method (Eigen benchmark: QR is about 4–5x slower at tall, small-p shapes). The QR fallback is a rank-handling choice and should stay. | [Householder QR (lm.fit) + HC2] A single Lin fit is O(np²) in compiled LINPACK QR, followed by the C++ HC2 post-fit. The fastglm benchmark vignette shows LLT-Cholesky about 2× faster than pivoted QR at n=1e3, p=30 (logistic: 0.67 vs 1.26 ms), but per fit that is sub-millisecond and costs accuracy on ill-conditioned X. The real cost is the per-draw R loop, which is already a Prototype item (C++ batch kernel, catalog §10).

brute-force-distance.note: [direct pairwise distance matrix] It is used only by method='ompr' (solve_optimal_blocks), where the MILP has n²B binary z variables and dwarfs the O(n²p) distance build. The GEMM trick (||x||²+||y||²−2x·y) loses accuracy through cancellation and makes results depend on BLAS threading. The Mahalanobis explicit-inverse issue is already tracked in row U (v1.0.5 TODO-29). | [brute-force pairwise distance matrix] The output is n² (or m²), so the brute-force O(n²p) loop is order-optimal. The only faster variant is the GEMM/Gram expansion, which the catalog already rejects for catastrophic cancellation on near-duplicates. scikit-learn's docs (fetched) still describe that cancellation and the loss of exact symmetry for the dot-product form, so there is no new evidence to overturn the rejection. The column-major stride is an implementation detail (incidental 9). The Mahalanobis whitening item is already v1.0.5 TODO-29. | [brute-force pairwise distance matrix (R callback)] A black-box R function inherently needs O(n²) calls. However, EDI already has cppXPtr plumbing for other user functions (helper_user_compiled_fn.R), and the parallelDist package (CRAN, GPL ≥2) shows a compiled-pointer custom distance pattern. Accepting an XPtr distance would remove the per-pair R-call overhead. Low priority, because the matrix is cached per design and the ompr MILP dominates.

gauss-jordan-elimination.note: [Gauss–Jordan elimination (partial pivoting)] The faster option, Cholesky/LLT of (S + ridge) followed by whitening Z = X·L⁻ᵀ, is already adopted (catalog §8 TODO-1, folded into v1.0.5 TODO-29). The Eigen decomposition table (fetched) rates LLT 'very fast' and LU 'fast', which agrees. I found nothing new beyond that existing Adopt verdict. | [sample covariance + Gauss–Jordan inverse] Replacing the hand-rolled Gauss–Jordan with LLT is already Adopt (subsumed by catalog §8 TODO-1 / v1.0.5 TODO-29). The Eigen benchmark puts LLT at about 1.5x PartialPivLU and 1.9x FullPivLU at 8x8, and LLT also avoids forming the inverse. Since the cost is O(p^3) once per design, end-to-end impact is nil. Confirmation only.

mahalanobis-quadratic-forms.note: [per-pair Mahalanobis quadratic form] Cholesky whitening once, then squared Euclidean distances, brings the kernel from O(n^2 p^2) to O(np^2 + n^2 p). This is already the Adopt verdict (v1.0.5 TODO-29 and catalog §8 TODO-1), and the sources fetched this run confirm it is standard practice. It is reported below only as confirmation; no new option was found. The Gram-matrix BLAS-3 variant was already rejected for cancellation on near-duplicate rows, and I found no new evidence that overturns that.

findings.label: brute-force pairwise distance matrix (R callback)
findings.candidate: Also accept a compiled user distance (RcppXPtrUtils::cppXPtr external pointer, routed through EDI's existing normalize_user_cpp_fn plumbing) and call it directly from C++. This is the pattern parallelDist uses for method='custom'. Keep the R-function path as is. Independently, reuse the two xi/xj buffers across pairs instead of allocating per pair.
findings.claimed_speedup: Not quantified for this exact comparison. parallelDist's README (fetched) calls its compiled custom-distance path 'fast' but gives no number against R-level functions. The gain is the removal of per-pair R interpreter call overhead.
findings.suggested_action: Re-look, low priority: consider adding XPtr support for custom optimal-blocks distances, consistent with the other user-compiled-function entry points, and hoist the per-pair NumericVector allocation. Otherwise keep the verdict 'Keep (inherent to a black-box R fn)'.

findings.label: per-pair Mahalanobis quadratic form
findings.candidate: LLT of (S + relative ridge), whiten once with Z = X·L^-T, then a direct per-pair squared-Euclidean loop on Z (not the Gram expansion): O(np^2 + n^2 p). This is the same option the audit already adopted. The sources fetched this run confirm it is the standard route: skfolio computes squared Mahalanobis distance via Cholesky with a relative ridge escalated on failure, and Eigen ranks LLT fastest among dense decompositions.
findings.claimed_speedup: Not quantified for this kernel by any source. The audit's theoretical estimate is about p× on the pair loop. Eigen's benchmark table at 8x8 gives LLT 0.05 ms against FullPivLU 0.1 ms, which affects only the O(p^3) part.
findings.suggested_action: No new action: this confirms the existing Adopt verdict (v1.0.5 TODO-29, catalog §8 TODO-1). When it is implemented, make the ridge relative (scaled by mean(diag S)) as planned.

inverse-transform-sampling.note: [conditional inversion sampling (Clayton copula)] For bivariate Clayton, conditional inversion is closed form and uses d=2 uniforms. Marshall-Olkin needs d+1=3 uniforms plus a gamma frailty draw, so it is not cheaper (copula qrng vignette). The per-pair R loop could be vectorized, but that is an implementation fix, not an algorithm change, and it would change RNG consumption order. | [inverse-CDF categorical sampling] Each observation has its own probability vector (eta_i differs), so the alias method's O(K) table setup has to be rebuilt per draw and gives no gain over an O(K) inverse-CDF scan when K is small. Sources on alias vs inverse transform agree: alias wins only for static distributions. The per-observation R loop is an implementation issue (vectorise with a cumulative-probability matrix compared to runif(n)), and that cost is minor next to the ordinal refit that follows. | [inverse transform sampling (linear scan)] The code still uses which(cumhaz >= tgt), which is O(nK). Replacing it with findInterval (already Adopt, §12 TODO-7) is the right fix. R's docs (fetched) give O(n log N), close to O(n) for sorted x. cumhaz is non-decreasing, so findInterval(tgt, cumhaz, left.open=TRUE)+1 picks the same index, the same answer. A vectorised runif(length(idx)) returns the same uniforms in the same order as per-subject runif(1), so the RNG stream is kept. Nothing faster than O(n log K) without sorting targets, which is the same order.

parametric-bootstrap.note: [parametric bootstrap] SMC early stopping (TODO-8), memoization (TODO-1) and a fixed critical value (TODO-9) are already tracked. Betting-based anytime-valid MC tests (Fischer & Ramdas) are already tracked under randomization_ci_search_precision.md. New for this driver: the Davidson–MacKinnon k-step bootstrap (Andrews 2002 shows it is higher-order equivalent), which caps the per-replicate refits at k Newton steps from the MLE. It is an estimator change at finite n. | [parametric null simulation] Vectorized r* draws at O(nK) cost, negligible next to the refits. Vectorizing the per-observation ordinal sample.int (one runif against cumulative probabilities) is already listed as incidental I16. Nothing new.

random-variate-generation.note: [R's built-in random variate samplers] Simulation DGP only, O(n) per dataset and not inside resampling loops. Faster samplers (e.g. the ziggurat in dqrng, AGPL-3) would change the stream and break parity with R, for no gain at EDI's sizes.

findings.label: parametric bootstrap
findings.candidate: k-step parametric bootstrap. Each bootstrap sample gets a fixed, small number k of Newton (or Gauss–Newton) steps from the original-sample estimate instead of a full refit. Offer it as an opt-in mode.
findings.claimed_speedup: Not quantified in the sources. The Davidson & MacKinnon (1999) abstract says only that 'very few steps are needed', and fewer for LR tests and for Newton than quasi-Newton. The saving would be the iteration count beyond k per refit, which is modest because replicates are already warm-started.
findings.suggested_action: Re-look: record the k-step bootstrap (Davidson–MacKinnon 1999; Andrews 2002) as an estimator-change option in the catalog §9 J options table. If it is pursued, prototype it as an opt-in for count-family LR bootstraps and measure the iteration counts the warm-started workers actually use first. If they already converge in 2–3 Newton steps, drop the idea.

linear-scan.note: [linear scan for non-constant columns] which_cols_vary in compute_all_subject_data.cpp is an O(tp) early-exit scan that has to read each column at least until it finds the first differing value, so nothing asymptotically faster exists. The real cost in that row is the duplicate ColPivHouseholderQR (pivot pass, then a second QR only for rank), which is already tracked as v1.0.5 TODO-29 'drop the redundant QR' and kk14_incremental_covariance.md TODO-1/2.

qr-decomposition.note: [full rebuild with rank-revealing QR] Row-append QR updating (fastQR qrupdate/rupdate, https://cran.r-project.org/package=fastQR; the Chan RRQR and Stewart URV updating literature) does not fit for two reasons. First, the matrices are re-centred and re-scaled every t, which changes every row. Second, column-pivot (independent-column) decisions must match ColPivHouseholderQR, and fastQR's updates assume full rank and do not pivot. The tracked plan (kk14_incremental_covariance.md: recompute only when the varying set changes; drop the redundant second QR, catalog P8) is already the practical win. Pivoted Cholesky on a running Gram was already rejected because it changes collinearity decisions. | [column-pivoted (rank-revealing) QR] Eigen master's new RandColPivHouseholderQR (BQRRP, Gaussian sketch) lifts the BLAS-2 ceiling only for large matrices. It falls back to unblocked CPQR when min(m,n) < 2·blocksize (auto threshold ~192), and its pivots differ from classical CPQR, so the selected columns could change. HQRRP/BQRRP papers show wins only at n in the thousands. At EDI's t×p (p ≲ 50) there is no gain. The redundant second QR and the varying-set caching are already tracked (v1.0.5 TODO-29, kk14 plan TODO-1/2).

streaming-moments.note: [column z-score standardization] Closed form, two-pass, O(tp); nothing faster per call. That needs fewer repetitions. The source does not quantify the saving.

findings.label: interleaved A/B timing, unpaired median rule
findings.candidate: Analyze the per-round paired differences a_i − b_i, as zenbench does: a Wilcoxon signed-rank p-value plus a 10k-resample bootstrap percentile CI on the differences. Accept only when the CI excludes zero and lies entirely outside a ±noise band (zenbench default 1%; EDI could keep 5%). Stop adaptively once the CI is narrow and stable, with a minimum number of rounds. perfgate-paired uses the same alternate-and-difference design. Use a fixed seed for the bootstrap so results stay deterministic.
findings.claimed_speedup: Not quantified. The zenbench methodology only says paired tests on per-round differences have 'far more power' than unpaired tests. The only number it quotes is Google Benchmark's figure of about 40% variance reduction from random interleaving, which EDI already does.
findings.suggested_action: No verdict change. Use this as the design reference for the paired-difference half of v1.0.5-TODO-12: paired Wilcoxon or bootstrap CI on the differences, a noise-band acceptance rule, and adaptive stopping with a sequential correction.

permuted-blocks.note: [Fisher–Yates shuffle (permuted blocks)] Block templates are small (a few to tens of entries), shuffled once per block. Batched bounded draws (arXiv 2408.06213) would save at most a handful of MT words per block and change the stream. The per-stratum std::map lookup in random_block_size_redraw_w_cpp costs more than the shuffle. Not worth it. | [permuted-block randomization (random block size)] Per-arrival queue pop is O(bs), so the algorithm is optimal. The known problem is correctness (catalog F1/F1b: the generic redraw uses the last subject's stratum, and sample() misbehaves when there is one block size). The fix is already sketched: wire up the existing dead random_block_size_redraw_w_cpp. No new algorithmic evidence. | [stratified permuted-block randomization] generate_permutations_spbr_internal uses dense integer stratum ids, one explicit Fisher–Yates shuffle per new block and pop_back. That is O(n) per draw, which is optimal because every draw must write n assignments, and it is already portable (v1.0.5-TODO-23 closed). The R-level assign_wt is O(1) amortized per arrival. spbr_redraw_w_cpp is dead code. Drawing one arrival at a time with a hypergeometric step would change the seed stream and would not be faster.

pocock-simon.note: [Pocock–Simon minimization] pocock_simon_assign_internal computes G_k for K=2 arms over only the subject's J levels, so each arrival costs O(J). That is the minimum, since the rule has to read every one of the subject's factor levels. Fetched sources describe nothing faster: Wikipedia lists the same per-patient procedure, and carat 2.3.0 (2026-09-08) and Minirand 0.1.3 on CRAN claim no algorithmic speedup. Minor implementation detail (catalog incidental #10): a std::vector is allocated per (arm, covariate) inside the loop. It is not an algorithm choice. | [Pocock–Simon minimization (incremental marginal counts)] Updating the counts in place costs O(sum of the subject's levels) per arrival. That is optimal and keeps the same rule and the same RNG stream. A possible inventory issue: at fa2fe36d, ensure_factor_metadata in design_seq_one_by_one_pocock_simon.R:161 rescans all rows only on the first call (full_scan). After that it registers only row t through match() on the per-column map, so the 'rescans all t rows ... O(n²k)' wording in the inventory details and complexity columns may be out of date (see bug_fix_plans/v1_0_5/pocock_simon_per_arrival_rebuild.md). draw_ws_raw still calls get_subject_levels_idx once per row, an R-side cost (incidental #9), not an algorithm choice. | [Pocock–Simon minimization (sequential simulation)] Exact Monte Carlo null draws, i.e. replaying the sequential rule with flat int counts, cost O(B·n·J). Each draw depends on its whole path, so a draw cannot cost less than one O(nJ) replay, and exact enumeration would mean up to 2^n paths. The only newer speedup found is Kojima, arXiv:2608.05527 (Aug 2026), a Gaussian approximation (SIGA). It replaces the randomization distribution instead of drawing from it, so it changes the test (see the finding). Fast rerandomization methods such as fastrerandomize and Metropolis–Hastings samplers target threshold-based rerandomization, not path-dependent minimization.

pvalue-combination-rules.note: [Cauchy combination test] O(k) closed form, so nothing is faster. The only known improvement is the tail-accurate form: 1/(p·pi) for p<1e-16 and a Cauchy upper-tail for large statistics, as in Liu & Xie's ACAT code (search this run showed the ICSKAT ACAT implementation). That is already Adopt (v1.0.5 TODO-7) and is still unimplemented: inference_suite.R:4062-4063 uses tan/atan directly. | [Fisher / Stouffer / min-p p-value combination] The current combination is O(1) after the two component p-values, so there is no speed gap. The open issue is conservativeness with discrete p's (Investigate). New comparator: DPComb 1.0.1 on CRAN (2026-08-22) and Contador & Wu (SJS 2025). This is an estimator change, reported below as such.

findings.label: Fisher / Stouffer / min-p p-value combination
findings.candidate: Wasserstein-adjusted discrete combination (Contador & Wu 2025, SJS 52(3):1281-1300; arXiv:2508.02647). Each discrete component is replaced by an adjusted statistic, and a continuous null (e.g. an optimal gamma instead of chi^2) is fitted to the combination statistic. Lancaster's mid-p and mean-value chi^2 come out as special cases. It is implemented in DPComb 1.0.1 (CRAN, 2026-08-22, MIT), which explicitly supports binomial and noncentral hypergeometric components, i.e. EDI's exact pair.
findings.claimed_speedup: Not a speedup. Its cost is O(d + S) like the current method, and cheaper than the O(d·S) exact convolution. This is an estimator (test) change: it reduces the conservativeness the Investigate verdict flags. The sources give no runtime numbers.
findings.suggested_action: Add as a third comparator row in catalog §11 (KK combination) when resolving the Investigate verdict. Prefer exact convolution if exactness is required, and treat DPComb/Lancaster mid-p as the cheap less-conservative non-exact option. Possibly use DPComb as a test oracle for a mid-p/Wasserstein variant.

No source found an O(n log n) evaluation of the smoothed Gehan equation; it is O(n²) per pair sum. interior-point-lp.note: [Frisch–Newton interior point / Barrodale–Roberts simplex] No new evidence. At EDI's n, br and fn run at about the same speed (fn 0.02 s at n=500 in CFM 2022, Table 1). That is a correctness issue, not a speed one, and the existing Prototype (one method for both paths) is unchanged. See the preprocessing finding for the BB replicates.

sandwich-estimator.note: [Hendricks–Koenker sandwich (nid)] The quantreg ChangeLog shows no change to the nid/ker/iid SEs since 5.74, which lets nid reuse sfn. The fast new methods (conquer, ppro, pfnb, qfnb) are smoothed or large-n/many-τ methods: they change the estimator or only pay off far above EDI's n ≤ low thousands. The two extra rq fits at τ±h are inherent to nid. 'ker' (Powell) is a different estimator.

findings.label: Frisch–Newton interior point / Barrodale–Roberts simplex
findings.candidate: Preprocessing bootstrap (Chernozhukov, Fernández-Val & Melly 2022, Algorithm 4), extending Portnoy–Koenker 1997. Use the full-sample β̂(τ) to predict residual signs in each replicate, solve the reduced LP on the M = m·(kn)^{1/2} uncertain observations plus two glob observations, verify the signs and repair any that are wrong. The result is the exact LP solution.
findings.claimed_speedup: ar5iv 1909.05782, bootstrap panel (median regression, k=20, 50 replications): Stata bsqreg simplex 2.63 s vs preprocessing 0.42 s at n=500 (~6×), 3.14 vs 0.63 s at n=1,000 (~5×), 8.19 vs 1.89 s at n=5,000 (~4×). For a single fit with k=8, preprocessing gives no gain at n=500 (fn 0.02 s vs pfn 0.04 s) and pays off only from about n=5,000.
findings.suggested_action: Re-look only if profiling shows replicate QR fits dominate at n ≳ 1,000 after the rq.fit Adopt lands. Otherwise record it in the catalog's options table as considered: exact, but no evidence of a gain at EDI's small p and n.

inverse-transform-sampling.note: [inverse transform sampling (AS 241)] Bit-for-bit parity with R's 'Inversion' norm_rand is the binding constraint. Ziggurat or Box–Muller are faster but give a different stream, and no hot loop calls norm_rand. Closed form, O(1), keep.

lemire-bounded-integer.note: [Lemire nearly-divisionless bounded integer] Single draws are already optimal. Batched ranged generation (Brackett-Rozinsky & Lemire 2024) packs several bounded draws into one generator word and could cut MT words per Fisher-Yates shuffle. It changes the seed→output stream, and its benefit is unmeasured with MT at EDI sizes. See finding.

mersenne-twister.note: [Mersenne Twister MT19937] SFMT (~2x per Wikipedia), xoshiro, PCG and Philox are all faster, but each breaks bit-identity with R's MT stream. The catalog's P1 table already considered and rejected them. Nothing newer than this row's 2026-11-16 review overturns that, and the throughput question is still tracked as performance_profiling_and_upgrades.md TODO-149(c). | [MT19937 seeding via LCG scramble] Its 675 LCG steps (about 1-2 µs) are required to reproduce R's RNG_Init. Matsumoto's improved init_genrand would give a different state, so R parity would be lost. Cost per construction is negligible next to one r-column draw. | [scaled 32-bit word (R fixup)] One multiply and two compares; it must match R's unif_rand bit for bit, so nothing faster or more acceptable exists.

seed-derivation.note: [SplitMix64 seed derivation] The SplitMix64 hash is O(1) and fine as a mixer. The cost is downstream: each draw index builds a fresh 2.5 KB Mersenne Twister RRng (675 LCG steps plus a 624-word regeneration on the first draw). In hot acceptance-rejection loops (rerandomization_helpers.cpp:230, design_fixed_greedy.cpp, optimal_design_search.cpp, binary_match_search.cpp) that is comparable to or larger than the per-draw work at EDI's n of about 100–500. A counter-based generator keyed by (master, index) removes the setup cost and keeps index-based determinism. See findings. | [seed derivation from one R uniform] O(1), one R::unif_rand() per call. Cost is negligible. Seed-quality and collision concerns belong to the per-index derivation (see the SplitMix64 finding), not this step.

findings.label: Lemire nearly-divisionless bounded integer
findings.candidate: Batched ranged random integer generation (Brackett-Rozinsky & Lemire 2024). It draws k bounded integers from one L-bit word whenever the product of the ranges is ≤ 2^L, still unbiased, with one multiply per value in the common case. The paper gives L=32 batch thresholds, so 32-bit MT words work: for example 2 draws per word when the remaining length is ≤ 2^16.
findings.claimed_speedup: The arXiv 2408.06213 HTML reports that shuffle_6 beats unbatched Fisher-Yates by 1.4-1.8x (Lehmer), 1.8-2.5x (PCG) and 2.9-4.7x (ChaCha) on Xeon, and says slower generators gain more. Arrays were cache-resident with 64-bit generators. MT19937 and 32-bit words were not benchmarked, so the gain for EDI is not quantified.

findings.label: Monte Carlo permutation p-value
findings.candidate: Anytime-valid sequential Monte Carlo testing by betting (Fischer & Ramdas, JRSS-B 2025, arXiv 2401.07365). Test martingales bet on whether each permuted statistic is ≥ or ≤ the observed one. The p-process Q_t = 1/sup_{s≤t} W_s is a valid p-value at any stopping time, including a budget cap. The binomial and binomial-mixture strategies stop early for rejection as well as futility. The framework contains Besag–Clifford as a special case. The formulas are closed form, so no external code is needed.
findings.claimed_speedup: Section 7.4 of https://arxiv.org/html/2401.07365v5 (Fisher sharp-null example, 53 units, p = 0.026, α = 0.05): binomial strategy mean 85 permutations (median 53), binomial mixture mean 147 (median 97), Besag–Clifford h = 10 mean 200, all with essentially full rejection. Section 7.2: power similar to Besag–Clifford with 'substantially fewer' permutations, especially under strong alternatives, where Besag–Clifford saves nothing because it stops early only for futility. Smaller savings and some power loss at α = 0.01. Against EDI's fixed 501, that is roughly 3–6× fewer draws in that example, on the paper's numbers; this is not an EDI measurement.
findings.suggested_action: When TODO-156 (Besag–Clifford) is designed, add the Fischer–Ramdas binomial / binomial-mixture betting test as a compared option for the standalone p-value. Reuse the betting machinery v1.2.0-TODO-34 already plans for the CI search. Correct the catalog §7 P4 claim that Besag–Clifford saves draws when the result is clearly significant. Keep fixed r as the default; ship any sequential rule as opt-in after the A/B correctness check.

findings.label: Monte Carlo randomization distribution
findings.candidate: Anytime-valid sequential Monte Carlo test by betting (Fischer & Ramdas, JRSS-B 2025, doi:10.1093/jrsssb/qkaf014). It generalizes Besag–Clifford with test martingales: a valid p-value at any stopping time, early stopping under both null and alternative (classical BC saves draws only under the null), and bounded resampling risk. The anytime-valid BC variant and the binomial-mixture strategy are both closed form, O(1) per draw.

Fig. 3: mean 327 (anytime-valid BC) and 462 (binomial mixture) permutations per rejection. The gain relative to EDI's default r = 501 is not quantified and would be much smaller.
findings.suggested_action: When TODO-156 (Besag–Clifford) is designed, evaluate the anytime-valid BC / betting p-value as the stopping rule, since it also stops early under the alternative. Add it to catalog P4.

findings.label: rerandomization (acceptance–rejection sampling)
findings.candidate: Early abandoning (partial-distance elimination). Store M row-major and accumulate d_j² (or |d_j|) one row at a time. Reject as soon as the running sum exceeds the cutoff. Both objectives are sums of nonnegative per-component terms, so the decision cannot change except by floating-point rounding exactly at the cutoff. Because M is whitened, under complete randomization the components are approximately iid N(0,1) (Morgan & Rubin 2012). Most rejected candidates should therefore exit after a few of the p rows when p_acc is small.
findings.claimed_speedup: Not quantified by any source for this problem. arXiv 2102.05221 reports only 'substantial speedup' from early abandoning in threshold-based search, for elastic distances. The Fisher–Yates O(n) part of each draw is not reduced, so the gain is bounded by the share of time spent in the O(np) check.
findings.suggested_action: Add as a row in catalog §P6. If it gets prototyped, benchmark at n=100–1000, p=5–20, p_acc=1e-2–1e-4 against the current kernel before adopting.

findings.label: rejection sampling (rerandomization)
findings.candidate: PSRSRR (Lu, Zhang & Zhu, arXiv 2602.07613, Feb 2026). It runs a pair-switching Metropolis–Hastings chain, checks the threshold along the way, and adds an 'inverse back' correction aimed at a uniform law on {w : M(w) ≤ a}. The idealized Algorithm 2 is exactly uniform (Thm 3.2) but far too slow (Table 7: 37,208 s at n=250, p=2). The practical Algorithm 3 is only asymptotically justified and is checked by KS tests.
findings.claimed_speedup: From arXiv 2602.07613: 10–10,000× in simulations, and over 1,800× median (Fig. 2) for 100 assignments at p_a = 1e-3 or 1e-5. Reserpine (n=30): 0.47 s vs 22.70 s (~48×). STAR (n≈974, 5 covariates): 2.95 s vs 193.65 s (~66×, Table 1). Simulations cover n=50–3000 and p=2–25, which overlaps EDI's sizes.
findings.suggested_action: Keep the default sampler. Add arXiv 2602.07613 to catalog P6's MCMC row, noting the asymptotic-only uniformity and the absence of FRT validity results. Also correct the v2.0.0 rerandomization_criterion_variants.md §B wording ('MR theory intact' / 'uniform law'): per 2602.07613, PSRR is not uniform, and PSRSRR is uniform only asymptotically.

irls.note: [IRLS M-estimator (Huber / bisquare)] Two low/medium-confidence leads. (1) For Huber at fixed scale, which is convex with a piecewise-quadratic objective, finite-termination Newton (Madsen–Nielsen 1990; Chen & Pınar 1998 prove finite termination with no extra assumptions). It gives the same estimator, and each iteration costs the same O(np²) as IRLS. Catalog O8 rejected Newton citing only the need for safeguards; the finite-termination proof was not considered there. I found no timing at EDI's sizes. (2) For the planned true-MM prototype (v1.0.5 algorithm_choice_audit TODO-31/catalog §1 TODO-4), a deterministic Peña–Yohai start (RobStatTM lmrobdetMM, pyinit; both GPL) fills the catalog's 'regression variant [cite needed]' and removes the RNG-seed-contract disadvantage of FAST-S. Neither recent arXiv paper (ROBU 2606.26611; FAMM 2606.27638) gives numbers at EDI's sizes, and FAMM is an approximation, i.e. an estimator change for replicates. | [IRLS M/MM-estimation] These R-level entries call the C++ IRLS above, with MASS::rlm as a fallback. robustbase NEWS 2023–2026 has no algorithmic speedup for lmrob/FAST-S beyond lmrob.fit(bare.only=), a reduced-output option. The KK classes use Huber 'M' with maxit capped at 10–25, and they would benefit from finding (1) on the C++ kernel, where it would make convergence exact. No separate R-level change is needed.

sandwich-estimator.note: [closed form (Huber sandwich)] Closed form, O(n + p³) using the already-cached OLS R factor, so nothing is faster. The known issues (no guard for mean ψ′→0; small-sample anti-conservatism per Koller & Stahel 2011) are about accuracy and estimators, not speed, and are already recorded (Incidental 10, catalog O8).

findings.label: IRLS M-estimator (Huber / bisquare)
findings.candidate: Finite-termination Newton for Huber's M-estimator (Madsen & Nielsen 1990; Chen & Pınar 1998, BIT). It exploits the piecewise-quadratic Huber objective: once the active set (|r_i|≤c·σ) is right, one Newton step lands exactly on the minimizer. Each iteration factorizes XᵀDX over the inlier set, at the same O(np²) as IRLS.
findings.claimed_speedup: Not quantified. The Chen & Pınar abstract says the enhancements 'improve its efficiency' and prove finite termination with no assumptions, but gives no numbers and no IRLS comparison.
findings.suggested_action: Re-look at catalog O8's 'Newton instead of IRLS' row for the Huber ('M') path only. Prototype a Madsen–Nielsen/Chen–Pınar active-set Newton and A/B its iteration counts against IRLS at EDI's sizes (n≈50–1000, p≲10), especially for the KK randomization draws.

sandwich-estimator.note: [OLS + HC0 sandwich] Linear-probability-model OLS delegates to fast_ols (normal equations + LDLT). HC0 needs only residuals and the bread, so it is O(np²) and needs no leverages. Nothing faster exists for the same estimator. | [cluster-robust sandwich + delta method] The cost is O(np² + p³): one pass of cluster score sums plus a p×p bread, which every sandwich needs. Grouping with unordered_map<int,VectorXd> allocates one vector per cluster; dense integer-indexed grouping would be a constant-factor micro-optimization, not an algorithm change. The search turned up no faster method. | [CR2 (Bell–McCaffrey) sandwich + Satterthwaite df] There is an exact p×p route for both the CR2 meat and the Bell–McCaffrey df. dfadjust vignette Lemma 2 does the meat by spectral decomposition of Q_gᵀQ_g with a generalized inverse. The df uses G'G = diag(a_gᵀa_g) − BBᵀ with B of size G×p. This replaces the per-cluster n_g×n_g eigen() and the dense n×G Umat. MacKinnon–Nielsen–Webb report the n_g×n_g (residual) method is fastest only when clusters have ≤4 observations. See finding. | [cluster-robust sandwich estimator] One hash-map pass for the score sums plus G rank-1 updates, O(np + Gp²). That is the cost of reading the data plus forming the meat. Nothing asymptotically or practically faster exists. Faster jackknife (CV3) methods change the estimator. | [HC0 sandwich estimator] Closed form, O(np² + p³). The catalog's (j) option already covers replacing solve() with chol2inv(chol()): about 2× on a p³ term that is negligible at p in the tens. Nothing new was found. | [HC2 sandwich estimator] Leverages via rowSums((XB)∘X) plus a weighted crossprod is O(np²), the minimum for exact leverages. Thin-QR leverages (catalog O13) cost more flops. Randomized or approximate leverage methods change the answer and only pay off at n far beyond EDI's. | [Lin–Wei robust sandwich (prefix sums)] Exact and deterministic, but the gain is negligible. Because sd.y is sorted ascending, the per-subject binary search for k_last can become a monotone pointer, giving O(n+K) instead of O(n log K). survival's coxscore2.c does the whole thing in one backward pass. The cost is dominated by the (n+K)p terms at EDI's p and n. The open accuracy item I-6 (forward running subtraction) matters more.

findings.label: CR2 (Bell–McCaffrey) sandwich + Satterthwaite df
findings.candidate: The exact p×p formulation. Take a QR (or (XᵀX)^{-1/2}) once. Per cluster, take the p×p spectral decomposition Q_gᵀQ_g = Σ λ_i r_i r_iᵀ and set D_g = Σ_{λ_i≠1} (1−λ_i)^{-1/2} r_i r_iᵀ. Then A_gᵀQ_g = Q_g D_g (dfadjust vignette Lemma 2, a generalized inverse, so clusters with I−H_gg singular are handled). The full CR2 meat follows as s_g = Rᵀ D_g Q_gᵀ e_g, the same idea as the 'score' method of Niccodemi et al. 2020 as revised in MacKinnon–Nielsen–Webb eq. 12–13. For the df, a_g = Q_g D_g ℓ̃ and B (G×p) with B_gk = a_gᵀQ_{g,k}. G'G = diag(a_gᵀa_g) − BBᵀ, so f_BM = tr(G'G)²/tr((G'G)²) needs only G×p and p×p matrices. Total O(np² + Gp³), with no n_g×n_g or n×G objects.
findings.claimed_speedup: Not quantified at EDI's sizes. MacKinnon, Nielsen & Webb (arXiv 2301.04527, §4/Fig. 1, N=2^20, k=20/40, Fortran) find the n_g×n_g residual method fastest only for cluster size M ≤ 4. It became 'prohibitively costly' above M = 4096, while the k×k score method is 'much faster … unless all the clusters are very small'. The dfadjust vignette says the p×p route is what makes large clusters feasible, but gives no timing. A 2025 blog benchmark (160 clusters, HSB data) shows the k×k NCR2 agreeing with clubSandwich to 7 decimals, but its median time is not faster than clubSandwich's.
findings.suggested_action: Re-look. First check whether cluster_robust_cr2_variance runs inside any resampling loop and what cluster sizes the cluster-capable designs use. If clusters typically have >4 subjects or the function is called per draw, prototype the p×p Lemma-2 meat and the B-matrix df. A/B test against the current implementation and clubSandwich::coef_test(vcov='CR2', test='Satterthwaite'), including a cluster-fixed-effect case where I−H_gg is singular. Otherwise leave as is; this is a speed tidy-up, not a correctness issue.

sequential-monte-carlo-stopping.note: [sequential Monte Carlo randomization p-value] Hot path: each draw for the GEE family is a full GEE refit. Fischer & Ramdas (arXiv 2401.07365) give anytime-valid betting tests (binomial and binomial-mixture strategies) with closed-form wealth. They report stopping earlier than Besag–Clifford with similar power, and they control error across repeated looks, which EDI's per-look 99% Clopper–Pearson band does not. The reported p-value would change, so this is a re-look rather than a drop-in replacement. See the finding. | [sequential Monte Carlo stopping (Clopper–Pearson band)] The catalog's options table cites only Besag–Clifford 1991 and Gandy 2009. It misses Fischer & Ramdas (JRSS-B 2025), whose anytime-valid betting tests stop sooner than Besag–Clifford and also bound resampling risk across looks, which is the gap the current per-look Clopper–Pearson band leaves open. It also misses Gandy, Hahn & Ding (2020) on p-value buckets. See the finding.

findings.label: sequential Monte Carlo randomization p-value
findings.candidate: Fischer & Ramdas 'Sequential Monte-Carlo testing by betting': an anytime-valid test martingale on the indicators 1[T_b ≥ T_obs]. The binomial strategy has p = 1/⌈√(2πe^{1/6})/α⌉, and the binomial mixture has closed-form wealth (1 − Bin(ℓ; t+1, c))/c with c < α. Stop when wealth ≥ 1/α (reject) or < α (futility). The p-process 1/max-wealth is valid at any stopping time.
findings.claimed_speedup: Not benchmarked against EDI's CP-band rule. Section 7.4 of https://arxiv.org/html/2401.07365v5 (Fisher sharp null, α=0.05, 1000 runs) reports mean/median permutations of 85/53 (binomial) and 147/97 (binomial mixture), against 200 (Besag–Clifford h=10, which failed to reject 3 times) and a fixed T=1000. Section 7 text says the method stops earlier than Besag–Clifford under both null and alternative with 'quite similar' power. At EDI's default r=501 this suggests on the order of 2–5x fewer GEE refits than a fixed r when the result is clearly significant (inferred, not measured).
findings.suggested_action: Re-look under performance_profiling_and_upgrades.md TODO-156 and catalog NEW-seq-mc-stopping. Compare the binomial-mixture betting rule with the current CP-band rule on draws used and decision agreement at r=501, α=0.05, in the GEE and other refit-per-draw classes. Decide whether to report the betting p-value or use it only as a stopping rule.

findings.label: sequential Monte Carlo stopping (Clopper–Pearson band)
findings.candidate: Anytime-valid sequential Monte Carlo tests by betting (Fischer & Ramdas, JRSS-B 2025): the binomial strategy, or the binomial mixture with c<α, plus a futility stop. They generalise Besag–Clifford, give an anytime-valid p-value or decision at any stopping time, and bound resampling risk. A related option the catalog also misses is p-value buckets with bounded resampling risk (Gandy, Hahn & Ding, Scand. J. Stat. 2020).
findings.claimed_speedup: From the Fischer & Ramdas arXiv v5 HTML, Section 7.4 (Fisher sharp null, α=0.05, 1000 runs, at most 5000 permutations): binomial strategy mean 85 / median 53 permutations, versus Besag–Clifford mean 200 (h=10) or 160 (h=8); the binomial mixture averaged 147. Section 5.3 (analytic): rejection possible after 39 permutations at c=0.04. Neither paper compares against EDI's Clopper–Pearson band, so the speedup over the current rule is not quantified.
findings.suggested_action: Add Fischer & Ramdas 2025 and Gandy–Hahn–Ding 2020 to the NEW-seq-mc-stopping options table and to performance_profiling_and_upgrades.md TODO-156. Before changing anything, A/B the binomial betting stop against the current Clopper–Pearson band on the existing CI-search workloads: compare mean draws and decision agreement with the fixed-r answer.

multistart.note: [deterministic multistart] Cloglog (.cloglog_full_data_multistart): the cumulative cloglog likelihood in the raw (α, β) parametrisation EDI uses is concave (Pratt 1981, since the extreme-value density is log-concave). The 4 extra refits per fit, including every estimate_only resampling draw, therefore cannot find a different optimum; they only repair non-convergence. A convergence certificate or Newton polish is cheaper and gives the same estimator (see finding). Stereotype (.stereotype_full_data_multistart / _candidates): the likelihood is genuinely nonconcave and no faster method with the same answer was found. The early-termination and global-optimality-test literature (arXiv 1906.00101) needs a generalized location family, which the stereotype model is not, and it is heuristic. The alternating algorithm was already rejected in the catalog. Keep.

newton-raphson.note: [Newton then L-BFGS fallback] The catalog (§5) already lists LM/trust-region Newton, damped Fisher scoring, alternating RR-VGLM fits and multistart, and v1.0.5 catalog TODO-6 tracks them. The only new method found is the MM algorithm of de Rooij (arXiv 2402.07634, v3 dated 2025-01-22), which the paper itself says has a linear rate and needs more iterations than IRLS, with no timings reported. VGAM 1.1-13 and 1.1-14 NEWS show no rrvglm/stereotype solver change; 1.1-14 only adds a 'bhhh' control option, with no claimed speedup. Nothing found that beats the current approach at EDI's sizes while keeping the same estimator.

profile-likelihood.note: [finite-difference profile curvature] Fallback only, used when the observed-information inverse is not finite: 3 profile refits. The obvious alternative (a Schur complement of the observed information) is exactly what failed when the fallback fires, so nothing cheaper is available. Not a hot path. | [profile likelihood (damped Newton)] Used only as a variance fallback: 3 profile refits when the observed-information diagonal inverse is not finite. It is warm-started from the MLE, and the analytic-Hessian damped Newton converges quadratically on a small nuisance block. The literature found (warm-start continuation, Newton with good starts) matches what the code already does. A possible micro-change, LDLT/LLT instead of FullPivLU on the small d×d system, is not algorithmic and not quantified.

reparameterization.note: [cumulative-softmax reparametrization] O(K²) Jacobian once per likelihood evaluation, with K ≤ about 10. The O(nK) likelihood dominates it, so a prefix-sum O(K) form would not change wall-clock time.

findings.label: deterministic multistart
findings.candidate: For the cumulative cloglog model, F(z) = 1 − exp(−exp(z)) has a log-concave density, so the log-likelihood is concave in the raw (α, β) parametrisation EDI uses (Pratt 1981, as cited in Kosmidis arXiv 1204.0105; that paper covers the G = 1 − exp(−exp(η)) case explicitly). When the MLE exists it is unique, and a restart that finds a strictly lower NLL means the primary solve stopped early, not that it found a different local optimum. Two cheaper checks fit this: (a) a convergence certificate on the primary fit, either the Newton decrement already in ordinal_scale_guard.h or a maximum-absolute-gradient plus positive-definite-Hessian test like ordinal::clm's maxGradient/cond.H, running the restarts only when it fails; or (b) a damped Newton polish from the primary solution, which is what clm does with step halving and gradTol 1e-6.
findings.claimed_speedup: Not quantified by any source. Based on the code structure, it avoids up to 4 extra fits per call when the primary fit passes the certificate, so up to about 5× fewer fits per estimate_only resampling draw. This is a theoretical figure, not a measurement.
findings.suggested_action: Re-examine the cloglog multistart. Gate the 4 restarts on a failed convergence certificate (gradient norm or Newton decrement with a PD Hessian), or replace them with a Newton polish. Before changing the default, A/B the result against the current multistart on the cases in ordinal_cumulative_link_null_refit_multistart.md. Apply the same reasoning to the cloglog fit_null 2-start, which is already marked Investigate.

m-out-of-n-subsampling.note: [m-out-of-n bootstrap] Cost is B fits of size m < n, and nothing replaces them for the same √m-scaled pivot. Bag of Little Bootstraps (Kleiner et al., arXiv 1112.5016) targets massive n, not EDI's n ≤ low thousands, and the search found no 2025–2026 speedup work for m-out-of-n. Choosing m (minimum volatility) is a separate inventory row. | [subsampling (Politis–Romano–Wolf)] Costs B·fit(b), with B=501 by default and b=n^0.7. No faster algorithm gives the same subsampling distribution. Lam's cheap bootstrap, which covers subsampling variants, gets valid CIs from very few resamples, but it builds a different interval, so it is an estimator change, reported as such.

minimum-volatility.note: [minimum-volatility method] In moonboot (arXiv 2412.05032), Bickel–Sakov costs O(Rn) and Götze–Račkauskas O(Rn²) by exhaustive search, so neither is cheaper than EDI's 9-point grid. moonboot does report poor coverage for Politis minimum volatility, but that is with a search up to m < n/2, where m is effectively proportional to n. EDI's n^0.5…n^0.9 grid keeps m/n → 0, so the criticism may not carry over. It is an accuracy and estimator question, not a speed one, and worth a look under the existing Bickel–Sakov option.

The new point is that two published approaches remove the catalog's two objections to AGQ: the per-evaluation mode-solve cost and the exact gradient through û(θ). See the AGQ finding. Golub–Welsch caching is already tracked (small_kernel_hoists_batch Item D). | [Gauss–Hermite quadrature (fixed 20-node)] WeibullFrailtyNormalLikelihood is covered by the same AGQ finding. The O(nKp)→O(nK+np) gradient rewrite (catalog §5 TODO-4) is already tracked and was not re-reported. | [Gauss–Hermite quadrature GLMM] Covered by the non-adaptive GH finding. Stringer (arXiv 2310.01589 v2, Nov 2024) gives an exact gradient for adaptive quadrature that works with L-BFGS (via LBFGSpp), which removes the obstacle the catalog recorded for v1.0.5 TODO-153. Against EDI's fixed 20 nodes the speed gain is not quantified and probably modest; against Poisson's 60 nodes it is likely larger. Not a drop-in: results change at quadrature tolerance.

lbfgs.note: [L-BFGS] The generic LBFGSpp driver uses backtracking strong-Wolfe. The Newton alternative for the concave ordinal/CR/AC/beta/logistic fits is already catalogued (catalog §2 TODO-1/2, §1 TODO-7). LBFGSpp releases add a More–Thuente / Nocedal–Wright line search but no performance claim. The literature found (arXiv 1911.04584, 2310.07296) suggests Wolfe/More–Thuente searches use more evaluations than Armijo backtracking, so switching the line search is not a demonstrated win. | [L-BFGS (closed-form Clayton copula likelihood)] The closed-form marginal already avoids quadrature. The open options (L-BFGS-B for the dependence bound, multistart, analytic Hessian) are already catalogued under NEW-nonconcave-dependence-mle and NEW-fd-hessian. The fit is a single small-p optimization, and no newer faster method for Clayton-copula AFT pairs was found.

multistart.note: [deterministic multistart] Cloglog (.cloglog_full_data_multistart): the cumulative cloglog likelihood in the raw (α, β) parametrisation EDI uses is concave (Pratt 1981, since the extreme-value density is log-concave). The 4 extra refits per fit, including every estimate_only resampling draw, therefore cannot find a different optimum; they only repair non-convergence. A convergence certificate or Newton polish is cheaper and gives the same estimator (see finding). Stereotype (.stereotype_full_data_multistart / _candidates): the likelihood is genuinely nonconcave and no faster method with the same answer was found. The early-termination and global-optimality-test literature (arXiv 1906.00101) needs a generalized location family, which the stereotype model is not, and it is heuristic. The alternating algorithm was already rejected in the catalog. Keep. | [multistart L-BFGS (BFGS / Nelder–Mead fallback)] Clayton–Weibull AFT: 3 θ starts with C++ L-BFGS; the R fallbacks fire only on failure. Searches found no newer fast algorithm for Clayton-copula AFT MLE (Copula.surv and CopulaCenR use other estimators). L-BFGS-B and a 1-D θ profile were already considered in the catalog and have about the same cost. | [multistart L-BFGS (BFGS fallback)] Dependent-censoring bivariate-lognormal model: 3 ρ starts with C++ L-BFGS and an analytic gradient. The FD-gradient optim fallback is slow, but it runs only on failure. Searches found no faster algorithm; packages from the same research group (SemiPar.depCens, depCensoring) use pseudo-likelihood or semiparametric estimators, which are estimator changes.

findings.label: deterministic multistart
findings.candidate: For the cumulative cloglog model, F(z) = 1 − exp(−exp(z)) has a log-concave density, so the log-likelihood is concave in the raw (α, β) parametrisation EDI uses (Pratt 1981, as cited in Kosmidis arXiv 1204.0105; that paper covers the G = 1 − exp(−exp(η)) case explicitly). When the MLE exists it is unique, and a restart that finds a strictly lower NLL means the primary solve stopped early, not that it found a different local optimum. Two cheaper checks fit this: (a) a convergence certificate on the primary fit, either the Newton decrement already in ordinal_scale_guard.h or a maximum-absolute-gradient plus positive-definite-Hessian test like ordinal::clm's maxGradient/cond.H, running the restarts only when it fails; or (b) a damped Newton polish from the primary solution, which is what clm does with step halving and gradTol 1e-6.
findings.claimed_speedup: Not quantified by any source. Based on the code structure, it avoids up to 4 extra fits per call when the primary fit passes the certificate, so up to about 5× fewer fits per estimate_only resampling draw. This is a theoretical figure, not a measurement.
findings.suggested_action: Re-examine the cloglog multistart. Gate the 4 restarts on a failed convergence certificate (gradient norm or Newton decrement with a PD Hessian), or replace them with a Newton polish. Before changing the default, A/B the result against the current multistart on the cases in ordinal_cumulative_link_null_refit_multistart.md. Apply the same reasoning to the cloglog fit_null 2-start, which is already marked Investigate.

multistart.note: [Newton–Raphson with random-restart multistart] robust_survreg_with_surv_object starts its non-Weibull (and Weibull-fallback) loop from init = 0. This overrides survreg's own data-driven start (the distribution's init(x, weights) mean/variance estimate). It then random-walks with unscaled N(0,1) jitter. This supports the existing 'Prototype deterministic data-driven starts' verdict with a concrete first step (see findings).

newton-raphson.note: [Newton–Raphson (survreg)] The Newton–Raphson in survreg is the right algorithm. The per-draw cost is R overhead: a formula and model.frame build for each Bayesian-bootstrap draw. The Cox sibling already calls coxph.fit directly; the Weibull sibling has no such interim path (see findings). The native weighted C++ kernel is already planned in bayesian_bootstrap_performance.md. | [Newton–Raphson (Weibull AFT MLE)] fast_weibull_regression / KK21 reduced fit / univariate_weibull_tstat use damped Newton on the analytic Hessian with an L-BFGS fallback, at p ≤ ~10. Newton is already the fastest-converging option. The BRT warm-start and Newton-default item was already reported by batch A.1 (2026-11-16). The Burridge reparametrization is already in the catalog (§ Weibull options) and changes robustness, not speed. survival 3.7-3 fixed survreg's step-halving NaN check, which is irrelevant to EDI's own kernel.

sandwich-estimator.note: [MLE + cluster-robust sandwich] Weibull AFT: Newton MLE plus a pair-cluster meat built from per-cluster score sums (rowsum + crossprod), O(np^2). This is the standard and minimal computation. Changing the variance estimator would be an estimator change, not a speedup.

findings.label: Newton–Raphson with random-restart multistart
findings.candidate: Make the first attempt survreg with init omitted (NULL). survreg then uses the distribution's documented init(x, weights) mean/variance estimate, which is deterministic and data-driven. Before any random jitter, add deterministic starts that are scale-aware: intercept = mean log-time, log-scale from the residual SD (the existing weibull_smart_cold_start pattern applied to lognormal and loglogistic). Keep the seeded jitter only as a last resort, scaled by the start's SE or by |start|.
findings.claimed_speedup: Not quantified. Expected to come from fewer failed survreg calls before a converged fit. A zero intercept is far from log(time) for typical time scales, so the zero-start first call is the one most likely to fail.
findings.suggested_action: Fold into multistart_nonconcave_likelihoods.md as the concrete 'deterministic data-driven starts' prototype. First start init=NULL (survreg default), then a moment start, then scaled jitter. A/B the convergence-failure rate and the attempts per fit.

findings.label: Newton–Raphson (survreg)
findings.candidate: Interim fast path for the unclustered case, mirroring the coxph.fit path in the same file: call survival::survreg.fit(x = cbind(1, X), y = Surv(...), weights =, offset = 0, init = warm, controlvals = survreg.control(), dist = survreg.distributions$weibull, scale = 0) on the prebuilt matrix. Fall back to the formula path on error. Same Newton–Raphson, same likelihood, same start. The native weighted C++ Weibull kernel (bayesian_bootstrap_performance.md item 2) remains the end state.
findings.claimed_speedup: Not quantified. No source benchmarks survreg.fit against survreg. The gain is removal of per-draw formula and model-frame overhead, multiplied by B.
findings.suggested_action: Add as an interim sub-item next to the coxph.fit interim in bug_fix_plans/v1_0_5/bayesian_bootstrap_performance.md item 2. Benchmark per-draw time on a Weibull Bayesian-bootstrap fixture before adopting.

analytic-derivatives.note: [analytic NLL + gradient] Closed-form O(n·p) objective and gradient (ZIP/hurdle-Poisson, truncated NB, ZOIB, ZINB), already using distinct-y special-function tables. No asymptotically or practically faster way to evaluate an exact likelihood exists. The dead `mu` pass in ZOIB is already recorded as incidental. | [analytic observed information] Closed-form Hessians costing O(n·p²) (LMM trace identities, hurdle NB, ZIP/hurdle, ZOIB block-diagonal). The cost equals forming XᵀWX, which is optimal for an exact Hessian. Finite differences or BFGS approximations would be less accurate. | [closed form] These are direct O(1), O(n) or O(np²) formulas: link cdf/pdf, analytic scores and Hessians, Wald/RD/BRS variances, ridit DeLong SE, lgamma sums. Each is at the lower bound of reading its inputs. Some are dead exports (beta_*_cpp, neg_loglik_nb_cpp). The micro-optimizations already noted (distinct-y lgamma caching in NegBinNoZiLikelihood, SYRK/weighted_crossprod reuse) are constant-factor and trivial. | [closed-form expected information] Both inventoried entries (ZAP and ZOIB expected_hessian) are closed forms at O(n k²), the minimum work for an information matrix. Both are dead code with no caller, so speeding them up gains nothing.

closed-form.note: [closed form] These are direct O(1), O(n) or O(np²) formulas: link cdf/pdf, analytic scores and Hessians, Wald/RD/BRS variances, ridit DeLong SE, lgamma sums. Each is at the lower bound of reading its inputs. Some are dead exports (beta_*_cpp, neg_loglik_nb_cpp). The micro-optimizations already noted (distinct-y lgamma caching in NegBinNoZiLikelihood, SYRK/weighted_crossprod reuse) are constant-factor and trivial.

finite-differences.note: [closed form + FD Hessian] ZipLimitLikelihood is a fallback-only boundary refit. Its objective and gradient are closed-form O(nk). The FD Hessian costs 2k gradient evaluations, which is O(nk²): the same order as an analytic ZIP Hessian, which would only buy accuracy (~1e-7 FD error). Nothing faster exists; the catalog's Keep stands.

laplace-approximation-tmb.note: [TMB automatic differentiation + nlminb (glmmTMB)] The structural fix (weighted C++ kernels per Bayesian-bootstrap replicate, catalog §10 TODO-3) is still the right one; glmmTMB 1.1.15.x NEWS adds no weight-refit or re-tape-avoidance feature (RTMB back-end only 'as fast as' TMB). Cheap interim win found in the code: the weighted replicate paths call glmmTMB() with default se=TRUE even when estimate_only=TRUE, so every estimate-only replicate still pays for sdreport. Passing se = !estimate_only keeps the estimate identical. TMB's DATA_UPDATE (re-use one tape across weight vectors) would need changes inside glmmTMB's C++ template, so it is not actionable from EDI.

lbfgs.note: [L-BFGS (joint, block-separable)] Hurdle-Poisson. Block-separate Newton/IRLS, which gives the same unique MLE, is already Prototype (catalog §3 TODO-3, pscl::hurdle precedent). Nothing newer or faster was found for a strictly concave two-block objective. | [L-BFGS then Newton fallback chain] Truncated NB count part. The first converged run returns, usually after one L-BFGS fit, and the chain only runs on failure. Catalog P3 already weighs the α=1/θ L-BFGS-B reparametrization. The search found nothing newer that is faster: Newton-type ztnb fits exist, but their speed is not quantified. An analytic Hessian exists (fast_hurdle_negbin.cpp:399), so Newton by default is possible but unbenchmarked; same pattern as TODO-3. | [L-BFGS (single start, joint)] No benchmark shows a faster algorithm at EDI's sizes. New software evidence: fastglm 0.1.4 (CRAN, published 2026-11-11, GPL≥2) ships a C++ EM driver for ZIP/ZINB with SQUAREM acceleration (NEWS 0.1.0/0.1.1), with M-steps by IRLS. It could serve as a reference implementation and comparator for em_algorithm_zero_inflated_mixtures.md TODO-3/TODO-5. Its speed is not quantified, so this is a low-confidence re-look. The catalog's conditional-likelihood start (catalog §3 TODO 1) and α=1/θ L-BFGS-B (TODO 4) remain the main open items. I found no 2025–2026 paper with a ZIP/ZINB-specific optimizer benchmark. | [Newton / L-BFGS (mixture MLE)] This is the R-level dispatch to the same C++ kernels (fast_zinb_cpp / fast_zero_augmented_poisson_cpp). The hurdle-Poisson path already exploits exact block separability, which matches fastglm's own hurdle design ('likelihood separates into a binary component and a positive-count component'). Nothing beyond the C++ kernel findings and the existing catalog §3 TODO 1/3/4.

likelihood-factorization.note: [factorized two-part fit (logistic + truncated NB)] The CRAN pscl manual confirms the reference implementation does the same thing: hurdle.control(separate=TRUE) is the default, with 'the two components of the model ... estimated separately using two optim calls' (BFGS, numerical Hessian). EDI's factorization plus analytic-Hessian L-BFGS/Newton is at least as fast. The known sub-item (fit the logistic part by IRLS instead of L-BFGS with maxit 100) is already in the catalog §3 incidentals. No new evidence.

newton-raphson.note: [Newton (block-separable hurdle MLE)] Newton on separable binary and truncated-NB blocks, with count-block-only null refits, already exploits the structure. Comparators (pscl-style optim/BFGS) are slower by construction. No newer method found.

truncated-series-summation.note: [brute-force series expected information] Dead code (no caller). The θ-part of the expected information can be written as a scalar tail-probability series per observation, so there is no need to rebuild a functor and a p×p Hessian for each y. See the finding.

findings.label: brute-force series expected information
findings.candidate: Compute the expected information analytically. The β-block is a closed-form weight times x xᵀ. The θ-related terms reduce to a scalar series over tail probabilities, Σ_j c_j(θ)·Pr(Y≥j), as in Eq. (2.12)–(2.13) of the source; the zero-truncated version renormalizes by 1−P(0). The series is built in one pass with the pmf/cdf recurrence, stopped adaptively once the tail mass is negligible, then added as a single rank-1/diagonal update per observation. Cost is O(n+·(Y_eff + p²)).
findings.claimed_speedup: Not quantified by the source. Analytically the per-term work drops from an O(p²) Hessian plus allocations to O(1) scalar work, roughly p²× fewer flops, and Y_eff ≈ μ+k·sd instead of ≥10⁴.
findings.suggested_action: Delete the dead expected_hessian, or, if expected information is ever needed for the truncated NB, rewrite it with the tail-probability series and an adaptive cutoff instead of per-y Hessian calls.

findings.label: TMB automatic differentiation + nlminb (glmmTMB)
findings.candidate: Thread estimate_only into the glmmTMB call as se = !estimate_only, so estimate-only replicates skip sdreport. Optionally also set glmmTMBControl(conv_check='skip', eigval_check=FALSE) on estimate-only replicates. Keep parallel=1 when the replicate loop is already parallel; the catalog §10 incidental finding already flags thread oversubscription.
findings.claimed_speedup: Not quantified. The glmmTMB reference manual documents se as 'whether to return standard errors' and eigval_check as possibly 'very slow' for many fixed-effect parameters, but gives no timing.
findings.suggested_action: Small low-risk change: pass se = !estimate_only (and skip conv/eigval checks) in the estimate-only weighted glmmTMB replicate paths, and time one B=200 run before and after. Also correct the inventory 'details' text, which wrongly says sdreport is skipped under estimate_only.

findings.label: L-BFGS (single start, joint)
findings.candidate: C++ EM with SQUAREM acceleration for ZIP/ZINB (Lambert-style E-step posterior of structural zero, IRLS M-steps, θ by 1-D update), as now shipped in fastglm::fastglm_zi. Use it as a reference implementation and comparator (or EM warm-up start) in the em_algorithm_zero_inflated_mixtures.md A/B, not as a dependency.
findings.claimed_speedup: Not quantified for ZI. fastglm NEWS 0.1.1 adds SQUAREM 'to speed up EM convergence' and gives no ZI timings. Its vignette reports coefficients and log-likelihood matching pscl to ~1e-5 for the ZI fit. The SQUAREM paper reports large gains over plain EM on Poisson mixtures (e.g. ~40× fewer fixed-point evaluations on the Hasselblad example), but that is not a comparison with L-BFGS.
